children.translated_text: Becoming what one must grieve over during the day. And whatever it touches — the hands, the feet, or any other limb — must be hidden from oneself and from others. From that cause arise many bodily afflictions in the body, such as: boils, abscesses, ringworm, eczema, itching, leprosy, <s>kiṭibha</s> (a skin disease), <s>kilāsa</s> (vitiligo), fever, cough, swelling, consumption, epilepsy, jaundice, hemorrhaging, bilious fistula — and other such bodily afflictions arise in the body. Or the food consumed causes disorder, whereby <s>viṣūcikā</s> (cholera) establishes itself in the body. This is called
The danger connected with transformation, that is, with regard to food.

body.translated_text: And essentially, when it has been fully transformed, it passes downward,

body.text: tatra katamaḥ paryeṣaṇānna(nva)yaādīnava āhāre | paryeṣaṇānvaya ādīnavo [a]nekavidha[ḥ]-samudānanākṛtaḥ | ārakṣākṛtaḥ | snehaparibhraṃśakṛtaḥ | atṛptikṛtaḥ | asvātantryakṛtaḥ duścaritakṛtaśca |
body.translated_text: Therein, what is the danger in food connected with pursuit? The danger connected with pursuit is of many kinds: caused by the effort of acquisition, caused by the need for protection, caused by the breakdown of affection, caused by insatiability, caused by lack of independence, and caused by misconduct.

body.text: tatra katama ādīnava āhāre [|] samudānanā kṛtaḥ [|] yathāpīhaikatyaḥ āhārahetorāhāranidānaṃ śīte śītena hanyamānaḥ, uṣṇe uṣṇena hanyamānaḥ, utsahate, ghaṭate, vyāyacchate | kṛṣiṇā vā, gorakṣyeṇa vā, vāṇijyena vā, lipigaṇanāvyasanasaṃkhyāmudrayā [a]nekavidhena śilpasthānakarmasthānenāpratilabdhasya vāhārasya pratilambhāya, upacayāya vā [|] yathā āhārasye (syai)vamāhāranidānasya [|] tasyaivamutsahato, ghaṭata(to), vyāyacchata (ḥ), sa cette karmāntā vipadyante | sa taṃ nidānaṃ (tannidānaṃ) śocati klāmyati, paridevate | urastāḍayati | krandati- saṃgo vā [mā] māpadyate | moho bata me svāyāso [a]tiphala iti | ayamu(yaṃ samu)dānanā sahagataḥ ādīnavo yaduta āhāre [|]
body.translated_text: Therein, what is the danger in food caused by the effort of acquisition? Just as here, someone, for the sake of food and on account of food, being struck by cold in the cold, being struck by heat in the heat, makes effort, exerts himself, and strains — through farming, cattle-herding, trade, writing, calculation, accounting, enumeration, seal-craft, and through many kinds of craft-practices and work-practices — for the obtainment and accumulation of food not yet obtained. As with food itself, so too with what is caused by food. For that person who thus makes effort, exerts himself, and strains — if those enterprises fail, then on that account he grieves, languishes, laments, beats his chest, and cries out; or he falls into confusion, [thinking:] 'Alas, my effort has been exceedingly fruitless!' This is the danger associated with the effort of acquisition, that is, with regard to food.

body.text: sa cetsaṃpadyate sa tasyārakṣādhikaraṇahetostīvramautsukyamāpadyayate | kaccinme bhogā rājñā vā apahriyeraṃścaurairvā, agninā vā dahyerannudakena vā uhyeyuḥ | kuniha(hi)tā vā nidhayaḥ praṇaśyeyuḥ (

children.text: ) kuprayuktā vā karmāntāḥ pralujyeran, apriyo(yā)vā dāyādā adhigaccheyuḥ | kulevā kulāṃgāra utpadyeta | yastānbhogānanayena vyasanamāpādaye [da]yamārakṣāsahagata ādīnavo yaduta āhāre |
children.translated_text: Will my poorly managed enterprises perhaps fail? Will unwanted heirs perhaps come forward? Or will a destroyer of the family arise in the family, who would bring those possessions to ruin?' This is the danger associated with protection, that is, with regard to food.

body.translated_text: If he does succeed, he falls into intense anxiety on account of having to protect his wealth: 'Will my possessions perhaps be seized by the king, or by thieves? Will they perhaps be burned by fire, or carried away by water? Will my poorly concealed treasures perhaps be lost?

body.text: katama ādīnava[ḥ] snehaparibhraṃśakṛtaḥ | yathāpi tadāhāranidānamāhārādhikaraṇahetormātā putrasyāvarṇambhāṣate | putro mātyaḥ (mātuḥ), pitā putrasya, putro (traḥ) pituḥ, bhrātā bhaginyā, bhaginī bhrātuḥ | sahāyakaḥ | sahāyakasya | prāgeva jano janasya [|] te (|) cānyonyaṃ vigṛhītā bhavanti, vivādamāpannāstathāudārā brāhmaṇakṣatriyagṛhapatimahāsālā āhārādhikaraṇahetorevaṃ vigṛhītāvivādamāpannāḥ anyonyaṃ pāṇinā praharanti | loṣṭhenāpi, daṇḍenāpi, śastreṇāpi praharantyayamucyate snehaparibhaṃśakṛta ādīnavaḥ |
body.translated_text: What is the danger caused by the breakdown of affection? Just as on account of food and for the sake of food, a mother speaks ill of her son, a son of his mother, a father of his son, a son of his father, a brother of his sister, a sister of her brother, a companion of his companion — let alone stranger against stranger. They become quarrelsome with one another and fall into disputes. Thus even eminent <s>Brāhmaṇas</s>, <s>Kṣatriyas</s>, householders, and great lords, for the sake of food, becoming quarrelsome and falling into disputes with one another, strike each other with fists, with clods, with sticks, and with weapons. This is called the danger caused by the breakdown of affection.

body.text: tatra katamaḥ | atṛptikṛta ādīnavaḥ | yathāpi tadrājānaḥ kṛtiyā (kṣatriyā) mūrddhābhiṣiktāḥ, sveṣu grāmanigamarāṣṭrarājadhānīṣu asaṃtuṣṭā viharanta ubhayato [a]bhyūhakāni saṃgrāmānīkāni pratisaranti | śaṃkhai(ḥ) kampa(mpya)mānaiḥ, paṭāhairvādyamānaiḥ, iṣubhiḥ kṣipyamāṇairvividhaiste tatra bhrāntenāśvena sārdhaṃ samāgacchanti || bhrāntena hastinā, sthena, pattinā sārdhaṃ samāgacchanti | iṣubhiḥ śaktibhirvā apakṛttagātrā (

children.text: ) maraṇamvā ni (vi)gacchanti | maraṇamātraṃ vā duḥkhamayamucyate | atṛptikṛta ādīnava iti yo vā punarapyevaṃbhāgīyaḥ ||
children.translated_text: They either meet death, or [experience] suffering that is equivalent to death. This is called the danger caused by insatiability, and whatever else is of the same kind.

body.translated_text: Therein, what is the danger caused by insatiability? Just as <s>Kṣatriya</s> kings, anointed upon the head [in consecration], dwelling unsatisfied in their own villages, towns, kingdoms, and capital cities, mobilize their battle-formations on both sides. With conch-shells being blown, drums being beaten, and arrows being shot, there with a charging horse they meet in battle, with a charging elephant, with a foot-soldier. With limbs severed by arrows and lances,

body.text: tatra katamaḥ | asvātantryakṛta ādīnavaḥ | yathāpi tadrājñaḥ pauruṣeyā āvarodhikāni nagarāṇyanupraskandataḥ (nte) | taptenāpi ti (tai)lenāvasicyante | taptayā vasayā, taptayā gomayalo (lau)hikayā, taptena tāmreṇa, taptenāyasā, iṣubhiḥ santibhi (śaktibhi)ścāpakṛttagātrā maraṇaṃ vā ni (vi)gacchanti | maraṇamātrakaṃ vā duḥkhaṃ | ayamucyate asvātantrayakṛta ādīnava iti yo vā punarapyevaṃbhāgīyaḥ |
body.translated_text: Therein, what is the danger caused by lack of independence? Just as the servants of kings assault fortified cities; they are doused with boiling oil, with boiling fat, with heated cow-dung balls, with molten copper, with molten iron; and with limbs severed by arrows and lances, they either meet death, or [experience] suffering that is equivalent to death. This is called the danger caused by lack of independence, and whatever else is of the same kind.

body.text: tatra [katamo] duścaritakṛta ādīnavaḥ [|] yathāpi tadekatyenāhāranidānaṃ prabhūtaṃ kāyena duścaritaṃ kṛtaṃ bhavatyupacitaṃ, yathā kāyenaivamvācā, manasā [|] sa ca ya(thā kā)ya ābādhiko bhavati, duḥkhito, bāḍhaglānaḥ, tasya tatpūrvakaṃ kāyaduścaritaṃ vāṅmanoduścarita(taṃ), parvatānāṃ vā parvatakūṭānāmvā, sāyāhne [yā]cchayā(cchāyā) avalambate | avyā(dhya)valambate | abhipralambate | [tasyai]vaṃ bhavati | kṛtaṃ bata me pāpaṃ, na kṛtaṃ bata me puṇyaṃ, kāyena vācā, manasā, (

children.text: ) so [a]haṃ yā gati[ḥ] kṛtapāpānāṃ [tāṃ] gatiṃ pretya gamiṣyāmīti | vipratisārī kālaṃ karoti | akālañca kṛtvāpāyeṣūpapadyate | yaduta narakeṣu, tiryakpreteṣu [|] ayamucyate duścarita kṛta ādīnavaḥ |
children.translated_text: 'And I shall go, after death, to the destination of those who have done evil' — thus filled with remorse, he meets his end. And having met his end, he is reborn in the lower realms — namely, in hells, among animals, or among <s>pretas</s> (hungry ghosts). This is called the danger caused by misconduct.

body.translated_text: Therein, what is the danger caused by misconduct? Just as here someone, on account of food, has committed and accumulated much misconduct of body; as of body, so too of speech and mind. And when that one becomes sick in body, suffering, severely ill, that former misconduct of body, speech, and mind, like the shadow of mountains or mountain peaks in the evening, descends upon him, overwhelms him, overtakes him. He thinks thus: 'Alas, evil has been done by me! No merit has been done by me, in body, speech, or mind.'

body.text: tasyaivambhavati | ityayamāhāra[ḥ] paryeṣa(ṣya)māṇo [a]pi sādīnavaḥ | paribhujyamāno [a]pi sādīnavaḥ | paribhukto [a]pi pariṇāma ādīnavaḥ | evamasti punarasyāhārasya kācidanuśansa (śaṃsa)mātrā sā punaḥ katamā | āhārasthitiko [a]ya(yaṃ) [kāya] āhāraṃ niśritya tiṣṭhati | nānāhāra iyamasyānuśansa(śaṃsa)mātrā [|]
body.translated_text: It occurs to him thus: 'This food, even when being sought, is fraught with danger; even when being enjoyed, it is fraught with danger; and when consumed, it involves the danger of transformation.' Yet is there any benefit whatsoever in this food? What then is that? 'This body is sustained by food; depending on food, it endures; not without food' — this alone is its meager benefit.

body.text: evamāhārasthitiko [a]yaṃ kāyaṃ(ḥ) suciramapi tiṣṭhan varṣaśatamvā tiṣṭhati | kiṃcidvā punarbhūyaḥ samyak parihriyamāṇaḥ | asti cāsyārvāguparatiḥ | tatra yaḥ (ye) kāyasthitimātre pratipannāḥ na te supratipannā[ḥ] kāye kāyasthitimātrakena (ṇa) saṃtuṣṭā na (na) te asaṃtuṣṭā, na ca punaste āhārakṛtaṃ paripūrṇamanavadyamanuśansaṃ (śaṃsaṃ) pratyanubhavanti | ye punarnakāyasthitimātrakeṇa (na) saṃtuṣṭā[ḥ] kāyasthitimātrake pratipannā, na te supratipannā, api tu tāmeva kāyasthitiṃ (

children.text: ) niściṃ[tya] (niśritya) brahmacaryaṃ (rya)samudāgamāya pratipannāḥ, supratipannāḥ, ta eva ca punaḥ paripūrṇamanavadyamanuśansaṃ (śaṃsaṃ) pratyanubhavanti | tanme pratimaṃ syād yada(d)vā pratyavareṇa āhārānuśansa (śaṃsa)mātrakeṇa saṃtuṣṭo vihareyaṃ | na me pratirūpaṃ syādyadahaṃ bālasabhāgatāṃ bālasahadhārmikatāmadhyāpadyeyamevamāhāre sarvākāraṃ paripūrṇamādīnavaṃ jñātvā sa itaḥ pratisaṃkhyāyādīnava darśī, niḥsaraṇānveṣī cāhāraniḥsaraṇārthameva putramāṃ(mān) so dharmamāhāramāharati |
children.translated_text: ) having determined, relying on it, those who have entered the practice for the accomplishment of the holy life are well-entered; and they again experience the blameless and complete benefit. It would be fitting for me if I were to dwell content with merely the benefit of the lesser food. It would not be fitting for me if I were to fall into the company of fools and the nature of fools. Having thus known the complete fault of food in every respect, he, reflecting from this standpoint, seeing the danger and seeking escape, partakes of food only for the purpose of escaping from food — that is, he partakes of the <s>Dharma</s> regarding food as nourishment for his sons [i.e., his faculties].

body.translated_text: This body, sustained by food, even if it endures for a long time, endures for a hundred years, or slightly more when properly cared for. And its cessation comes sooner [than expected]. Those who are devoted merely to the sustaining of the body are not well-devoted; those who are contented merely with sustaining the body are not [truly] contented, nor do they experience the full, blameless benefit produced by food. But those who are not contented merely with sustaining the body [yet] are devoted to the mere sustaining of the body — they are not well-devoted; rather, that very sustaining of the body

body.text: tasyaivaṃ bhavati | evamete dāyakadānapatayaḥ kṛcchreṇa bhogān samudānīya, mahāntaṃ paryeṣaṇākṛtamādīnavaṃ pratyanubhavantaḥ, prapīḍya, prapīḍya, tvaṅmānsa (māṃsa)śoṇitamasmākamanuprayacchanti | ya [ete] [a]nukampāmupādāya viśeṣaphalārthinaḥ tasyāsmākaṃ tathā pratilabdhasya piṇḍapātasyāyamevaṃ rūpo [a]nurūpaḥ paribhogaḥ syādyadahaṃ tathā paribhūtamātmānaṃ (|) sthāpayitvā paribhuṃjīya, yathā teṣāṃ kārāḥ kṛtā atyarthaṃ mahāphalā[ḥ] syurmahānuśaṃsā, mahādyubha(ta)yo, mahāvistārāḥ, candropamaśca kulānyupasaṃkrameyaṃ vyavakṛṣya kāyaṃ, vyavakṛṣya cittaṃ, hrīmānapragalbhaḥ, anātmotkarṣī aparapansī, (

children.text: ) yathāsvena lābhena citta (sucittaḥ) syāṃ, sumanāḥ, evaṃ parasyāpi lābhena citta (sucittaḥ) syāṃ sumanā, evaṃ cittaśca punaḥ kulānyusaṃkrameyaṃ | tatkuta etallabhyaṃ pravrajitena parakuleṣu yadvadatra pare me māna (naṃ) dadatu | satkṛtya, mā asatkṛtya, prabhūtaṃ mā stokaṃ, praṇītaṃ mā lūhaṃ, tvarita[ṃ] mā gatvaṃ (baddham) | evaṃ caritasya me kulānyusaṃkramataḥ sa cet pare na dadyustenāhaṃ na teṣāmantike āghātacittatayā pratighacittatayā vyavadīyeyaṃ | na ca punastannidānaṃ kāyasya bhedādapāyopapattyā vighātamāpadyeya (yaṃ) | yaduta tāmevāghātacittatā (tāṃ) [pratighacittā]madhipatiṃ kṛtvā sa cedasatkṛtya na satkṛtya, sa cetstokaṃ na prabhūtaṃ | sa cellūhaṃ na praṇītaṃ, sa cedvaddhaṃ na tvaritaṃ dadyuḥ | da (ta)yāhamāghātacittatayā, pratighacittatayā ca vyavadīyeyamiti vistareṇa pūrvavat | imaṃ cāhaṃ kabaḍīkāramāhāraṃ niśritya tathā tathā pratipadyeya(yaṃ), tāñca mātrāṃ prativedhyeyaṃ | yena me jīvitendriyanirodhaśca na syānnaca piṇḍakena klāmyeyaṃ | brahmacaryānugrahaśca me syādevaṃ ca me śrava(ma)ṇabhāve, pravrajitabhāve sthitasyāyaṃ piṇḍapātaparibhogarūpaśca | (
children.translated_text: ) content with my own gains, well-pleased and cheerful; likewise content and cheerful with others' gains as well — thus minded, I should again approach families. How then can this be obtained by a renunciant in the homes of others — that others there should give me respect, not disrespect; abundantly, not scantily; fine food, not coarse; quickly, not slowly? And if I, conducting myself thus and approaching families, they should not give — then I should not on that account become one of hostile mind, one of resentful mind toward them. Nor again should I, on that account, incur harm through rebirth in a lower state at the breaking up of the body — that is, making that very hostility of mind and resentment of mind the governing factor. And if they give with disrespect rather than respect, if they give scantily rather than abundantly, if they give coarse rather than fine, if they give slowly rather than quickly — even then, I should not become one of hostile mind, one of resentful mind' — and so on in detail as before. 'And relying on this morsel-food, I should practice in such and such a way, and I should understand the proper measure, so that there would be no cessation of my life-faculty, nor would I be fatigued by alms-rounds, and there would be support for the holy life. And for me, established in the state of an ascetic, in the state of a renunciant, this proper partaking of alms-food
) would be purified and blameless in these respects.' Thus reflecting, he partakes of food.

body.translated_text: This thought arises in him: 'These donors and alms-givers, having gathered their goods with difficulty, experiencing the great danger incurred by seeking them, pressing and pressing, give us their skin, flesh, and blood. Those who, out of compassion and desiring special fruit, [give to us] — for the food thus obtained by us, this would be the appropriate way of partaking: that I should place myself in such a condition and partake in such a way that their deeds would be of exceedingly great fruit, of great benefit, of great splendor, and of great extent. And I should approach families like the moon — with body withdrawn, with mind withdrawn, possessed of modesty and conscience, not exalting myself, not disparaging others,

body.text: āhāraḥ punaḥ katamaḥ [|] catvāra āhārāḥ [|] kabaḍaṃkāraḥ, sparśo, manaḥsaṃcetanā, vijñānaṃ cāsmiṃstvarthe kabaḍaṃkāra āhāro 'bhipretaḥ | sa punaḥ katamastadyathā manthā vāpūpā vā odanakulmāṣamvā, sarpistailaṃ, phaṇitaṃ, māṃsaṃ, matsyā, vallūrā, lavaṇaṃ, kṣīraṃ, dadhi, navanītamitīmāni cānyāni caivaṃ rūpāṇyupakaraṇāni yāni kabaḍāni (

children.translated_text: ) by making them into morsels. Therefore it is called morsel-food.

body.translated_text: What then is food? There are four kinds of food: <s>kabaḍīkāra</s> (morsel-food), <s>sparśa</s> (contact), <s>manaḥsaṃcetanā</s> (mental volition), and <s>vijñāna</s> (consciousness). In this context, morsel-food is intended. What then is that? Namely: gruel, cakes, boiled rice and barley, ghee, oil, molasses, meat, fish, dried meat, salt, milk, curds, butter — these and other such provisions that are consumed

body.text: āharatīti bhuṃkte | pratiniṣevatyabhyavaharati, khādati, bhakṣayati | svādayati, pibati, cūṣatīti paryāyāḥ [|]
body.translated_text: 'Partakes' means eats. The synonyms are: consumes, ingests, chews, devours, savors, drinks, sips.

body.text: na dravārthamiti | yaścaite (ye caite) kāmopabhogina ityarthaḥ | yāharanti (ya āharanti) yadvayamāhāreṇa prīṇitagātrāḥ saṃtarpitagātrāḥ pratyupasthite sāyāhnakāle samaye, atikrāntāyāṃ rajanyāṃ, maulībaddhikābhiḥ sārddhaṃmalābu-romaśabāhubhiḥ kandukastanibhirnārībhiḥ (kandukastanībhirnārībhiḥ) (

children.text: ) krīḍato (nto), ramamāṇāḥ, paricārayan (nta), auddhatyaṃ dravaṃ prāviṣkariṣyāma iti [|] drava eṣa ārye dharmavinaye yadutakāmarāgopasaṃhitā, maithunopasaṃhitā[ḥ] pāpakā akuśalā dharmā, vitarkā, yairayaṃ khādyamāno, bādhyamāna, uddhatendriyo bhavatyanuddhatendriyaśca, drutamānasaḥ, plutamānasaḥ, asthitamānaso [a]vyupaśāntamānasaḥ, te punaratyantamāhāramāharanto dravārthamāharantītyucyate |
children.translated_text: ) sporting, delighting, and amusing themselves, 'We shall display excitement and intoxication.' This is intoxication in the noble <s>Dharma</s> and <s>Vinaya</s>: namely, evil and unwholesome states, thoughts connected with sensual desire and connected with sexual intercourse, by which this person, being consumed and afflicted, becomes one of agitated faculties and unagitated faculties, of an excited mind, of a leaping mind, of an unsteady mind, of an unquieted mind. Those who partake of food excessively are said to partake for the purpose of intoxication.

body.translated_text: 'Not for the purpose of intoxication' — the meaning is: those who are enjoyers of sensual pleasures. Those who partake, whose limbs are satisfied and nourished by food, at the arrival of the evening time, when the night has passed, with women who are like gourds with hairy arms and breasts like balls,

body.text: śrutavāṃstvāryaśrāvaka[ḥ] pratisaṃkhyānabalika ādīnavadarśī niḥsaraṇaṃ prajānaṃ (nan) paribhuṃkte | na tathā yathā te kāmopabhogino bhuṃjante | tenāha- na dravārthaṃ na madārthaṃ, na maṇḍanārthaṃ na vibhūṣaṇārthamiti | yathāpi ta eva kāmopabhogina ityartha māhāramāharanti | adya vayamāhāramāhṛtavanto yaduta prabhūtañca tṛptito yathāśaktyābalaṃ | snigdhaṃ ca, vṛṣyañca, bṛṃhaṇīyañca, varṇasaṃpannaṃ, gandhasampannaṃ, rasasampannaṃ | endhābhūte (aindhībhūte), nirgatāyāṃ rajanyāṃ śaktā bhaviṣyāmaḥ | pratibalā, vyāyāmakaraṇo (ṇā), yaduta atartkāyā (ātatīkriyayā) vā, nirghātena, vyāyāmaśilayā (

children.text: ) vā, ulloṭhanene (na) vā, pṛthivīkhātena vā, bāhuvyāyāmena vā, pādāvaṣṭambhanena vā, plavanena vā, (a)laṃghanena vā [|] tatra vyāyāmena bāha(hu)ñca punarvyāyāmaṃ niśritya balavantobhaviṣyāmaḥ | (a)vyāyatagātrā, dīrghaṃ cārogāḥ, cirakālaṃ cāsmākaṃ yauvanamanuvartakaṃ bhaviṣyati, no tu tvaritaṃ (|) virūpakaraṇī jarā dehamabhibhaviṣyantī (tī)ti | cirataraṃ ca jīviṣyāma iti | prabhūtabhakṣaṇe ca pratibalā bhaviṣyāmaḥ | bhuktaṃ ca (bhuktaṃ) samyakpariṇamiṣyati | doṣāṇāṃ cāpaca (kṣa)yaḥ kṛto bhaviṣyati | ityārogyamadārthaṃ, [yauvana]madārthaṃ, jīvitamadārthaṃ paribhuṃjate |
children.translated_text: ) or by rolling exercises, or by earth-digging, or by arm-exercises, or by leg-exercises, or by swimming, or by jumping. And through exercise, relying on much exercise, we shall become strong, with well-exercised limbs, and we shall be healthy for a long time, and our youth will continue for a long time and will not quickly be overtaken by the disfiguring old age that overcomes the body. And we shall live for a longer time. And we shall be capable of abundant eating, and what is eaten will be properly digested, and the diminution of the bodily humors will be effected.' Thus they partake for the purpose of pride in health, pride in youth, and pride in life.

body.translated_text: But the learned noble disciple, empowered by reflection, seeing the danger, knowing the escape, partakes — not in the way that those enjoyers of sensual pleasures partake. Therefore he says: 'Not for the purpose of intoxication, not for the purpose of pride, not for the purpose of adornment, not for the purpose of decoration.' Just as those very enjoyers of sensual pleasures partake of food — the meaning is — 'Today we have partaken of food, that is, abundantly and to our fill, to the extent of our ability and strength, rich, potent, nourishing, excellent in color, excellent in fragrance, excellent in taste. When it has become dark, when the night has passed, we shall be capable, powerful enough for exercise — that is, through archery practice, or wrestling, or by exercise disciplines,

body.text: teṣāṃ punarevaṃ bhavati | kṛtavyāyāmā vayaṃ snātrasaṃvidhānaṃ kariṣyāmo, yaduta-śucinā toyena gātrāṇi prakṣāliṣyāmaḥ | prakṣālitagātrāśca keśāni ca (keśāṃśca) prasādhayiṣyāmaḥ | vividhena cānulepanena kāyamanupalipya (-manulipya) vividhairvastrairvividhairmālyairvividhairalaṃ[kāraiḥ] kāyaṃ bhūṣayiṣyāmaḥ | (

children.translated_text: ) Therein, the bathing, grooming, and anointing is said to be their adornment.

body.translated_text: Furthermore, this thought arises in them: 'Having exercised, we shall make arrangements for bathing — that is, we shall wash our limbs with clean water. Having washed our limbs, we shall groom our hair. Having anointed the body with various unguents, we shall adorn the body with various garments, various garlands, and various ornaments.'

body.text: tathā maṇḍanajātānāṃ yadvastramālyābharaṇadhāraṇamidamucyate | vibhūṣaṇamiti | maṇḍanārthaṃ vibhūṣaṇārthaṃ paribhuṃja[to 'ta] evaṃ (paribhuṃjanto 'ta evaṃ) madamattā maṇḍanajātivibhūṣitagātrāḥ | madhyāhnasamaye, sāyāhna samaye vā, bhaktasamaye tṛṣitā bubhukṣitāśca, pareṇa harṣeṇa, parayā nandyā, pareṇāmodena | ādīnavadarśino niḥsaraṇamaprajānanta (nto) yathopapannamāhāramāharanti | yāvadeva punaḥ punardravārthaṃ, maṇḍanārthaṃ, vibhūṣaṇārtha ca [|]
body.translated_text: Similarly, for those who are adorned, the wearing of garments, garlands, and ornaments is said to be their decoration. Partaking for the purpose of adornment and decoration, thus proud and intoxicated, with adorned and decorated bodies, at midday or in the evening, at mealtime, thirsty and hungry, with supreme delight, supreme joy, and supreme pleasure, not seeing the danger, not knowing the escape, they partake of food as it is available — again and again for the purpose of intoxication, adornment, and decoration.

body.text: śrutavāṃstvāryaśrāvakaḥ | pratisaṃkhyānabalika ādīnavadarśī niḥsaraṇaṃprajānan paribhuṃkte | na tu tathā yathā te kāmopabhoginaḥ paribhuṃjate | nānyatremamasaṃniveṣaṇāprahātavyamāhāraṃ pratiniṣevamāṇa eva prahāsyāmīti | yāvadevāsya kāyasya sthitaye iti bhuktvā nābhuktvā yaśca jīvitasya kāyasthitirityucyate | so [a]hamimamāhāramāhṛtya jīviṣyāmi, na mariṣyāmīti āhārati | tenāhaṃ (ha) yāvadevāsya kāyasya sthitaye |
body.translated_text: But the learned noble disciple, empowered by reflection, seeing the danger, knowing the escape, partakes — not in the way those enjoyers of sensual pleasures partake. 'There is nothing other than this: while consuming the food that is not to be abandoned from this body, I shall [through practice] abandon it [i.e., attachment].' 'For the maintenance of this body' — having eaten or not eaten, that which is called the maintenance of bodily life. 'I, having partaken of this food, shall live, shall not die' — thus he partakes. Therefore it is said: 'For the maintenance of this body.'

body.text: kathaṃ yāpanāyai āharati | dvividhā yātrā-asti kṛcchreṇa astyakṛcchreṇa [|] kṛcchreṇa yātrā katamā [|] yadrūpamāhārato jighatsā daurbalyaṃ vā bhavati | duḥkhito vā bāḍhaglānaḥ | adharmeṇa vā piṇḍapātaṃ paryeṣate, na dharmeṇa | raktaḥ paribhuṃkte, saktaḥ, gṛddho, grathito, mūrchito 'dhyavasito [a]dhyavasāyamāpannaḥ | guruko vāsya kāyo bhavatyakarmaṇyaḥ, aprahāṇakṣamaḥ, yenāsya dhandhaṃ cittaṃ samādhiyate (dhīyeta) | kṛcchreṇa vā āśvāsa-praśvāsāḥ pravartante | styānamiddhaṃ vā cittaṃ paryavahīya (paryavanahyatīya)mucyate kṛcchreṇa yātrā |
body.translated_text: How does he partake for sustenance? Sustenance is of two kinds: with difficulty and without difficulty. What is sustenance with difficulty? When, from that kind of food, hunger or weakness arises, or one becomes afflicted and severely ill, or one seeks alms-food by unrighteous means rather than righteous ones, or one partakes with attachment, clinging, greed, entanglement, infatuation, excessive involvement, and having adopted [wrong] resolve; or one's body becomes heavy, unfit for work, incapable of abandonment, whereby one's mind settles sluggishly in <s>samādhi</s>, or breathing in and out proceeds with difficulty, or the mind is seized by torpor and drowsiness — this is called sustenance with difficulty.

body.text: akṛcchreṇa yātrā katamā [|] yathāpi tadrūpamāhāramāharato yathā jighatsā daurbbalyaṃ vā na bhavati | nābhyadhiko bhavati | duḥkhito vā bāḍhaglānaḥ | dharmeṇa vā piṇḍapātaṃ paryeṣate, na vā [a]dharmeṇa | surakto vā paribhuṃktesaktaḥ (paribhuṅkate 'saktaḥ), agṛdhraḥ, agrathitaḥ, anadhyavasito [a]nadhyavasāyamāpannaḥ, na cāsya kāyo guruko bhavati | karmaṇyo bhavati | prahāṇakṣamaḥ | yenāsya tvaritaṃ cittaṃ samādhīyate | alpakṛcchreṇāśvāsapraśvāsāḥ pravarttante | styānamiddhaṃ (

children.translated_text: ) this is called sustenance with little difficulty.

body.translated_text: What is sustenance without difficulty? When, from that kind of food, neither hunger nor weakness arises, nor does one become excessive, afflicted, or severely ill; one seeks alms-food by righteous means rather than unrighteous ones; one partakes without attachment, without clinging, without greed, without entanglement, without infatuation, without having adopted [wrong] resolve; one's body does not become heavy; it is fit for work; it is capable of abandonment; one's mind settles quickly in <s>samādhi</s>; breathing in and out proceeds with little difficulty; the mind is not seized by torpor and drowsiness —

body.text: tatra yā kṛcchreṇa yātrā tayā jīvitasthitirbhavati | kāyasya sāvadyā sasaṃkliṣṭā [|] tatra yeyamalpakṛcchreṇa yātrā tayā jīvitasthitirbhavati (|) kāyasya [|] sā ca punaranavadyā | asaṃkliṣṭā [|] tatra śrutavānāryaśrāvakaḥ | sāvadyāṃ saṃkliṣṭāṃ yātrāmparivarjayati | anavadyāmasaṃkliṣṭāṃ yātrāṃ gacchati | pratiṣevate | tenāha yāpanāyai |
body.translated_text: Therein, the sustenance that is with difficulty — by that, the maintenance of life and body is blameworthy and defiled. Therein, the sustenance that is with little difficulty — by that, the maintenance of life and body is blameless and undefiled. Therein, the learned noble disciple avoids the blameworthy and defiled sustenance, and follows, practices the blameless and undefiled sustenance. Therefore it is said: 'for sustenance.'

body.text: sā punaranavadyā asaṃkliṣṭā yātrā yā pūrvamuktā | tāṃ kathaṃ yāpayati | āha | yadyayaṃ jighatsoparataye, brahmacaryānugrahāya iti, paurāṇāṃ ca vedanāṃ prahāsyāmi navāñca notpādayiṣyāmi | yātrā ca me bhaviṣyati | balaṃ ca, sukhaṃ cānavadyatā ca, (

children.text: ) sparśavi[hāra]tā ceti | evaṃ pratiṣevamāṇaḥ anavadyāmasaṃkliṣṭāṃ yātrāṃ kalpayati |
children.translated_text: ) and the state of dwelling in comfort.' Thus practicing, he establishes blameless and undefiled sustenance.

body.translated_text: That blameless, undefiled sustenance is what was previously described. How does he sustain? He says: 'By this, the cessation of hunger, for the support of the holy life — I shall abandon former painful feelings and shall not generate new ones. There shall be sustenance for me, and strength, and happiness, and blamelessness,

body.text: kathaṃ ca punarjighatsoparataye āharati [|] pratyupasthite bhaktasamaye, utpannāyāṃ kṣudhāyāṃ, yadā paribhuṃkte tasyaiva kṣutparyavasthānasya jighatsādaurbalyasya ca prativigamāya tāñca mātrāṃ paribhuṃkte | yathāsya bhuktavataḥ akāle punarjighatsādaurbalyanna bādhate | sāyāhnasamaye vā, abhi(ti?)krāntāyāmvā rajanyāṃ, śvobhūte, pratyupasthite bhaktasamaye [|] evaṃ jighatsoparataye āharati |
body.translated_text: And how does one eat for the cessation of hunger? When mealtime has arrived and hunger has arisen, when one eats, one eats just that measure for the removal of that very state of hunger and the weakness of appetite, such that, having eaten, hunger and weakness do not trouble one again at an improper time — whether in the evening, or when the night has passed, or on the next day, when mealtime arrives. Thus one eats for the cessation of hunger.

body.text: kathaṃ brahmacaryānugrahāyārati | tāṃ mātrāṃ paribhuṃkte tadrūpamāhāramāharati | yenāsya kuśalapakṣe prayuktasya dṛṣṭa eva dharme bhuktasamanantaraṃ tasminneva vā divase agurukaḥ kāyo bhavati | karmaṇyaśca bhavati, prahāṇakṣamaśca, yenāsya tvaritatvaritaṃ cittaṃ samādhīyate | alpakṛcchreṇāśvāsapraśvāsāḥ pravartante | styānamiddhaṃ cittaṃ na paryavanaha(hya)ti | yenāyaṃ bhavyo bhavati | pratibalaśca | kṣipramevāprāptasya prāptaye, anadhigatasyādhigamāya, asākṣātkṛtasya sākṣātkriyāyai | evaṃ brahmacaryānugrahāyāharati ||
body.translated_text: How does one eat for the support of the holy life (<s>brahmacarya</s>)? One eats that measure and takes such food by which, when engaged in the wholesome side, in this very life, immediately after eating, on that very day, the body becomes not heavy, becomes fit for work, and capable of striving, by which one's mind quickly becomes concentrated, by which the in-breaths and out-breaths proceed with little difficulty, by which <s>styānamiddha</s> (sloth and torpor) does not overwhelm the mind, and by which one becomes capable and competent to quickly attain what has not been attained, to realize what has not been realized, to directly experience what has not been directly experienced. Thus one eats for the support of the holy life.

body.text: kathaṃ paurāṇāṃ vedanāṃ prahāsyāmītyāharati | (

children.text: ) tathāpi tadatītamadhvānamupādāya | amātrayā vā paribhuktambhavatyapaśyamvā (pathyaṃ vā), apariṇate (taṃ) vā, yenāsya vividhaḥ kāyika ābādhaḥ samutpanno bhavati | tadyathā kaṇḍū[ḥ], kuṣṭa[ḥ], kiṭibha[ḥ] kilāsa iti vistareṇa pūrvavat | tasya cābādhanidānā utpadyante śārīrikā vedanā duḥkhāstīvrāḥ, kharāḥ, kaṭukā, amanāpā (amana āpā)[ḥ |] tasyābādhasyopaśamāya tāsāṃ ca tannidānānāṃ duḥkhānāṃ vedanānāmupaśamāya hitaṃ paśyamanu(pathyamanu)kūlamānulomikaṃ vaidyopadiṣṭena vidhinā bhaiṣajyaṃ pratiṣevate [|] sāṃpreyaṃ cāhāramāharati | yenāsyotpannasyābādhasya tannidānānāṃ ca duḥkhānāṃ vedanānāṃ prahāṇaṃ bhavatyevaṃ paurāṇāmvedanāṃ prahāsyāmītyāhāramāharati | sa varttamānamadhvānamupādāya sukhī, arogo, balavānnāmātrayā vā paribhuṃkte | apathya tā apariṇate, kāye nāsyāgatamadhvānamupādāya (cāsyānāgatamadhvānamupādāya) śvo vā, uttaraśvo vā, viṣūcikā vā kāye saṃtiṣṭheta | anyatamānyatamo vā kāye kāyika ābādhassamutpadyeta | tadyathā kaṇḍū[ḥ], kuṣṭa[ḥ], kiṭibha[ḥ], kilāsa iti vistareṇa pūrvavat | yannidānā utpadyeranchā (ñchā)rīrikā vedanā[ḥ] pūrvavat | evaṃ ca navāṃ vedanāṃ notpādayiṣyāmītyāharati |
children.translated_text: Considering the past: if one has eaten immoderately, or [eaten] unwholesome [food], or undigested [food], whereby various bodily afflictions have arisen — such as itching, leprosy, skin disease, vitiligo, and so on in detail as before — and due to that affliction, painful bodily feelings arise that are intense, sharp, harsh, bitter, and disagreeable — for the alleviation of that affliction and for the alleviation of those painful feelings caused by it, seeing what is beneficial, appropriate, suitable, and in accordance with the method prescribed by a physician, one takes medicine and consumes food suitable for the present, by which the arisen affliction and the painful feelings caused by it are eliminated. Thus one eats [thinking] 'I shall eliminate former feelings.' He, considering the present time: being happy, free from illness, and strong, does not eat immoderately, [does not eat] unwholesome or undigested [food], so that considering the future time, tomorrow or the day after, neither dysentery may settle in the body, nor any other bodily affliction may arise — such as itching, leprosy, skin disease, vitiligo, and so on in detail as before — which would cause painful bodily feelings to arise, as before. Thus one eats [thinking] 'I shall not produce new feelings.'

body.translated_text: How does one eat [thinking] 'I shall eliminate former feelings (<s>vedanā</s>)'?

body.text: kathaṃ yātrā me bhaviṣyati | varṇaṃ ca sukhaṃ cānavadyatāṃ(tā) ca | sparśavihāratā cetyāharati | yattāvad bhukto jīvatītyevaṃ yātrā bhavati | yatpunarjighatsādaurbalyamu(ma)panayati | evamasya varṇaṃ bhavati | yatpunaḥ paurāṇāṃ vedanāṃ prajahāti | navāṃ co (ca no)tpādayatyevamasya sukhaṃ bhavati | yat punardharmeṇa piṇḍapātaṃ paryeṣṭyāraktaḥ (paryeṣyāraktaḥ), asaktaḥ iti vistareṇa pūrvavadevamanavadyatā bhavati | yatpunarbhuktavato na gurukaḥ kāyo bhavati, karmaṇyaśca bhavati, prahāṇakṣamo vistareṇa pūrvavadevamasya sparśavihāratā bhavati | tenāha pratisaṃkhyāyāhāramāharati | na dravārthaṃ, na madārthaṃ, na maṇḍanārthamiti | vistareṇa pūrvavadayaṃ tāvad bhojane mātrajñatāyā vistaravibhāgaḥ |
body.translated_text: How does one eat [thinking] 'There will be sustenance for me, and complexion, and comfort, and blamelessness, and comfortable dwelling'? Insofar as having eaten one lives — thus there is sustenance. Insofar as one removes the weakness of hunger — thus there is complexion. Insofar as one eliminates former feelings and does not produce new ones — thus there is comfort. Insofar as one seeks <s>piṇḍapāta</s> (almsfood) by <s>dharma</s>, unattached, unbound, and so on in detail as before — thus there is blamelessness. Insofar as having eaten the body does not become heavy, becomes fit for work, and capable of striving, in detail as before — thus there is comfortable dwelling. Therefore it is said: 'One eats having reflected (<s>pratisaṃkhyāya</s>). Not for amusement, not for intoxication, not for adornment,' and so on in detail as before. This, then, is the detailed analysis of moderation in eating.

body.text: samāsārthaḥ punaḥ katama[ḥ] āha [|] yaśca (yañca) paribhuṅakte | yathā ca paribhuṃkte | yaduta kabaḍaṃkāramāhāraṃ, manthā vā, [a]pūpā vā, odanakulmāṣaṃ vā vistareṇa pūrvavat |
body.translated_text: What is the summary meaning? He says: What one eats and how one eats — namely, <s>kabaḍaṃkāra āhāra</s> (morsel food), whether porridge, or cakes, or rice and barley gruel, and so on in detail as before.

body.text: kathaṃ paribhuṃkte | pratisaṃkhyāya paribhuṃkte | na dravārthaṃ, na madārthaṃ na maṇḍanārthamiti vistareṇa pūrvavat |
body.translated_text: How does one eat? One eats having reflected. Not for amusement, not for intoxication, not for adornment, and so on in detail as before.

children.translated_text: As it is said: 'One eats having reflected.'

body.translated_text: Furthermore, the summary meaning: one eats having embraced the antidote, and free from the extreme of sensual indulgence, and free from the extreme of self-mortification, for the support of the holy life.

body.text: kathaṃ kāmasukhallikāntavivarjitaṃ | yadāha | na dravārthaṃ, na madārthaṃ, na maṇḍanārtha, na vibhūṣaṇārthamiti |
body.translated_text: How is it free from the extreme of sensual indulgence? As it is said: 'Not for amusement, not for intoxication, not for adornment, not for embellishment.'

body.text: kathamātmaklamathāntavivarjitaṃ | yadāha [|] jighatsoparataye, paurāṇāṃ ca vedanāṃ prahāsyāmi | navāñca notpādayiṣyāmi | yātrā ca me bhaviṣyati | balaṃ ca sukhaṃ ceti |
body.translated_text: How is it free from the extreme of self-mortification? As it is said: 'For the cessation of hunger; and I shall eliminate former feelings; and I shall not produce new ones; and there will be sustenance for me, and strength, and comfort.'

body.text: kathaṃ bahmacaryānugrahāya paribhuṃkte | yadāha | brahmacaryānugrahāya | anavadyatā ca | sparśavihāratā ca me bhaviṣyatīti |
body.translated_text: How does one eat for the support of the holy life? As it is said: 'For the support of the holy life; and there will be blamelessness; and comfortable dwelling for me.'

body.text: punaraparaḥ samāsārthaḥ [|] dvayamidaṃ bhojanaṃ, cābhojanaṃ ca | tatrābhojanaṃ yat sarveṇa sarvaṃ sarvathā kiṃcinna paribhuṃkte | abhuṃjānaśca mriyate | tatra bhojanaṃ dvividhaṃ | samabhojanaṃ, viṣamabhojanaṃ ca | tatra samabhojanaṃ | yannātyalpaṃ nātiprabhūtaṃ, nāpathyaṃ, nāpariṇatena saṃkliṣṭaṃ | tatra viṣamabhojanaṃ | yadya(da) tyalpamatiprabhūtaṃ ca | apariṇate (taṃ) vā, apathyaṃ vā, saṃkliṣṭaṃ vā paribhuṃkte | tatra samabhojane nātyalpabhojane jighatsādaurbalyamanutpannaṃ (|) notpādayati | utpannaṃ prajahāti | tatra nātiprabhūtabhojane (na) [sama]viṣamabhojanena (

children.text: ) gurukaḥ kāyo bhavatyakarmaṇyaḥ aprahāṇakṣamo vistareṇa pūrvavat | tatra pariṇatabhojanena, samabhojanena paurāṇāṃ ca vedanāṃ prajahāti | navāñca notpādayiṣyatyevamasya yātrā bhavati | balaṃ ca, sukhaṃ ca, asaṃkliṣṭabhojanena | samabhojanena anavadyatā ca bhavati | sparśavihāratā ca |
children.translated_text: the body does not become heavy, unfit for work, incapable of striving, and so on in detail as before. Therein, by digested and balanced eating, one eliminates former feelings and will not produce new ones — thus there is sustenance, strength, and comfort. By uncontaminated and balanced eating, there is blamelessness and comfortable dwelling.

body.translated_text: Furthermore, the summary meaning: There are two [categories]: eating and not-eating. Therein, not-eating is when one does not eat anything at all in every way and in every respect, and not eating, one dies. Therein, eating is of two kinds: balanced eating and imbalanced eating. Therein, balanced eating is that which is neither too little nor too much, neither unwholesome, nor contaminated by being undigested. Therein, imbalanced eating is when one eats too little or too much, or undigested, or unwholesome, or contaminated food. Therein, in balanced eating that is not too little, hunger and weakness that have not arisen are not produced, and those that have arisen are eliminated. Therein, in eating that is not too much, by balanced [rather than] imbalanced eating,

body.text: tatrātyalpabhojanaṃ yena jīvati | atiprabhūtabhojanaṃ | yenāsya gurubhārādhyākrāntaśca kāyo bhavati | na ca kālena bha(bhu)ktampariṇamati | tatrāpariṇatabhojanena viṣūcikā kāye saṃtiṣṭhate | anyatamānyatamo vā kāye kāyika ābādhaḥ (|) samutpadyate | yathā apariṇatabhojanenaivamapathyabhojanena [|] tatrāyamapathyabhojane viśeṣaḥ [|] doṣaḥ pracayaṃ gacchati | kharaṃ vābādhaṃ spṛśati | tatra saṃkliṣṭabhojanena adharmeṇa piṇḍapātaṃ paryeṣya raktaḥ paribhuṃkte | sakto, gṛddho, grathita iti vistareṇa pūrvavat | iti yaḥ samabhojanaṃ ca paribhuṃkte | viṣamabhojanaṃ ca parivarjayati | tasmād bhojane samakārītyucyate | bhojane samakāritaiṣā ebhirākaurarākhyātā, uttānā, vivṛtā, saṃprakāśitā | yaduta pratisaṃkhyāyāhāramāharati | na dravārthaṃ, na madārthaṃ, na maṇḍanārthaṃ, na vibhūṣaṇārthamiti vistareṇa pūrvavat |
body.translated_text: Therein, eating too little is that by which one merely survives. Eating too much is that by which the body becomes weighed down as if laden with a heavy burden, and the food eaten does not digest in due time. Therein, from undigested food, dysentery settles in the body, or some other bodily affliction arises — just as from undigested food, so too from unwholesome food. Therein, with unwholesome food there is this distinction: the <s>doṣa</s> (humoral imbalance) accumulates, or one touches a severe affliction. Therein, by contaminated eating, one seeks <s>piṇḍapāta</s> by non-<s>dharma</s> and eats attached, bound, greedy, entangled, and so on in detail as before. Thus one who eats balanced food and avoids imbalanced food — therefore he is called 'one who is balanced in eating.' This balance in eating has been explained, made manifest, opened up, and made clear by these [phrases] — namely, 'One eats having reflected. Not for amusement, not for intoxication, not for adornment, not for embellishment,' and so on in detail as before.

body.text: tatra yastā(yattā)vadāha | pratisaṃkhyāyāhāramāharati | na dravārthaṃ, na madārthaṃ, na maṇḍanārthaṃ, na vidū(bhū)ṣaṇārthaṃ (|), yāvadevāsya kāyasya sthitaye, yāpanāyai, anena tāvadabhojanaṃ na (ca) pratikṣipati | yatpunarāha | jighatsoparataye, brahmacaryānugrahāya vistareṇa yāvat sparśavihāratāyai, anena viṣamabhojanaṃ pratikṣipati |
body.translated_text: Therein, when it is said 'One eats having reflected. Not for amusement, not for intoxication, not for adornment, not for embellishment — just for the maintenance and sustenance of this body' — by this, not-eating is rejected. But when it is said 'For the cessation of hunger, for the support of the holy life,' and so on in detail up to 'for comfortable dwelling' — by this, imbalanced eating is rejected.

body.text: kathaṃ ca punarviṣamabhojanaṃ (punaratiprabhūtabhojanaṃ) pratikṣipati | yattāvadāha brahmacaryānugrahāyānenātiprabhūtabhojanaṃ pratikṣipati | yadāha [|] paurāṇāṃ ca vedanāṃ prahāsyāmi (|), navāṃ ca notpādayiṣyāmītyanenāpariṇatabhojanata me (tāma)pathyabhojanatāṃ ca pratikṣipati | yadāha | yātrā ca me bhaviṣyati, balaṃ cānenātyalpabhojanatāṃ pra(tāmapra)bhūtabhojanatāṃ ca darśayati (pratikṣipati) | yadāha | sukhaṃ ca me bhaviṣyatītyanena pariṇatabhojanatāṃ ca darśayati [|] yadāha (|) sukhaṃ ca me bhaviṣyatīti pathyabhojanatāṃ ca darśayati | yadāha | anavadyatā ca me bhaviṣyati, sparśavihāratā cetyanenāsaṃkliṣṭabhojanatāṃ darśayati | yosāvadharmeṇa piṇḍapātaṃ paryeṣya raktaḥ (

children.text: ) paribhuṃkte | sakto vistareṇa pūrvavat | sa saṃkliṣṭaśca paribhuṃkte, sāvadyatā cāsya bhavati | tasyaiva ca kuśalapakṣaprayuktasya pratisaṃlayane, yoge, manasikāre, svādhyāye, arthacintāyāṃ ta eva pāpakā akuśalā vitarkāścittamanuvasravanti ye [a]sya taṃ nityāṃ (tannityāṃ), tatpravaṇāṃ, tatprābhorāṃ (tatprābhārāṃ) cittasantatiṃ pravarttayanti | yenāsya sparśavihāreṇa (sparśavihāro na) bhavati | sā ceyaṃ dvividhā sparśavihāratā atiprabhūtabhojanaparivarjanācca yenāsya na gurukaḥ kāyo bhavatyakarmaṇyaḥ, aprahāṇakṣama iti vistareṇa pūrvavat | aparenā (ṇā) svādākaraṇād yenāsya vitarkasaṃkṣobhakṛtāṃ (tā) asparśavihāratā na bhavati | tadevaṃ sati sarvairebhiḥ padairbhojane samakāritā vyākhyātā bhavati | iyamucyate bhojane mātrajñatā || vistarataḥ saṃkṣepataśca ||
children.translated_text: bound, and so on in detail as before — he eats in a contaminated way, and there is blame for him. And for that very one who is engaged in the wholesome side, in his retreat, in <s>yoga</s>, in mental attention, in self-study, and in reflection on meanings — those very evil, unwholesome <s>vitarkas</s> (discursive thoughts) flow into his mind that make his mental continuum constant in that [unwholesome direction], inclined toward it, and burdened by it, whereby comfortable dwelling does not arise for him. And this comfortable dwelling is of two kinds: from the avoidance of eating too much, whereby the body does not become heavy, unfit for work, incapable of striving, and so on in detail as before; and from not making [food] into a matter of relishing, whereby the non-comfortable dwelling caused by disturbance of discursive thoughts does not arise. Thus, when this is so, balance in eating has been explained by all these phrases. This is called moderation in eating — in detail and in summary.

body.translated_text: And how is imbalanced eating rejected? When it is said 'For the support of the holy life' — by this, eating too much is rejected. When it is said 'I shall eliminate former feelings and I shall not produce new ones' — by this, eating undigested food and eating unwholesome food are rejected. When it is said 'There will be sustenance for me, and strength' — by this, eating too little and eating too much are indicated [as rejected]. When it is said 'There will be comfort for me' — by this, eating digested food is indicated. When it is said 'There will be comfort for me' — by this, eating wholesome food is indicated. When it is said 'There will be blamelessness for me, and comfortable dwelling' — by this, eating uncontaminated food is indicated. That one who seeks <s>piṇḍapāta</s> by non-<s>dharma</s> and eats attached,

body.text: pūrvarātrāpararātraṃ jāgarikānuyuktatā katamā | (

children.text: ) tatra katamaḥ pūrvarātraḥ (-mat pūrvarātram) | katamo (mada)pararātraḥ (tram) | katamojāgarikāyogaḥ | katamā jāgarikāyogasyānuyuktatā | tatrāya(yaṃ)-(tredaṃ) sāyāhnaṃ ardharātraḥ (traṃ), sāyāhnaṃ sūryāstaṃgamanamupādāya yo rātryāḥ pūrvabhāgaḥ, so 'tirekaṃ prahāraṃ (sātirekaḥ praharaḥ) | tatrāyaṃ jāgā(ga)rikāyogaḥ | yadāha | divā caṃkramaniṣadyābhyāmāvaraṇīyebhyo dharmebhyaścittaṃ pariśodhayati | pariśodhya, bahi[r]vihārasya pādau prakṣālya vihāraṃ praviśya dakṣiṇena pārśvena śayyāṃ kalpayati | pāde pādamādhāya ālokasaṃjñī smṛtaḥ | saṃprajāna(n) utthānasaṃjñāmeva manasi kurvan, sa rātryāḥ paścime yāmelaghu laghveva prativibudhya caṃkramaniṣadyābhyāmāvaraṇīyebhyo dharmebhyaścittaṃ (
children.translated_text: Therein, what is the first watch? What is the last watch? What is the practice of wakefulness? What is the dedication to the practice of wakefulness? Therein, this is the evening [until] midnight — from the setting of the sun, it is the first portion of the night, slightly more than one <s>prahara</s> (watch). Therein, this is the practice of wakefulness — as it is said: 'During the day, by walking meditation and seated meditation, one purifies the mind of obstructive <s>dharmas</s>. Having purified it, having washed the feet outside the dwelling, one enters the dwelling and arranges the bed on the right side, placing foot upon foot, with the perception of light, mindful, clearly comprehending, mentally forming the intention of rising. In the last watch of the night, lightly and quickly awakening, by walking meditation and seated meditation, one purifies the mind of obstructive <s>dharmas</s>.'

children.text: ) pariśodhayati | tatreyaṃ jāgarikānuyogasyānuyuktatā | yathāpi tadbuddhasya bhagavataḥ śrāvakajāgarikāyogasya śrotā | tatra śikṣitukāmo bhavati | yathābhūtasyāsya yajjāgarikāyogamārabhya buddhānujñātaṃ jāgarikānuyogaṃ sampādayiṣyāmīti yaśchando, vīyaṃ (vīryaṃ), vyāyāmo, niṣkramaḥ | parākramasthānaprārambhaḥ | utsāha utsūḍhiraprativāṇiścetasaḥ | saṃgrahaḥ sāvadyaṃ (dyaḥ) |
children.translated_text: ) one purifies the mind. Herein, this is the practice of devotion to wakefulness: Just as one hears from the <s>Buddha</s> <s>Bhagavān</s> about the yoga of a <s>śrāvaka's</s> (disciple's) wakefulness, and therein one desires to train — the wish, the vigor, the exertion, the effort, the undertaking of a firm stand, the enthusiasm, the energy, the non-retreat of the mind, and the restraint from what is blameworthy [arise in one thinking]: 'I shall accomplish the practice of devotion to wakefulness as authorized by the <s>Buddha</s> regarding the yoga of wakefulness as it truly is.'

body.translated_text: What is the practice of wakefulness in the first and last watches of the night (<s>pūrvarātrāpararātraṃ jāgarikānuyuktatā</s>)?

body.text: tatra kathaṃ caṃkramaniṣadyābhyāmāvaraṇīyebhyo dharmebhyaścittaṃ pariśodhayati | divā ucyate | sūya(rya)syābhyudgamanasamayamupādāya yāvadastagamanasamayā[c], caṃkrama ucyate | āyatāni (āyatanāni) (|) vipulamāpite pṛthivīpradeśe gamanapratyāgamanapra[yoga]yuktaṃ | satkāyakarmaniṣadyā ucyate | yathāpīhaikatyo maṃcevā, pīṭhe vā, tṛṇasaṃstare vā niṣīdati | paryaṅkamābhujya | ṛjuṃ kāyaṃ praṇidhāyābhimukhīṃ smṛtimupasthāpya [|] āvaraṇānyucyante pañca nivaraṇāni | āvaraṇīyā dharmā ye nivaraṇasthānīyā dharmā nivaraṇāparakāste (

children.text: ) punaḥ katame | kāmachando (kāmacchando), vyāpāda[ḥ], styāna(naṃ), middhauddhatyaṃ, kaukṛtyaṃ, vicikitsā, [a]śubhatā, pratighanimittamandhakāraḥ, jñātijanapadāmaravitarkapaurāṇasya ca hasitakrīḍitarasitaparivāritasyānusmṛtiḥ, trayaścādhvānaḥ | tryadhvagatā cāyoniśo dharmacintā [|]
children.translated_text: ) And what are these? Sensual desire (<s>kāmacchanda</s>), ill-will (<s>vyāpāda</s>), sloth (<s>styāna</s>), torpor-and-restlessness (<s>middhauddhatya</s>), remorse (<s>kaukṛtya</s>), doubt (<s>vicikitsā</s>), [the perception of] the unattractive (<s>aśubhatā</s>), the sign of hostility, darkness, the recollection of laughter, play, conversation, and company of kinsmen, countrymen, and the deceased of former times, and the three periods of time — and improper mental attention (<s>ayoniśo dharmacintā</s>) regarding the three temporal periods.

body.translated_text: Therein, how does one purify the mind of obstructive qualities by walking meditation and sitting? 'Day' is said [to mean]: from the time of the rising of the sun until the time of its setting. 'Walking meditation' (<s>caṃkrama</s>) is said [to mean]: the practice of going back and forth in an extensive, spacious area of level ground. 'Sitting with proper bodily posture' (<s>niṣadyā</s>) is said [to mean]: just as here a certain person sits on a couch, or on a seat, or on a grass mat, having crossed the legs, holding the body upright, and establishing mindfulness before oneself. 'Obstructions' are said [to mean] the five hindrances (<s>nīvaraṇa</s>). 'Obstructive qualities' are the qualities that are the basis for the hindrances — those that are secondary to the hindrances.

body.text: ebhyaḥ kathaṃ caṃkramaṇacittaṃ pariśodhayati | katibhyaśca pariśodhayati [|] styānamiddhātsyānamiddhāhārakāccāvaraṇāt pariśodhayati | ālokanimittamanena sādhu ca, suṣṭhu ca, sugṛhītaṃ bhavati | sumanasikṛtaṃ, suja(ju)ṣṭaṃ | supratividdhaṃ | sa ālokasahagatena, suprabhāsasahagatena cittena channe vā, abhyavakāśe vā, caṃkrame caṃkramyamāṇaḥ (caṃkramamāṇaḥ), anyatamānyatamena prasadanīyenālambanena cittaṃ saṃdarśayati | samuttejayati | saṃpraharṣayati | yaduta buddhānusmṛtyā vā, dharmasaṃghaśīlatyāgadevatānusmṛtyā vā, (|) kāye vā punaranena styānamiddhādīnavapratisaṃyuktā dharmāḥ śrutā bhavantyadgṛhītā, dhṛtāḥ | tadyathā sūtraṃ, gū(ge)yaṃ, vyākaraṇaṃ, gāthodānanidānāvadānetivṛttakajātakavaipulyādbhutadharmopadeśā, yeṣu styānamiddhamamanekaparyāyeṇa vigarhitaṃ, vijugupsitaṃ [|] styānamiddhaprahāṇaṃ punaḥ (|)stutaṃ, varṇitaṃ, praśastaṃ [|] tān teṣāṃ vistareṇa svareṇa svādhyāyaṃ karoti | pareṣāmvā (

children.text: ) prakāśayatyarthamvā cintayati | tulayatyupaparīkṣate, diśo vā vyavalokayati | caturnakṣatragrahatārāsu vā dṛṣṭiṃ dhārayatyudakena mukhamākledayati | evamasya tatstyānamiddhaparyavasthānaṃ anutpannaṃ ca notpadyate, utpannaṃ ca prativigacchatyevamanena tasmādāvaraṇīyā[d] dharmāccittaṃ pariśodhitaṃ bhavati |
children.translated_text: ) he expounds them to others, or he reflects upon the meaning, weighs it, investigates it, or he looks at the directions, or he fixes his gaze upon the stars, planets, and constellations in the four [directions], or he moistens his face with water. Thus, for him, the mental state of sloth-and-torpor, when unarisen, does not arise, and when arisen, it subsides. In this way, his mind is purified from that obstructive quality.

body.translated_text: How does one purify the mind of these during walking meditation? And from how many does one purify? One purifies from sloth-and-torpor, from the nourishment of sloth-and-torpor, and from the obstruction [thereof]. The sign of light is well grasped, truly grasped, well attended to, well practiced, and well penetrated by him. With a mind accompanied by light, accompanied by radiance, whether under a roof or in the open, while walking in the walking-meditation [path], he inspires, uplifts, and gladdens the mind with one or another object that produces serenity — namely, through the recollection of the <s>Buddha</s>, or the recollection of the <s>Dharma</s>, the <s>Saṃgha</s>, moral discipline, generosity, and the deities. Furthermore, regarding sloth-and-torpor, the teachings concerning the danger [of it] have been heard by him, grasped, retained — namely, <s>sūtra</s>, <s>geya</s> (songs), <s>vyākaraṇa</s> (explanations), <s>gāthā</s> (verses), <s>udāna</s> (inspired utterances), <s>nidāna</s> (origins), <s>avadāna</s> (heroic tales), <s>itivṛttaka</s> (historical narratives), <s>jātaka</s> (birth stories), <s>vaipulya</s> (extensive discourses), <s>adbhutadharma</s> (marvelous teachings), and <s>upadeśa</s> (instructions) — in which sloth-and-torpor is condemned in many ways, criticized, and regarded with disgust, and the abandonment of sloth-and-torpor is praised, extolled, and commended. He recites those [texts] aloud in full detail, or

body.text: tatra niṣadyayā katamebhya āvaraṇīyebhyo dharmebhyaḥ [cittaṃ] pariśodhayati | kāmacchandād, vyāpādādauddhatyakaukṛtyādvicikitsāyāstadāhārakebhyaśca dharmebhyaḥ [|] sa utpanne vā kāmacchandaparyavasthāne prativinodanāyānutpanne vā dūrīkaraṇāya, niṣadya, paryaṅkamābhujya, ṛjuṃ kāyaṃ praṇidhāya, pratimukhāṃ (khīṃ) smṛtimupasthāpya, vinīlakaṃ vā, vipūyakamvā, vima(bha)drāma(tma)kamvā, vyādhmātakamvā, vi[khādi]takamvā, vilohitakamvā, asthiṃ (asthi) vā, śaṃkalikāṃ vā, anyatamānyatamaṃ vā bhadrakaṃ samādhinimittaṃ manasi karoti | ye vā dharmāḥ kāmarāgaprahāṇamevārabhya kāmarāgaprahāṇāyodgṛhītā bhavanti | dhṛtā, vacasā parijitā, manasā anvīkṣitā[ḥ], dṛṣṭyā supratividdhā[ḥ], tadyathā sūtraṃ, geyaṃ, vyākaraṇamiti vistareṇa pūrvavat | ye anekaparyāyeṇa kāmarāgaṃ, kāmacchandaṃ, (

children.text: ) kāmālayaṃ, kāmaniyantiṃ, kāmādhyavasānaṃ vigarhanti, vivarṇayanti | vijugupsayanti | kāmarāgaprahāṇamanekaparyāyeṇa stuvanti | varṇayanti, praśansa(śaṃsa)yanti | tāṃ (tān) dharmāṃstathā niṣaṇṇo [a]yoniśo manasi karotyevamasyānutpannaṃ ca kāmacchandaparyavasthānaṃ notpadyate | utpannaṃ ca kāmacchandaparyavasthānaṃ prativigacchati |
children.translated_text: ) sensual clinging, sensual delight, and sensual resolve are condemned in many ways, disparaged, and regarded with disgust; and the abandonment of sensual attachment is praised in many ways, extolled, and commended. Seated thus, one attends to those teachings properly. In this way, the mental state of sensual desire, when unarisen, does not arise; and when arisen, the mental state of sensual desire subsides.

body.translated_text: Therein, while sitting, from which obstructive qualities does one purify the mind? From sensual desire, from ill-will, from restlessness-and-remorse, from doubt, and from the qualities that nourish them. When the mental state of sensual desire has arisen — in order to dispel it; or when it has not yet arisen — in order to distance it; sitting down, having crossed the legs, holding the body upright, establishing mindfulness before oneself, one contemplates [the sign of] the blue-discolored [corpse], or the festering [corpse], or the gnawed [corpse], or the bloated [corpse], or the cut-up [corpse], or the blood-smeared [corpse], or a bone, or a chain of bones, or one or another auspicious <s>samādhi</s> sign. Or [one reflects upon] those teachings that have been grasped and retained specifically for the purpose of abandoning sensual attachment, rehearsed verbally, examined mentally, well penetrated by insight — namely, <s>sūtra</s>, <s>geya</s>, <s>vyākaraṇa</s>, and so on in detail as before — in which sensual attachment, sensual desire,

body.text: tatra vyāpāde ayamviśeṣaḥ | tathā niṣaṇṇo maitrīsahagatena cittenāvaireṇāsaṃpathenāvyābādhena, vipulena, mahadgatenāpramāṇena subhāvitenaikāṃ diśamadhimucya smāritvopa (smṛtvopa-)sampadya viharati | tathā dvitīyāṃ, tathā tṛtīyāṃ, tathā caturthīmityūrdhvamadhastiryaksarvamanantaṃ lokaṃ smāritvā (smṛtvā) upasampadya viharati | śeṣaṃ pūrvavat |
body.translated_text: Therein, regarding ill-will, this is the distinction: seated thus, with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness (<s>maitrī</s>) — without enmity, without conflict, without harm — vast, great, immeasurable, and well cultivated — one pervades one direction with determination and, having recollected it, abides [therein]. Likewise the second [direction], likewise the third, likewise the fourth — above, below, across — the entire infinite world, having recollected it, one abides. The rest is as before.

body.text: tatrauddhatyakaukṛtye viśeṣaḥ | tadyathā niṣaṇṇe adhyātmameva cittaṃ sthāpayati | saṃsthāpayati | samviṣodayati (saṃviśodhayati) | ekotīkaroti | samādhatte | śeṣaṃ pūrvavat |
body.translated_text: Therein, regarding restlessness-and-remorse, the distinction is: seated thus, one settles the mind inwardly, establishes it, purifies it, unifies it, and concentrates it. The rest is as before.

body.text: tatra vicikitsānivaraṇe viśeṣaḥ | tathā sanniṣaṇṇaḥ | atītamadhvānaṃ nāyoniśo manasikaroti | anāgataṃ pratyutpannamadhvānaṃ nāyoniśo manasikaroti | kiṃ nvahamabhūvamatīte [a]dhvani konvahamabhūvaṃ | āhosvinnāhamatīte [a]dhvani ko nvahamabhūvaṃ | kathaṃ (

children.text: ) nvahamabhūvamadī(tī)te 'dhvani [|] ko nvahaṃ bhaviṣyāmi | anāgate [a]dhvani, kathaṃ bhaviṣyāmyanāgate [a]dhvani, ke santaḥ ke bhaviṣyāmaḥ | ayaṃ satva (sattvaḥ) kuta āgataḥ | itaścyutaḥ kutragāmī bhaviṣyati | sa ityevaṃ rūpamayoniśomanasikāraṃ varjayitvā yoniśo manasi karoti | atītamadhvānamanātī(ga)taṃ pra[tyutpanna]mapyadhvānaṃ [|] sa dharmamātraṃ paśyati | vastumātraṃ | sacca sataḥ, asaccāsataḥ | hetumātraṃ, phalamātraṃ, nāsadbhūtaṃ samāropaṃ karoti | na sadvastu nāśayatyapaca(va)dati | bhūtaṃ bhūtato jānāti | yadutānityato vā, [duḥkhato] vā, śūnyato vā, [anātmato vā], anityeṣu, duḥkheṣu, śūnyeṣu, anātmasu dharmeṣu sa evaṃ yoniśo manasi kurvan, buddhe [a]pi niṣkāṅkṣo bhavati, nirvicikitsaḥ | dharme, saṃghe, duḥkhe, samudaye, nirodhe, mārge, hetau, hetusamutpanneṣu dharmeṣu niṣkāṅkṣo bhavati | nirvicikitsaḥ | śeṣaṃ pūrvavat |
children.translated_text: ) was I in the past? Who shall I become in the future? How shall I be in the future? Being what, what shall we become? This being — where did he come from? Having departed from here, where will he go?' Having abandoned such improper mental attention, one attends properly — to the past, the future, and the present. One sees only phenomena, only entities — existing from what exists, non-existing from what does not exist — only causes, only effects. One does not make a false superimposition upon what is not real; one does not destroy or reject what is a real entity. One knows the real as it truly is — namely, as impermanent, [as suffering,] as empty, [as non-self.] With respect to phenomena that are impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, attending properly thus, one becomes free from doubt regarding the <s>Buddha</s>, free from hesitation; regarding the <s>Dharma</s>, the <s>Saṃgha</s>, suffering, the origin, cessation, the path, the cause, and phenomena arisen from causes — one becomes free from doubt, free from hesitation. The rest is as before.

body.translated_text: Therein, regarding the hindrance of doubt, the distinction is: seated thus, one does not attend improperly to the past, nor to the future, nor to the present: 'Did I exist in the past? Who was I in the past? Or did I not exist in the past? Who was I? How

body.text: tatra vyāpāde vaktavyaṃ | yo [a]nena pratighaṃ pratighanimittaṃ cārabhya, tasya ca prahāṇāya, dharmā udgṛhītā iti vistaraḥ [|]
body.translated_text: Therein, regarding ill-will, this should be stated: those teachings that have been grasped by him concerning hostility and the sign of hostility, and for their abandonment — as stated in detail.

body.text: auddhatyakaukṛtye vaktavyaṃ | anenauddhatyakaukṛtyamārabhya (

children.text: ) tasya ca prahāṇāya dharmā udgṛhītā iti vistareṇa pūrvavat |
children.translated_text: ) and for their abandonment — as stated in detail, as before.

body.translated_text: Regarding restlessness-and-remorse, this should be stated: [the teachings grasped] by him concerning restlessness-and-remorse,

body.text: vicikitsāyāmvaktavyaṃ | ye anena vicikitsāmārabhya tasyāśca prahāṇāya dharmā udgṛhītā iti vistareṇa pūrvavadityanena kāmacha(ccha)ndanivaraṇād vyāpādastyānamiddhauddhatyakaukṛtyavicikitsānivaraṇā[c] cittaṃ viśodhitaṃ bhavati | tadāhārakebhyaśca dharmebhya āvaraṇīyebhyastenāha caṃkramaniṣadyābhyāmāvaraṇīyebhyo dharmebhyaścittaṃ pariśodhayati |
body.translated_text: Regarding doubt, this should be stated: those teachings that have been grasped by him concerning doubt and for its abandonment — as stated in detail, as before. By this, the mind is purified from the hindrance of sensual desire, from the hindrances of ill-will, sloth-and-torpor, restlessness-and-remorse, and doubt, and from the obstructive qualities that nourish them. Therefore it is said: 'By walking meditation and sitting, one purifies the mind from obstructive qualities.'

body.text: yā caiṣā dharmādhipateyā āvaraṇīyebhyo dharmebhyaścittasya pariśodhanā [|] asti punarātmādhipateyā, lokādhipateyā cāvaraṇīyebhyo dharmebhyaścitta pariśodhanā [|]
body.translated_text: This purification of the mind from obstructive qualities has the <s>Dharma</s> as its governing principle. Is there also a purification of the mind from obstructive qualities with the self as governing principle and with the world as governing principle?

body.text: ātmādhipateyā katamā | yathāpi tadutpanne anyatamānyatamasminnivaraṇe ātmata eva pratirūpatāmviditvā, utpannaṃ nivaraṇaṃ nādhivāsayate (ti) | prajahāti, vinodayati, vyantīkaroti | tena nivaraṇenātmānaṃ na jñāyamānaḥ, cetasa upakleśakareṇa, prajñādaurbalyakareṇa, vighātapakṣyeṇaivamasāvātmānamevādhipatiṃ kṛtvā āvaraṇīyebhyo dharmebhyaścittaṃ pariśodhayati |
body.translated_text: Which is the one with the self as governing principle? Just as, when any one of the hindrances has arisen, knowing from oneself what is proper, one does not tolerate the arisen hindrance; one abandons it, dispels it, eliminates it. Through that hindrance, one does not allow oneself to be known as one afflicted by a defilement of the mind, by what weakens wisdom, by what belongs to the side of harm. Thus, making the self itself the governing principle, one purifies the mind from obstructive qualities.

body.text: kathaṃ lokamadhipatiṃ kṛtvā āvaraṇīyebhyo dharmebhyaścittaṃ pariśodhayati | ihāsyā (sya) nivaraṇe (

children.text: ) samutpanne, utpattikāle vā pratyupasthite | evaṃ bhavatyahaṃ cedanutpannaṃ nivaraṇamutpādayeyaṃ, śāstā me apavaded, devatā api, vijñā api, sabrahmacāriṇo [a]dharmatayā vigarhayeyuriti | sa lokamevādhipatiṃ kṛtvā āvaraṇīyebhyo dharmebhyaścittaṃ pariśodhayati | ihāsya nivaraṇe samutpanne, utpattikāle vā pratyupasthite, evaṃ bhavatyahaṃ cedanutpannaṃ nivaraṇamutpādayeyaṃ | śāstā me apavaded, devatā api | vijñā api, sabrahmacāriṇo [a]dharmatayā vigarhayeyuriti | sa lokamevādhipatiṃ kṛtvā, anutpannaṃ ca nivaraṇaṃ notpādayati, utpannaṃ ca prajahāti | evaṃ lokamadhipatiṃ kṛtvā āvaraṇīyebhyo dharmebhyaścittaṃ pariśodhayati | śayanāsanapratiguptyarthaṃ punarlokācārañcānuvṛtto bhaviṣyatīti yāvadrātryāḥ prathame yāme caṃkramaniṣadyābhyāmāvaraṇīyebhyo dharmebhyaścittaṃ pariśodhayati | āvaraṇīyebhyo dharmebhyaścittaṃ pariśodhya bahirvihārasya pādau prakṣālayati | prakṣālya, vihāraṃ praviśya, śayyāṃ kalpayati | yāvadeva svasyo (yau)pacayikānāmmahābhūtānāṃ upacayāya [|] upacito [a]yaṃ kāyaḥ karmaṇyataraśca bhaviṣyati | anukūlataraśca sātatyenai[ka]pakṣye kuśalapakṣaprayoge |
children.translated_text: ) has arisen, or when the time of arising is imminent, one thinks: 'If I were to allow an unarisen hindrance to arise, the Teacher would reprove me, the deities too, the wise too, and my fellow practitioners would censure me for unrighteousness.' Making the world itself the governing principle, one purifies the mind from obstructive qualities. Here, when a hindrance has arisen, or when the time of arising is imminent, one thinks: 'If I were to allow an unarisen hindrance to arise, the Teacher would reprove me, the deities too, the wise too, and my fellow practitioners would censure me for unrighteousness.' Making the world itself the governing principle, one does not allow the unarisen hindrance to arise, and one abandons what has arisen. Thus, making the world the governing principle, one purifies the mind from obstructive qualities. For the purpose of protecting the sleeping-quarters, and furthermore, following the conventions of the world — throughout the first watch of the night, one purifies the mind from obstructive qualities by walking meditation and sitting. Having purified the mind from obstructive qualities, one washes the feet outside the dwelling; having washed them, one enters the dwelling and prepares the bed — just for the restoration of one's own physical great elements; the body thus restored will become more workable and more conducive to constant, one-sided effort in the wholesome course of practice.

body.translated_text: How does one purify the mind from obstructive qualities making the world the governing principle? Here, when a hindrance

body.text: kenakāraṇena pārśvena śayyāṃ kalpayati | (

children.text: ) siṃhasya prāṇinaḥ sādharmyeṇa [|] kiṃ punaratra sādharmyaṃ [|] siṃhaḥ prāṇaṃ (prāṇī) sarveṣāṃ tiryagyonigatānāṃ prāṇināṃ vikrānta, utsāhī, dṛḍhaparākramaḥ | bhikṣurapi jāgarikānuyukta ārabdhavīryo viharati | vikrānta, utsāhī, dṛḍhaparākramaḥ | atastasya siṃhopamaiva śayyā pratirūpā bhavadi(ti), no tu pretaśayyā, devaśayyā, na kā[ma]bhogaśayyā | tathā hi te sarva eva kusīdā, hīnavīryā, ca(ma)ndabalaparākramāḥ | api tu dharmataiṣā yaddakṣiṇena pārśvena siṃhopamāṃ śayyāṃ kalpayato na tathā gātrāṇāṃ vikṣepo bhavati | na ca śayānasya smṛtisaṃpramoṣo bhavati | na ca gāḍhaṃ svapiti | pāpakāṃśca svapnāṃ (pnān) na paśyati | anyathā tu śayyāṃ kalpayato viparyayeṇa sarve doṣā veditavyāḥ | tenāha dakṣiṇena pārśvena śayyāṃ kalpayati |
children.translated_text: by analogy with the lion among living beings. What then is the analogy here? The lion, among living beings, is valiant, energetic, and of firm exertion among all beings born in the animal realm. Likewise, the <s>bhikṣu</s> devoted to wakefulness dwells with aroused vigor — valiant, energetic, and of firm exertion. Therefore the lion-posture alone is fitting for him, and not the posture of <s>pretas</s> (hungry ghosts), nor the posture of <s>devas</s> (gods), nor the posture of sensual indulgence. For all of those are lazy, of feeble vigor, and of weak exertion. Moreover, it is a natural law (<s>dharmatā</s>) that when one prepares the lion-posture on the right side, there is not such restlessness of the limbs, nor does one lose mindfulness while sleeping, nor does one sleep heavily, nor does one see evil dreams. But when one prepares the bed in another manner, all the opposite faults should be understood. Therefore the text says: 'one prepares the bed on the right side.'

body.translated_text: For what reason does one prepare the bed on one's side?

body.text: ālokanimittamanena sūdgṛhītaṃ bhavati | sumanasikṛtaṃ | sujuṣṭaṃ, supratividdhaṃ | yadeva manasi kurvan sa prabhā sahagatena cittena śayyāṃ kalpayati | suptasyāpi cāsya yena na bhavati cetasaḥ [|] andhakārāyitatvamevamālokasaṃjñīśayyāṃ kalpayati |
body.translated_text: The sign of light (<s>ālokanimittam</s>) has been well grasped by him, well attended to in mind, well practiced, and well penetrated. Accordingly, keeping this in mind, he prepares his bed with a mind accompanied by radiance. And even while sleeping, his consciousness does not become enveloped in darkness. In this way, he prepares his bed with the perception of light.

body.text: kathaṃ smṛta[ḥ] śayyāṃ kalpayati | ya (ye) anenadharmā[ḥ] śrutā bhavanti | cintitā, bhāvitā vā, (

children.text: ) kuśalā arthopasaṃhitāstadanvayā [a]sya smṛtiryāvatsvapanakālānuvarttinī bhavati | yathāsya suptasyāpi ta eva dharmā jāgrato vā abhilapanti, teṣveva ca dharmeṣu taccittaṃ bahulamanuvicarati | iti yathāsmṛtyā yathāsmṛtaḥ | kuśalacittaśayyāṃ kalpayati | avyākṛtacitto vā [|] evaṃ smṛtaḥ śayyāṃ kalpayati |
children.translated_text: wholesome and connected with beneficial meaning — his mindfulness that follows those teachings persists even during sleep. Just as, even while sleeping, those same teachings that were present while awake are expressed in his mind, and his mind frequently dwells upon those very teachings — thus, through mindfulness as mindfulness operates, he prepares his bed with a wholesome state of mind, or with an indeterminate (<s>avyākṛta</s>) state of mind. In this way, one prepares the bed mindfully.

body.translated_text: How does one prepare the bed mindfully? Whatever <s>dharmas</s> (teachings) have been heard by him, reflected upon, or cultivated —

body.text: kathaṃ saṃprajānanto (jānan) śayyāṃ kalpayati | suptasyāsya tathā smṛtasya yasminsamaye [a]nyatamānyatamenopakleśena cetasaḥ saṃkleśo bhavati | sa utpadyamānameva taṃ saṃkleśaṃ samyageva prajānāti, nādhivāsayati, prajahāti, pratividhyati | pratyudāvarttayati mānasaṃ | tenocyate saṃprajānaṃ(nan) śayyāṃ kalpayati |
body.translated_text: How does one prepare the bed with clear comprehension (<s>saṃprajānan</s>)? When, at any time during sleep, while he is thus mindful, defilement of the mind occurs through one or another of the secondary afflictions (<s>upakleśa</s>), he correctly comprehends that defilement the very moment it arises, does not tolerate it, abandons it, counteracts it, and turns the mind away from it. Therefore it is said that one prepares the bed with clear comprehension.

body.text: kathamutthānasaṃjñāmeva manasikurvan śayyāṃ kalpayati | sa vīryasaṃpragṛhītaṃ cittaṃ kṛtvā śayyāṃ kalpayati | supratibuddhikayā suharṣakta (suhṛṣṭacitta)stadyathā āraṇyako mṛgaḥ | no tu sarveṇa sarvaṃ viddhamavakramaṇanimnaṃ cittaṃ karoti | tatpravaṇaṃ | na tatprābho (bhā)ramapi (|) cāsyaivaṃ bhavati | aho batāhaṃ buddhānujñātāṃ jāgaritāṃ (kāṃ)sarveṇa sarvaṃ sarvathā sampādayeyamiti | tasyāśca sampādanārthaṃ tvāśaṃsena, rasena, prayogeṇa, chandagato viharatyabhiyuktaśca [|] api cāsyaivaṃ bhavati | yathāhamadya (

children.text: ) jāgarikārthamārabdhavīryo vyahārṣaṃ, kuśalānāñca dharmāṇāṃ bhāvanāyai, dakṣo [a]nalasa, utthānasampannaḥ, śvaḥ prabhāte, nirgatāyāṃ ca rajanyāṃ, bhūyasyā mātrayā ārabdhavīryo vihariṣyāmi utthānasampanna iti | tatraikayā utthānasaṃjñayā gāḍhaṃ svapiti | yenāhaṃ (yaṃ) śaknoti laghu laghveva utthānakāle utthātuṃ, na kālātikrāntaṃ pratibudhyati | dvitīyayotthānasaṃjñayā buddhānujñātāṃ siṃ[haśa]yyāṃ kalpayatyanyūnāmanadhikāṃ | tṛtīyayotthānasaṃjñayā chandaṃna sransa(sraṃsa)yati | sati smṛtisaṃpramoṣe, satyuttaratrottaratra samādānāya prayukto bhavati | evamutthānasaṃjñāmeva manasi kurvan śayyāṃ kalpayati |
children.translated_text: I was vigorous and joyful for the purpose of wakefulness, and for the cultivation of wholesome qualities — dexterous, not lazy, endowed with enterprise — so too tomorrow morning, when the night has passed, I shall dwell with even greater vigor, endowed with enterprise.' Therein, by the first perception of rising, he does not sleep heavily, whereby he is able to rise lightly and swiftly at the time of rising and does not awaken after the proper time has passed. By the second perception of rising, he prepares the lion-posture approved by the <s>Buddhas</s>, neither deficient nor excessive. By the third perception of rising, he does not let his zeal (<s>chanda</s>) slacken; and should there be a loss of mindfulness, he strives for ever-higher commitments. In this way, one prepares the bed while keeping the thought of rising in mind.

body.translated_text: How does one prepare the bed while keeping the thought of rising in mind (<s>utthānasaṃjñā</s>)? He prepares the bed having made the mind firm with vigor, with a well-awakened and joyful mind — like a forest-dwelling deer. He does not make the mind entirely sunken, inclined toward sinking, or tending toward it, nor does he give it excessive weight. And furthermore, this thought occurs to him: 'Oh, may I in every way and in all respects fully accomplish the wakefulness approved by the <s>Buddhas</s>!' And for the sake of accomplishing that, with aspiration, with relish, with effort, and with zeal, he dwells engaged [in practice]. Moreover, this thought occurs to him: 'Just as today

body.text: sa rātryāḥ paścime yāme laghu laghveva prativibudhyāvaraṇīyebhyo dharmebhyaścittaṃ pariśodhayatīti | paścimo yāma uccate | yo [a]pararātraḥ sātirekapraharaṃ (raḥ) | sa cāyamālokasaṃjñī smṛtaḥ | saṃprajāna[n], utthānasaṃjñāmeva manasi kurvan, madhyamaṃ yāmaṃ sātirekaṃ praharaṃ middhamavakrāmayitvā (krāmya), yasmiṃ (smin) samaye vyuttiṣṭhate | tatra tasmiṃ (smin) samaye vyuttiṣṭhate | karmaṇyakāyo bhavati | utthāya, nādhimātreṇa styānamiddhaparyavasthānenābhibhūtaḥ | yenāsyottiṣṭhato dhandhāyitatvaṃ vā syānmaṃdāyitacca(tva)mvā, ālasyakausīdyamvā [|] asati vā (

children.text: ) punastasmindhandhāyitatve, mandāyitatve, ālasyakausīdye, laghu laghvevotthānaṃ bhavatyābhogamātrādeva no saṃgrāmaṃ vā kṛtvā āvaraṇīyebhyo dharmebhyaḥ pariśuddhiḥ pūrvavadvedi tavyāḥ (vyā) | ayaṃ tāvatpūrvarātrāparaṃrātraṃ jāgarikānuyogasya vistaravibhāgaḥ |
children.translated_text: that sluggishness, dullness, laziness, or indolence, rising occurs lightly and swiftly, by mere inclination of attention alone, without having to wage a battle [against torpor]. The purification from obstructive qualities should be understood as before. This is the detailed analysis of devotion to wakefulness in the first and last watches of the night.

body.translated_text: The text says: 'In the last watch of the night, rising lightly and swiftly, one purifies the mind from obstructive qualities.' The last watch is said to be the latter part of the night, slightly more than one <s>prahara</s> (three-hour watch). And this person, with the perception of light, mindful, clearly comprehending, keeping the thought of rising in mind, having entered sleep for the middle watch — slightly more than one <s>prahara</s> — at whatever time he awakens, at that very time he rises. His body becomes workable upon rising, and he is not overwhelmed by an excessive degree of the sloth-and-torpor obstruction, such that upon rising there would be sluggishness, dullness, laziness, or indolence. Or, in the absence of

body.text: samāsārthāḥ punaḥ katame | iha jāgarikāyogamanuyuktasya puruṣapudgalasya catvāri samyakkaraṇīyāni bhavanti | katamāni catvāri | yāvajjāgrati (gati) tāvatkuśalapakṣaṃ na riṃcati | sātatyenai[ka]pakṣyakuśaladharmabhāvanāyāṃ kālena ca śayyāṃ kalpayati | nākālena | suptaścāsaṃkliṣṭacitto middhamavakrāmayati | na saṃkliṣṭacittaḥ [|] kālena ca prativibudhyate(ti) | notthānakālamativartate | itīmāni catvāri samyakkaraṇīyānyāramya bhagavatā śrāvakāṇāṃ jāgarikānuyogo deśitaḥ |
body.translated_text: What then are the summarized meanings? Here, for a person devoted to the practice of wakefulness, there are four things to be done correctly. Which four? As long as one is awake, one does not abandon the wholesome side; one constantly cultivates wholesome qualities belonging to the one [correct] side; one prepares the bed at the proper time, not at an improper time; having slept, one enters sleep with an undefiled mind, not with a defiled mind; and one awakens at the proper time, not allowing the time for rising to pass. These are the four things to be done correctly, on the basis of which the Blessed One taught the disciples the devotion to wakefulness.
