children.translated_text: a discourse should be given using varied, engaging, powerful, and eloquent modes of expression. When that discourse is being given, if the listener is of the <s>Śrāvaka</s> lineage (<s>gotra</s>), he is exceedingly delighted, joyful, glad, and happy with that discourse. He is [not merely] pleased — he becomes deeply convinced. But when a discourse connected with the <s>Mahāyāna</s> is being given, one who is of the <s>Mahāyāna</s> lineage is exceedingly delighted, joyful, and up to being deeply convinced and persuaded, whereas one of the <s>Śrāvaka</s> or <s>Pratyekabuddha</s> [lineage] is not so affected. If, furthermore, the listener is of soft faculties, he is exceedingly delighted, but for the discernment, grasping, and penetration of the meaning of the <s>Dharma</s> [he is slow]. One of middling faculties is not [so limited], but one of sharp faculties swiftly discerns, grasps, and penetrates the <s>Dharma</s> even when a profound discourse is being given. If, furthermore, the listener is of passionate temperament, when a faith-inspiring discourse is being given, he is exceedingly pleased and delighted, and even enters into meditation. His body displays tears, a tender disposition, a soft mind, and a pliant mind. If one is of hateful temperament, when a penetrating discourse connected with <s>Nirvāṇa</s> is being given, he attains a non-sensual state of spiritual urgency. As was stated for one of soft faculties, so too should it be understood here. If one is of the temperament that follows the <s>Dharma</s>, he understands the meaning and listens with care, but does not lend his ear; he does not establish a mind of wisdom as fully. Even

children.text: ) āvarjito 'pi na tathā sānukāramanuprayacchati | sa cetpunarvicarito (rvicārānucarito) bhavati | tasya svavahitasyāpi cittaṃ vikṣipyate | durgṛhītagrāhī bhavati | na dṛḍhaṃ gṛhṇāti | na sthiraṃ, udgṛhītañca nāśayati | na puna[ḥ] kaya(tha)yā paripṛcchana kaśca bhavati | evaṃ kathayā | gotramindriyaṃ caritaṃ ca samanveṣitavyaṃ | kathaṃ ceṣṭayā [|] yāni pūrvoktāni liṃgāni | śrāvakagotrasya, rāgacaritānāṃ ca pudgalānāṃ tāni ceṣṭetyucyate | tayā ca ceṣṭayā yathāyogaṃ gotramindriyaṃ caritaṃ ca samanveṣitavyaṃ |
children.translated_text: when drawn in, he does not respond with imitation in the same way. If, furthermore, one is of the discursive temperament, even when attentive, his mind becomes distracted. He grasps poorly, does not grasp firmly, does not grasp steadily, and loses what he has grasped. He is not one who asks questions about the discourse. In this way, through discourse, the lineage, the faculties, and the temperament are to be investigated. And how through behavior? The signs previously described — those of the <s>Śrāvaka</s> lineage and of persons of passionate temperament — these are called behavior. And through that behavior, the lineage, faculties, and temperament are to be investigated as appropriate.

body.translated_text: How should one be examined through questioning regarding <s>gotra</s> (lineage), faculties, and temperament? One should ask thus: 'Does the Venerable One know his own <s>gotra</s>, faculties, or temperament? Of what <s>gotra</s> am I? What are my faculties — soft, middling, or sharp? Am I of passionate temperament, or of hateful temperament?' — and likewise: 'Am I of discursive temperament?' If that person is wise, and his <s>gotra</s>, faculties, and temperament have been previously observed and noted through sequential [self-]analysis, then he will declare just that. But if he is capable yet has not previously observed or noted [these traits] through sequential [analysis], and does not declare [them] when asked — then his temperament at least may have been observed. In that case, the three [aspects of <s>gotra</s>, faculties, and temperament] should be further examined through conversation. Before him, [teachings] connected with the <s>Śrāvakayāna</s> (

body.text: tatra kathaṃ cetaḥparyāyajñānena gotrendriyacaritāni samanveṣitavyāni | yathāpi sa yogī yogajño lābhī bhavati cetaḥ paryāyajñānasya [|] sa tena paracittajñānena gotramindriyaṃ, caritaṃ ca yathābhūtaṃ prajānāti | (

children.text:
) etāni catvāri sthānānyebhiścaturbhiḥ kāraṇaissamanveṣya pañcasu sthāneṣu vinayate | tadyathā samādhisaṃbhārarakṣopacaye, prāvivekye, cittaikāgratāyāḥ(yāṃ), āvaraṇaviśuddhau, manaskārabhāvanāyāṃ ca | tatra samādhisaṃbhārarakṣopacayaḥ yāvatā śīlasamvareṇa samanvāgato bhavati | tatra
cāpramādavihārī bhavatyapapariṇāya buddhānuśiṣṭasya ca buddhānujñātasya pudgalasya, śīlaskandhasya śikśāpadapratipattyā vīryaṃ na sransa (sraṃsa)yati | evamayamavigatācchīlapratisamvarācchi kṣāmārgānna parihīyate | anadhigataṃ ca śikṣāmārgamadhigacchati | yathā śīlasamvara evamindriyasamvaraḥ, bhojane mātrajñatā, pūrvarātrāpararātraṃ jāgarikānuyogaḥ, saṃprajānadvihāritā, evaṃ yāvacchramaṇālaṃkāra iti | yasya yasya saṃbhāraparigṛhītasya dharmapravibhāgasya lābhī bhavati | sa taṃ vā rakṣatyuttari (raṃ) ca pravibhāgasya pāripūraye | yathoktādbhūrādhikakasamudācārāya [c]chandajāto viherayu(ret) mu(mū)kajāta ārubdhavīryaścāyamucyate samādhisaṃbhārarakṣopacayaḥ | sa evaṃ hānabhāgīyāṃśca dharmān virajyati, śeṣabhāgīyāṃśca dharmān pratiṣevamāṇaḥ praviviktavihārī bhavati |
children.translated_text: Having investigated these four matters by means of these four causes, one trains [the student] in five areas, namely: the accumulation and guarding of the prerequisites for <s>samādhi</s>, seclusion, one-pointedness of mind, purification from obstructions, and the cultivation of mental attention. Therein, the accumulation and guarding of the prerequisites for <s>samādhi</s>: insofar as one is endowed with moral restraint (<s>śīlasamvara</s>), one dwells therein with diligence, not declining — and as a person instructed and approved by the <s>Buddha</s>, one does not let vigor slacken in the practice of the rules of the moral aggregate. Thus, not having departed from the moral restraint, one does not fall away from the path of training, and one attains the path of training not yet attained. Just as with moral restraint, so too with sense-restraint, moderation in eating, devotion to wakefulness in the first and last watches, and dwelling with clear comprehension — all up to the ornaments of an ascetic. Whatever provisions of the <s>Dharma</s>-analysis one has obtained, one guards those and strives for the further fulfillment of those provisions. One who dwells with desire for proper conduct arising from what has been described and beyond, with eagerness, with aroused vigor — this is called 'the accumulation and guarding of the prerequisites for <s>samādhi</s>.' Thus, turning away from states that lead to decline, and cultivating states that lead to the remainder [of attainment], one becomes a dweller in seclusion.

body.translated_text: Therein, how are the lineage, faculties, and temperament to be investigated through the knowledge of others' minds (<s>cetaḥparyāyajñāna</s>)? When a <s>yogī</s> who is skilled in <s>yoga</s> attains the knowledge of others' minds, through that knowledge of others' minds he correctly knows the lineage, the faculties, and the temperament as they truly are.

body.text: prāvivekyaṃ katamat | yā sthānasampadīryāpathasampat | tatra sthānasampattadyathā | araṇyamvā, vṛkṣamūlamvā, śūnyāgāramvā-tatra parvatakandaraṃ vā, giriguhā vā, palālapuṃjāni vā śūnyāgāramityucyate | tatra vanaprasthaṃ vṛkṣamūlamityucyate | tatrābhyavakāśaṃ, śmaśānaṃ, prāntaśca śayanāsanamaraṇyamityucyate | tadidamabhisamasya sthānaṃ veditavyaṃ | yadutāraṇyavṛkṣamūlaśūnyāgāraparvatagiriguhāpalālapuṃjābhyavakāśaśmaśānavanaprasthāni prāntāni śayanāsanāni | sthānasampatpunaḥ pañcavidhā | iha sthānamādita evābhirūpaṃ bhavati | darśanīyaṃ prāsādikamārāmasampannaṃ, vanasampannaṃ, puṣkariṇīsampannaṃ, śubhaṃ, ramaṇīyaṃ, notkūlanikūlaṃ, na sthāṇukaṇṭakadhānaṃ | na bahupāṣāṇaśarkarakapālaṃ | yatrāsya dṛṣṭavā cittamabhiprasīdati | vāsāya, prahāṇāya, prayogāya | hṛṣṭacittaḥ | pramuditacittaḥ | prahāṇaṃ pradadhāti iyaṃ prathamā sthānasampat | punarayaṃ (ridaṃ) na divā alpavilokaṃ bhavati | rātrāvalpaśabdavanyanirghoṣamalpadaṃśamaśakavātātapasarīsṛpasaṃsparśamiyaṃdvitīyā sthānasampat | yatpunaraparaṃ siṃhavyāghradvīpitaskaraparacakramanuṣyāmanuṣyabhayabhairavāpagataṃbhavati | yatra viśvasto niḥśaṃkitamānasaḥ | sukhaṃ sparśaṃ viharati | itīyaṃ tṛtīyā sthānasampat | (

children.text: ) punaraparaṃ ye te ānulomikā jīvitapariṣkārāścī varādayaḥ | te [a]trālpakṛcchreṇa sampadyante | yenāyaṃ piṇḍakena na klāmyati | yatrāsamvidhāna iyaṃ caturthī sthānasampat | punarapatraṃ(raṃ) kalyāṇamitraparigṛhītaṃ bhavati | tadrūpā atra vijñāḥ sabrahmacāriṇaḥ prativasanti | yesyākṛtāni nottānīkurvanti | gaṃbhīraṃ cārthapadaṃ prajñayā pratividhya suṣṭhu ca prakāśayanti | jñānadarśanasya viśuddhaye | iyaṃ pañcamī sthānasampat |
children.translated_text: Furthermore, the life-requisites such as robes and the like are obtained there with little difficulty, so that one is not exhausted by alms-begging, and there is no lack of provisions. This is the fourth excellence of place. Furthermore, the place is attended by good spiritual friends; therein dwell wise fellow practitioners of the holy life, who do not leave unclear what is obscure, and who, having penetrated the profound meaning and expression with wisdom, explain it well — for the purification of knowledge and vision. This is the fifth excellence of place.

body.translated_text: What is seclusion (<s>prāvivekya</s>)? It is the excellence of place and the excellence of posture. Therein, excellence of place is as follows: a forest, the root of a tree, or an empty house — therein, a mountain cave or grotto or straw-heap is called an 'empty house'; therein, a forest clearing is called 'root of a tree'; therein, an open space, a cremation ground, and remote lodgings are called 'forest.' Comprehending all this, the place should be understood as follows: namely, forests, tree-roots, empty houses, mountain caves, grottoes, straw-heaps, open spaces, cremation grounds, forest clearings, and remote lodgings. The excellence of place is fivefold. Here, the place is from the very beginning beautiful, pleasing, gracious, endowed with a garden, endowed with a forest, endowed with a lotus-pond, pure, delightful, neither hilly nor sunken, free from stumps, thorns, and weeds, without many stones, pebbles, or potsherds — where, upon seeing it, one's mind becomes pleased for dwelling, for abandonment, and for practice; with a joyful and delighted mind, one undertakes the effort of abandonment. This is the first excellence of place. Furthermore, this place is not excessively disturbed during the day; at night, it is free from excessive noise and forest clamor, with few mosquitoes, flies, wind, sun-heat, and contact with creeping creatures. This is the second excellence of place. Furthermore, it is free from the fear and terror of lions, tigers, leopards, thieves, hostile armies, and both human and non-human dangers — where one dwells confidently, with an untroubled mind, in comfortable ease. This is the third excellence of place.

body.text: tatra katamā īryāpathasampat | divā caṃkrameṇa vātināmayati | niṣadya yāvatā evaṃ rātryāḥ prathamaṃ yāmaṃ, madhyame na (ca) yāme dakṣiṇena pārśvena (ṇa) śayyāṃ kalpayati | paścime ca yāme laghulaghvevottiṣṭhate | caṃkramaniṣadyayā vātināmayati | tasminnidaṃ sampanne śayanāsane, tathā buddhānujñāte mañce vā, pīṭhe vā, tṛṇe vā, saṃstaraṇe vā niṣīdati | paryaṅkamābhujya tu | kena kāraṇena pañca kāraṇāni samanupaśyan saṃpiṇḍitena kāyena praśrabdhirutpadyate | praśrabdhyutpattaye anukūloyamīryāpatha (

children.text: ) iti | tathā cārikā [kā]laṃ niṣadyayāśakto vyatināmayituṃ | nā cāsyāneneryāpathena kāyakleśo bhavati | tathā asādhāraṇoyamīryāpathonyatīrthikaiḥ | parapravādibhiḥ | tathā pare aneneryāpathena niṣaṇṇaṃ dṛṣṭvā atyarthamabhiprasīdanti buddhaiśca buddhaśrāvakaiścāyaṃ īryāpatho niṣevitaścānujñātaśca [|] imāni paṃcakāraṇāni | saṃpaśyati niṣīdati | paryaṅkamābhujya ṛjuṃ kāyaṃ praṇidhāya |
children.translated_text: Also, when one is unable to spend the walking period in sitting, there is no bodily fatigue from this posture. Also, this posture is not shared with other sectarians or teachers of other doctrines. Also, when others see one seated in this posture, they are exceedingly pleased. And this posture has been practiced and approved by the <s>Buddhas</s> and the disciples of the <s>Buddhas</s>. Seeing these five reasons, one sits with legs crossed, holding the body upright.

body.translated_text: Therein, what is the excellence of posture (<s>īryāpathasampat</s>)? During the day, one spends the time in walking and sitting. Likewise, in the first watch of the night; in the middle watch, one prepares the bed on the right side; and in the last watch of the night, one rises lightly and swiftly and spends the time in walking and sitting. In that excellent and accomplished lodging, as approved by the <s>Buddha</s>, one sits on a bed, a chair, on grass, or on a mat, having crossed the legs. For what reason? Seeing five reasons, with the body folded together, tranquility (<s>praśrabdhi</s>) arises; this posture is conducive to the arising of tranquility.

body.text: tatra katamā kāyasaṃjñatā | kāyasya spaṣṭocchritapraṇihitatā | cittena na niḥśocyena kuhanāpagatenārjavena | tatra ṛjunā kāyena pragṛhītena styānamiddhaṃ cittaṃ na paryādāya tiṣṭhati | niṣkuhakena citte bahirdhā vikṣepo na paryādāya tiṣṭhati | pratimukhāṃ (khīṃ) smṛtimupasthāpya |
body.translated_text: Therein, what is bodily composure (<s>kāyasaṃjñatā</s>)? It is the clear, erect, and settled posture of the body — with a mind that is not distressed, free from hypocrisy, and straight. Therein, with the body held upright, sloth-and-torpor does not overwhelm the mind. And with freedom from hypocrisy, outward distraction does not overwhelm the mind. One establishes mindfulness face-to-face (<s>pratimukhī smṛti</s>).

body.text: tatra katamā pratimukhā(khī) smṛtiḥ | yāmupasthāpayati yoniśo manasikārasaṃprayuktā smṛtiḥ pra[ti]mukhe (khī)tyucyate | sarvakṛṣṇapakṣapramukhatayā, prativilomatayā | api ca samādhinimittālambanā pratibhālambanā smṛtiḥ pratimukhe (khī) tyucyate | sarvasamāhitabhūmikālambanapramukhatayā iyamucyate īryāpathasampat |
body.translated_text: Therein, what is face-to-face mindfulness (<s>pratimukhī smṛti</s>)? The mindfulness that one establishes, conjoined with proper mental attention (<s>yoniśo manaskāra</s>), is called 'face-to-face' because it is foremost in opposing and countering the entire dark side [of unwholesome states]. Moreover, mindfulness that has as its object the sign of <s>samādhi</s> and the object of counterimage is called 'face-to-face' because it is foremost among all objects belonging to the concentrated level. This is called the excellence of posture.

body.text: vyapakarṣaḥ katamaḥ | āha | dvividhaḥ kāyavyapakarṣaḥ | cittavyapakarṣaśca | tatra kāyavyapakarṣo yo gṛhasthapravrajitaiḥ sārdhamavihāritā || tatra cittavyapakarṣaḥ yaḥ kliṣṭamavyākṛtaṃ ca manaskāraṃ ca varjayitvā | samāhitabhūmikaṃ vā samādhisaṃbhāraprāyogikaṃ vā manaskāraṃ bhāvayati | kuśalamarthopasaṃhitamayamucyate cittavyapakarṣaḥ | tatra sthānasampat yā ceyamīryāpathasampat | yaścāyaṃ kāyavyakarṣaḥ | yaśca cittavyapakarṣaḥ (yaścittavyapakarṣas)tadekatyamabhisaṃkṣipya prāvivekyamityucyate |
body.translated_text: What is withdrawal (<s>vyapakarṣa</s>)? He says: It is twofold — bodily withdrawal and mental withdrawal. Therein, bodily withdrawal is non-cohabitation with householders and renunciants. Therein, mental withdrawal is when, having abandoned defiled and indeterminate mental attention, one cultivates mental attention that belongs to the concentrated level or that is preparatory for the prerequisites of <s>samādhi</s> — wholesome and connected with beneficial meaning. This is called mental withdrawal. Therein, the excellence of place, the excellence of posture, bodily withdrawal, and mental withdrawal — all of this, taken together in summary, is called 'seclusion' (<s>prāvivekya</s>).

body.text: tatraikāgratā katamā | āha | punaḥ punaḥ smṛtisabhāgālambanā pravāhānavadyaratiyuktā | cittasantatiryā sā samādhirityucyate | kuśalacittaikāgratāpi [|] kiṃ punaḥ punaranusmarati | āha | ye dharmā udgṛhītā[ḥ] śrutā, yā cāvavādānuśāsanī pratilabdhā bhavati | gurubhyastāmadhipatiṃ kṛtvā samāhitabhūmikanimittaṃ saṃmukhīkṛtya tadālambanāṃ pravāhayuktāṃ smṛtimanuvarttayati | (

children.text: ) upanibadhnāti | tatra katamatsabhāgālambanaṃ | yatkiṃcitsamāhitabhūmikamālambanamanekavidhaṃ | bahunānāprakāraṃ | yenālambane cittaṃ paraṃ samāhitamidamucyate | sabhāgamālambanaṃ [|] kasyaitat | sabhāgaṃ [|] āha | kṣayasya vastunaḥ pratirūpakametattasmātsabhāgamityucyate | yā punarabhikṣayākārānichidrā (niśchidrā) nirantarā smṛtiḥ pravartate | tenālambanena satataṃ ca satkṛtya ceyaṃ pravāhayuktatā | yatpunastasminnevālambane abhiratasyāsaṃkliṣṭavihāritā | vāhimārgatā smṛtiriyamavadyaratiyuktatā | tenāha punaḥ punaraparānusmṛtisabhāgālambanapravāhānavadyaratiyuktā citta santatiḥ | samādhiriti sā khalveṣā ekāgratā śamathapakṣyā vipaśyanāpakṣyā ca | tatra yā navākārāyāṃ cittasaṃtathau (sthitau) vā [sā] śamathapakṣyā, yā punaścaturvidhe prajñādhāre sā vipaśyanāpakṣyā |
children.translated_text: and binds it. Therein, what is a similar object (<s>sabhāgālambana</s>)? Whatever object belonging to the concentrated level, of many kinds and various types, upon which the mind becomes supremely concentrated — this is called a similar object. Similar to what? He says: It is a likeness of the real thing that [leads to the] destruction [of defilements]; therefore it is called 'similar.' The mindfulness that operates with unbroken, uninterrupted, and continuous attention toward that object, and does so constantly and respectfully — this is the flowing continuity. The blameless dwelling of one who delights in that very object without defilement, without being carried away — this mindfulness is the blameless delight-connection. Therefore the text says: 'Again and again, mindfulness with a similar object, flowing, and joined with blameless delight — this mental continuum is <s>samādhi</s>.' That one-pointedness indeed belongs to both the side of <s>śamatha</s> (calm abiding) and the side of <s>vipaśyanā</s> (insight). Therein, that which pertains to the nine stages of mental settling (<s>cittasthiti</s>) belongs to the side of <s>śamatha</s>; that which pertains to the four bases of wisdom (<s>prajñādhāra</s>) belongs to the side of <s>vipaśyanā</s>.

body.translated_text: Therein, what is one-pointedness (<s>ekāgratā</s>)? He says: It is the mental continuum that is again and again conjoined with an object similar to mindfulness, flowing continuously, and joined with blameless delight. That is called <s>samādhi</s> (concentration) — the one-pointedness of the wholesome mind. What then does one again and again recollect? He says: Whatever teachings have been grasped and heard, and whatever instruction and admonition has been received from teachers — making that the dominant factor, bringing face-to-face the sign belonging to the concentrated level, one maintains the flow of mindfulness with that as its object,

body.text: tatra navākārā cittasthitiḥ katamā | iha bhikṣuradhyātmameva cittaṃ sthāpayati | saṃsthāpayati | avasthāpayatyupasthāpayati | damayati | śamayati | (

children.translated_text: thoroughly pacifies it (<s>vyupaśamayati</s>), makes it one-pointed (<s>ekotīkaroti</s>), and places it in equipoise (<s>samādhatte</s>).

body.translated_text: Therein, what are the nine stages of mental settling? Here a <s>bhikṣu</s> internally settles the mind (<s>sthāpayati</s>), continuously settles it (<s>saṃsthāpayati</s>), re-settles it (<s>avasthāpayati</s>), closely settles it (<s>upasthāpayati</s>), tames it (<s>damayati</s>), pacifies it (<s>śamayati</s>),

body.text: kathaṃ sthāpayati | sarvabāhyebhya ālambanebhyaḥ pratisaṃkṣipyādhyātmamavikṣepāyopanibaghnāti | yattatprathamopanibaddho vikṣepāya iyaṃ sthāpanā |
body.translated_text: How does he establish [the mind]? Withdrawing from all external objects, he binds it internally for the sake of non-distraction. That which is first bound — its distraction constitutes the establishment

body.text: kathaṃ saṃsthāpayati | tatprathamopanibaddhaṃ yadeva cittaṃ tadba[la]maudārikamasaṃsthitamaparisaṃsthitaṃ tasminnevālambane pravarddhanayogena prasādayogena sābhinigrahaṃ sūkṣmīkurvan abhisaṃkṣipan saṃsthāpayati |
body.translated_text: How does he re-establish [the mind]? That very mind which was first bound — when it becomes coarse, unsettled, and not properly settled — through the practice of intensification upon that very object, he re-establishes it.

body.text: kathamavasthāpayati | sa ceccittameva sthāpayataḥ | smṛtisaṃpramoṣādbahirdhā vikṣipyate | sa punarapi tathaiva pratisaṃharanti (ti) | evame(ma)va sthāpayati |
body.translated_text: How does he make [the mind] abide? If, while establishing the mind, it is distracted outward through the loss of mindfulness, he again withdraws it in the same way. Thus

body.text: kathaṃ damayati | yairnimittairasya taccittaṃ vikṣipyate | tadyathā gatvarasaṃspraṣṭavyanimittai rāgadveṣamohastrīpuruṣanimitaiśca [|] tatrānena pūrvamevādīnavasaṃjñodgṛhītā bhavati | tāmadhipatiṃ kṛtvā teṣu nimitteṣu tasya cittasya prasaraṃ na dadāti | evaṃ damayati ||
body.translated_text: How does he tame [the mind]? By whatever signs his mind is distracted — namely, by signs of taste, touch, and contact; by signs of passion, hatred, delusion, women, and men — therein,

body.text: kathaṃ śamayati | yairvitarkaiḥ kāmavitarkādibhiḥ | yaiścopakleśaiḥ | kāma[c]chandanivaraṇādibhiḥ | tasya cetasaḥ saṃkṣobho bhavati | tatrānena pūrvamevādīnavasaṃjñodgṛhītā bhavati | tāmadhipatiṃ kṛtvā tasya cetasaḥ | teṣu vitarkopakleśeṣu | prasaraṃ na dadātyevaṃ śamayati |
body.translated_text: How does he calm [the mind]? By whatever thoughts — thoughts of sensual desire and so on — and by whatever secondary afflictions — the hindrance of sensual desire and so on — there is disturbance of his mind. Therein, seeing the danger in them,

body.text: kathaṃ vyupaśamayati | smṛtisampramoṣāttadubhayasamudācāra [re] satyutpannotpannān vitarkopakleśān nādhivāsayati | prajahāti | evaṃ vyupaśamayati |
body.translated_text: How does he thoroughly calm [the mind]? When, through the loss of mindfulness, both of those [thoughts and afflictions] have arisen, he does not tolerate the arisen thoughts and afflictions — he abandons them. Thus he thoroughly calms.

body.text: kathamekotīkaroti | sābhisaṃskāraṃ nicchi(śchi)draṃ nirantaraṃ samādhipravāhamā (ma)vasthāpayatyeva mekotīkaroti |
body.translated_text: How does he unify [the mind]? With effort, without gaps, without interruption, he establishes the continuous flow of <s>samādhi</s> (concentration) — thus he unifies.

body.text: kathaṃ samādhatte | āsevanānvayādbhāvanānvayādbahulīkārānvayādanābhogavāhanaṃ | svarasavāhanaṃ | mārgaṃ labhate | yenānabhisaṃskāra (re)vā (ṇā) nābhogenāsya cittasamādhipravāhaḥ | avikṣepe pravarttate | evaṃ samādhatte |
body.translated_text: How does he concentrate [the mind]? Through repeated practice, through cultivation, through frequent engagement, he obtains the path of effortless flow, of spontaneous flow, by which, without deliberate effort,

body.text: tatra ṣaḍvidhabalairnavākārā cittasthitiḥ sampadyate | tadyathā śrutacintābalena | smṛtibalena | vīryabalena | (
body.translated_text: therein, the ninefold mode of mental stability is accomplished through six kinds of powers, namely: the power of hearing and reflection, the power of mindfulness, the power of vigor,

body.text: tatra śrutacintābalena tāvat | yacchrutaṃ, yā cintā [tā]madhipatiṃ kṛtvā cittamādita ālambane sthāpayati | tatraiva ca | prabandhayogena saṃsthāpayati | tatropanibaddhaṃ cittaṃ smṛtibalena pratisarannavasthāpayati | upasthāpayati | tataḥ saṃprajanyabalena nimittavitarkopakleśeṣu prasaramananuprayacchan damayati | śamayati | vīryabalena | tadubhayasamudācāraṃ ca nādhivāsayati | ekotīkaroti | paricaya balena samādhatte [|]
body.translated_text: Therein, first, through the power of hearing and reflection — making what has been heard and what has been reflected upon the predominant factor, one initially establishes the mind upon the object. And therein, through the practice of continuity, one re-establishes it.

body.text: tatra navākārāyāṃ cittasthitau catvāro manaskārā veditavyāḥ | balavāhanaḥ sa[c]chidravāhano nichi(śchi)dravāhanaḥ | anābhogavāhanaśca | tatra sthāpayataḥ, saṃsthāpayato balavāhano manaskāraḥ | avasthāpayata, upasthāpayato, damayataḥ, śamayataḥ, vyupaśamayataḥ, sacchidravāhano manaskāraḥ | ekotīkurvato nichi(śchi)dravāhano manaskāraḥ | samādadhataḥ | anābhogavāhano manaskāro bhavati | evamete manaskārāyāṃ cittasthitau śamathapakṣyā bhavanti | yaḥ punarevamadhyātmaṃ cetaḥśamathasya lābhī vipaśyanāyāṃ prayujyate | tasyaita eva catvāro manaskārā vipaśyanāpakṣyā bhavanti ||
body.translated_text: Therein, in the ninefold mode of mental stability, four kinds of mental attention should be understood: forceful engagement, engagement with gaps, engagement without gaps, and effortless engagement. Therein,

body.text: caturvidhā vipaśyanā | katamā | bhikṣurdharmān vicinoti | pravicinoti | parivitarkayati | parimīmānsā(māṃsā)māpadyate | yadutādhyātmaṃ cetaḥśamathaṃ niśritya [|]
body.translated_text: Fourfold is <s>vipaśyanā</s> (insight). What is it? The <s>bhikṣu</s> (monk) investigates <s>dharmas</s>, thoroughly investigates, deliberates, and engages in examination — namely, internally regarding the mind

body.text: kathaṃ ca vicinoti | caritaviśodhanaṃ vā ālambanaṃ | kauśalyālambanaṃ vā, kleśaviśodhanaṃ vā | yāvadbhāvikatayā vicinoti | yathāvadbhāvikatayā | pravicinoti | savikalpena manaskāreṇa prajñāsahagatena | nimittīkurvanneva parivitarkayati | santīrayatyadhimīmāṃsāmāpadyate |
body.translated_text: How does he investigate? He investigates the object for purifying temperament, or the object of skill, or the object for purifying afflictions — he investigates through <s>yāvadbhāvikatā</s> (extent-reality) and <s>yathāvadbhāvikatā</s> (mode-reality).

body.text: sā khalveṣā vipaśyanā trimukhī ṣaḍvastuprabhedālambanā veditavyā(ḥ) | katamāni trīṇi (|) mukhāni [|] vipaśyanā yannimittamātrānucaritā | vipaśyanā paryeṣaṇānucaritā, paryeṣi tā ca | pratyavekṣaṇānucaritā |
body.translated_text: This <s>vipaśyanā</s> should be understood as having three faces and as taking the six-object analysis as its basis. What are the three faces? <s>Vipaśyanā</s> that follows mere signs, <s>vipaśyanā</s> that follows

body.text: tatra nimittamātrānucaritā [|] yena (yayā) (

body.translated_text: therein, that which follows mere signs — by which (

body.translated_text: When, however, one thinks, determines, weighs, and examines — then it becomes [<s>vipaśyanā</s>] following investigation.

body.text: yadā punastīrayitvā upaparīkṣya yathā vyavasthāpitameva pratyavekṣate | tadā pratyavekṣaṇānucaritā bhavatīyaṃ trimukhā (khī) vipaśyanā |
body.translated_text: When, however, having determined and examined, one reviews exactly as it has been established — then it becomes [<s>vipaśyanā</s>] following review. This is the three-faced <s>vipaśyanā</s>.

body.text: katamāni ṣaḍvastuprabhedālambanāni | sa paryeṣamāṇaḥ | ṣaḍvastūni paryeṣate | arthaṃ, vastu, lakṣaṇaṃ, pakṣaṃ, kālaṃ, yuktiñca paryeṣyannetānyeva (paryeṣamāṇa etānyeva) pratyavekṣate |
body.translated_text: What are the six objects of analysis? One who is investigating searches for six objects: meaning, entity, characteristic, side, time, and reasoning. And by investigating these,

body.text: kathamarthaṃ paryeṣate | asya bhāṣitasyāyamartho [a]sya bhāṣitasyāyamartha (ta) ityevamarthaṃ paryeṣate |
body.translated_text: How does one investigate meaning? 'This is the meaning of this statement, this is the meaning of that statement' — thus one investigates meaning.

body.text: kathaṃ vastu paryeṣate | dvividhaṃ vastu [|] ādhyātmikaṃ bāhyañca [|] evaṃ vastu paryeṣate |
body.translated_text: How does one investigate entity? Entity is twofold: internal and external. Thus one investigates entity.

body.text: kathaṃ lakṣaṇaṃ paryeṣate | dvividhaṃ | svalakṣaṇaṃ sāmānyalakṣaṇaṃ ca | evaṃ lakṣaṇaṃ paryeṣate |
body.translated_text: How does one investigate characteristic? It is twofold: <s>svalakṣaṇa</s> (specific characteristic) and <s>sāmānyalakṣaṇa</s> (general characteristic). Thus one investigates characteristic.

body.text: kathaṃ pakṣaṃ paryeṣate | dvividhaḥ pakṣaḥ kṛṣṇapakṣaḥ śuklapakṣaḥ [|] kṛṣṇapakṣaṃ doṣataḥ | ādīnavataḥ | śuklapakṣaṃ punarguṇato 'nuśaṃsataścaivaṃ [pakṣaṃ] paryeṣate |
body.translated_text: How does one investigate side? Side is twofold: the dark side and the bright side. The dark side by its faults and dangers; the bright side by its qualities and benefits.

body.text: kathaṃ kālaṃ paryeṣate | trayaḥ kālāḥ [|] atīto 'nāgato vartamānaśca | evametadabhūdatītedhvani evametadbhaviṣyati | anāgatedhvani | evametadetarhi | pratyutpannedhvanītyevaṃ kālaṃ paryeṣate |
body.translated_text: How does one investigate time? There are three times: past, future, and present. 'Thus it was in the past period,' 'thus it will be in the future period,' 'thus it is

body.text: kathaṃ yuktimparyeṣate | catasro yuktayaḥ |[|] apekṣāyuktiḥ, kāryakāraṇayuktiḥ, upapattisādhanayuktirdharmatāyuktiśca || tatro (trā) pekṣāyuktyā saṃvṛtiṃ ca saṃvṛtitaḥ | paramārthaṃ ca paramārthataḥ | nidānaṃ ca nidānataḥ | paryeṣate | kāya (rya) kāraṇayuktyā kāritraṃ dharmāṇāṃ paryeṣate | ayandharmaḥ, idaṃ kāritraṃ, ayamidaṃ kāritra iti [|] upapattisādhanayuktyā trīṇi pramāṇāni paryeṣate | āptāgamamanumānaṃ pratyakṣaṃ ca [|] kimasti (|) atrātmā, nāstīti kiṃ pratyakṣamupalabhyate na veti, kimanumānena prayujyate na veti | tatra dharmatāyuktayā tathābhūtatāṃ dharmāṇāṃ prasiddhadharmatāmacintyadharmatāmavasthitadharmatāmadhimucyate, na cintayati | na vikalpayatyevaṃ yuktimparyeṣate |
body.translated_text: How does one investigate reasoning? There are four types of reasoning: <s>apekṣāyukti</s> (reasoning by dependency), <s>kāryakāraṇayukti</s> (reasoning by cause and effect), <s>upapattisādhanayukti</s> (reasoning by evidential proof), and <s>dharmatāyukti</s> (reasoning by the nature of things). Therein, the reasoning by dependency

body.text: iyaṃ ṣaḍvastuprabhedālambanā(ni) trimukhā (khī)vipaśyanā samāsataḥ | anayā sarvavipaśyanāsaṃgrahaḥ |
body.translated_text: This, in brief, is the three-faced <s>vipaśyanā</s> based on the six objects of analysis. By this, all <s>vipaśyanā</s> is encompassed.

body.text: kena punaḥ kāraṇena ṣaṭprabhedā vyavasthāpitā[ḥ |] āha | trividhamavabodhamadhikṛtya bhāṣitārthā (na)vabodhamvastuparyeṣantatāvabodhaṃ | yathābhūtāvabodhaṃ ca | tatrārthaparyeṣaṇayā bhāṣitārthāvabodhaḥ | vastuparyeṣaṇayā, svalakṣaṇaparyeṣaṇayā ca vastuparyeṣantatāvabodhaḥ | tatra sāmānyalakṣaṇaparyeṣaṇayā, pakṣaparyeṣaṇayā, kālayuktiparyeṣaṇayā yathābhūtāvabodhaḥ | etāvacca yoginā jñeyaṃ | yaduta bhāṣitasyārthaḥ, jñeyasya vastunaḥ yāvadbhāvikatā | yathāvadbhāvikatā ca | tatrāśubho (bhe) prayukto yogī ṣaḍvastūni paryeṣate | āha [|] aśubhādhipateyaṃ dharmaṃ śrutamudagṛhītamadhipatiṃ kṛtvā samāhitabhūmikena manaskāreṇaivamarthapratisaṃvedī bhavati | aśubhayā aśubhyetatpratirūpametpratika(gha)metad durgandhamāmagandhamiti | (

children.translated_text: ) by these aspects of this kind, for that very <s>dharma</s> whose subject is unattractiveness, previously heard — the experiential understanding of its meaning. Thus, with reference to unattractiveness, one investigates meaning.

body.translated_text: For what reason are the six types of analysis established? He says: With reference to threefold understanding — understanding of the meaning of the spoken word, understanding through investigation of the entity, and understanding of what has been

body.text: kathaṃ vastu paryeṣate [|] sa evamarthapratisaṃvedī tāmaśubhatāṃ dvayorbhāvayorvyavasthāpitāṃ paśyatyadhyātmambahirdhā ca |
body.translated_text: How does one investigate entity? One who has thus experienced the meaning sees that unattractiveness as established in two domains — internal and external.

body.text: kathaṃ svalakṣaṇaṃ paryeṣate | adhyātmaṃ tāvadantaḥ kāyagatāmaśubhatāṃ pratyaśubhatāmadhimucyate || santyasminkāye keśaromāṇi vistareṇa yāvanmastakaṃ mastakaluṃgaṃ praśrāva (prasrāva) iti | tāṃ punaranekavidhāmantaḥ kāyagatāmaśubhatāṃ dvābhyāṃ dhātubhyāṃ saṃgṛhītāmadhimucyate | pṛthivīdhātunā, abdhātunā ca [|] tatra keśaromāṇyupādāya | yāvadyakṛtpurīṣā pṛthivīdhāturadhimucyate | aśrudvedanāmupādāya yāvatprasrāvādabdhātumadhimucyate | bahirdhā vā punarbāhyagatāmaśubhatāṃ vinīlakādibhirākārairadhimucyate | tatra vinīlakamadhimucyate | yadanena mṛtakuṇapaṃ svayaṃ vā dṛṣṭaṃ bhavati | purato vā śrutaṃ parikalpitaṃ vā, puna[ḥ] striyā vā, puruṣasya vā, mitrasya vā, amitrasya vā, udāsīnasya vā | hīnamvā, madhyamvā, praṇītamvā, dahrasya vā, madhyasya vā, vṛddhasya vā [|]
body.translated_text: How does one investigate specific characteristic? Internally, one resolves upon the unattractiveness within the body — the direct unattractiveness: 'In this body there are head-hairs, body-hairs' — in detail up to

body.text: tatra nimittamudgṛhya ekāhamṛtaṃ pragaḍitaśoṇitamayaṃ prāptapūyabhāvaṃ vinīlakamityadhimucyate | dvyahamṛtaṃ (

children.text: ) prāptapūyabhāvaṃ | asaṃjātakṛmivipūyakamityadhimucyate | saptāhamṛtaṃ saṃjātakṛmi ādhmātaṃ ca vimadrāmakaṃ vyādhmātakamityadhimucyate kākaiḥ kuralai(rai)ḥ khādyamānaṃ gṛddhaiḥ śvabhiḥ śrṛgālairvikhādikamityadhimucyate | viravāditamvā punarapagatatvaṅmānsaśoṇitaṃ snāyumātropanibaddhaṃ vilohitakamityadhimucyate | diśodiśamaṃgapratyaṃgeṣu vikṣipteṣu viśleṣiteṣu samānse(māṃse)ṣu nirmānse (māṃse)ṣu kiṃcicchiṣṭamānse(māṃse)ṣu vikṣiptakamityadhimucyate || anyato vā hastāsthīnyanyataḥ pādāsthīnyanyato jānvasthīnyūrvasthīni, bāhvasthīni, prabāhvasthīni | pṛṣṭhā(ṣṭhī) vaṃśaḥ | hanunakraṃ dantamālā madhyataḥ | śiraskapālaṃ dṛṣṭvānyāsthīnyadhimucyate | yadā punaḥ sambaddhamarikṣakaraṃkamaviśīrṇaṃ manasi karoti | kevalaṃ nimittagrāhī bhavati | na tu tasyāṃga pratyaṃgeṣu vyaṃjanagrāhī | evaṃ śaṃkalikāmadhimucyate | yadā [tvanu] vyaṃjanagrāhī bhavati | tadāsthiśaṃkalikāmadhimucyate | api ca dve śaṃkalike dehaśaṃkalikā, pratyaṃgaśaṃkalikā ca | tatra deha śaṃkalikā śroṇīkaṭāhamupādāya | pṛṣṭhīvaṃśo yāvat, yatra śiraskapālaṃ pratiṣṭhitaṃ | pratyaṃgaśaṃkalikā sambaddhāni bāhvasthīni ca sambaddhāni | tatra yā dehaśaṃkalikā ca | tatra dehaśaṃkalikā śroṇīkaṭāhamupādāya | (
children.translated_text: that which has reached the state of being putrid; when worms have not yet appeared, one resolves upon it as <s>vipūyaka</s> (festering). Seven days after death, when worms have appeared and it is bloated, one resolves upon it as <s>vyādhmātaka</s> (swollen). When it is being devoured by crows, vultures, dogs, and jackals, one resolves upon it as <s>vikhādika</s> (gnawed). Or again, that from which the skin, flesh, and blood have departed, held together only by sinews, one resolves upon it as <s>vilohitaka</s> (discolored). When the limbs and secondary limbs are scattered in various directions, some with flesh, some without flesh, some with a little remaining flesh, one resolves upon it as <s>vikṣiptaka</s> (scattered). Or again, seeing the hand-bones in one place, the foot-bones in another, the knee-bones, thigh-bones, arm-bones, forearm-bones elsewhere, the spinal column, the jawbone, the row of teeth in the middle, and the skull — one resolves upon other bones. When, however, one attends to a connected, undisintegrated skeleton, one grasps only the sign, not the secondary marks of its limbs and secondary limbs. Thus one resolves upon the <s>śaṅkalikā</s> (chain of bones). When one also grasps the secondary marks, then one resolves upon the <s>asthiśaṅkalikā</s> (bone-chain). Moreover, there are two [types of] chain: the body-chain (<s>dehaśaṅkalikā</s>) and the limb-chain (<s>pratyaṅgaśaṅkalikā</s>). Therein, the body-chain extends from the hip-basin, along the spinal column, up to where the skull rests. The limb-chain consists of the connected arm-bones and connected [leg-bones]. Therein, the body-chain extends from the hip-basin,

children.text: ) pṛṣṭhīvaṃśo yāvat yatra śiraskapālaṃ pratiṣṭhitaṃ | pratyaṃgaśaṃkalikāsambaddhāni bāhvasthīni | ūrujaṃghāsthīni ca | tatra yā dehaśaṃkalikā | sā śaṃkalikaivocyate | yā punaḥ pratyaṃgaśaṃkalikā sā asthiśaṃkaliketyucyate |
children.translated_text: along the spinal column up to where the skull rests. The limb-chain consists of the connected arm-bones and the thigh-and-shin-bones. Therein, the body-chain is simply called "chain" (<s>śaṅkalikā</s>). The limb-chain, however, is called "bone-chain" (<s>asthiśaṅkalikā</s>).

body.translated_text: therein, having grasped the sign, one resolves: 'A corpse dead for one day, with coagulated blood, having reached the state of pus, is discolored.' 'A corpse dead for two days,' (

body.text: api ca dvau śaṃkalikāyānimittagrāhau citrakṛtāyāḥ pāṣāṇa kāṣṭhaśādakṛtāyā vā | bhūtaśaṃkalikāyā vā | abhūtaśaṃkalikāyā vā | nimittaṃ manasikaroti | tadāśaṃkalikāmevādhimucyate nāsthiśaṃkalikāṃ | yadā pūnarbhūtaśaṃkalikāyā nimittaṃ manasi karoti | tadāsthiśaṃkalikāmevādhimucyate | nāsthiśaṃkalikāṃ | (yadā punarbhūtaśaṃkalikāyā nimittaṃ manasi karoti | tadāsthiśaṃkalikāmadhimucyate) | sa khalveṣa bāhyāyā varṇanibhāyā upādāyarūpagatāyāstrividho (|) vipariṇāmaḥ | svarasavipariṇāmaḥ | parakṛtastadubhayapakṣyaśca |
body.translated_text: Moreover, there are two ways of grasping the sign of a chain: from one that is artificially made of stone or wood, or from an actual skeleton; or from a non-real or a real chain. When one attends to the sign of a non-real chain, one resolves upon the chain itself, not the bone-chain. When, however, one attends to the sign of a real skeleton, one resolves upon the bone-chain. This threefold transformation of the external attractive appearance belonging to derived form is: transformation by natural process, transformation caused by others, and that belonging to the side of both.

body.text: tatra vinīlakamupādāya | yāvad vyādhmātakāḥ (kāt) svarasavipariṇāmaḥ | tatra vikhāditakamupādāya yāvadvikṣiptakātparakṛto vipara(ri)ṇāmaḥ | tatrāsthikā (vā), śaṃkalikā vā ityayamubhayapakṣyo vipariṇāma iti | ya evaṃ yathābhūtaṃ prajānāti | (

children.text: ) bahirdhā aśubhatāmākārata evaṃ bahirdhā aśubhatāyāḥ svalakṣaṇaṃ paryeṣate |
children.translated_text: the external unattractiveness in its aspect — thus one seeks the particular characteristic (<s>svalakṣaṇa</s>) of external unattractiveness.

body.translated_text: Therein, from the discolored (<s>vinīlaka</s>) up to the swollen (<s>vyādhmātaka</s>) is transformation by natural process. From the gnawed (<s>vikhādika</s>) up to the scattered (<s>vikṣiptaka</s>) is transformation caused by others. Therein, the bones or the chain of bones — this is transformation belonging to the side of both. One who thus knows as it really is

body.text: kathamaśubhatāyā[ḥ] (|) sāmānyalakṣaṇaṃ paryeṣate | yathā cādhyātmaṃ bahiḥ kāyasyāśubhāvarṇanibhayā apariṇatā yāvadbahirdhā bahiḥ kāyasyāśubhā varṇanibhā vipariṇatā adhyātmikayā aśubhayā varṇanibhā samānadharmatāṃ tulyadharmatāmadhimucyate | iyamapi me śubhā varṇanibhā evaṃ dharmiṇīti | ye 'pi kecitsattvā anayā śubhayā varṇanibhayā samanvāgatāsteṣāmapi sāśubhāyāṃ evaṃ dharmiṇī tadyatheyambāhyā || evaṃ sāmānyalakṣaṇaṃ paryeṣate |
body.translated_text: How does one seek the general characteristic (<s>sāmānyalakṣaṇa</s>) of unattractiveness? Just as the internal, external body's unattractive appearance is untransformed, and just as the external, outer body's unattractive appearance is transformed — one resolves upon the sameness of nature, the equality of nature, of the internal unattractive appearance with the [external], [thinking:] "This attractive appearance of mine is also of such a nature." And whatever beings possess this attractive appearance — their [attractive appearance] too is of this unattractive nature, just like this external one. Thus one seeks the general characteristic.

body.text: kathaṃ pakṣaṃ paryeṣate | tasyaivaṃ bhavati | yadāha masyā (anayāśubhayā varṇanibhayā etāmaśubhamatā (tāṃ) yathābhūtamaprajānannadhyātmaṃ vā bahirdhā vā śubhāyāṃ varṇanibhāyāṃ saṃrāgamutpādayāmi viparyāsa eva kṛṣṇapakṣasaṃgṛhītaḥ | niḥsaraṇadharmaḥ saduḥkhaḥ savighātaḥ sopadravaḥ saparidāhaḥ | atonidānā utpadyante | āyatyāṃ jātijarāvyādhimaraṇaśokaparidevaduḥkhadaurmanasyopāyāsāḥ | yā punarasyāṃ śubhāyāmvarṇanibhāyāṃ | aśubhadharmatānugatā yathābhūtānupaśyanā śuklapakṣyā [|] eṣa dharmaḥ aduḥkhaḥ | avighātaḥ | yāvadato nidānā upāyāsā nirudhyante | tatra yoyaṃ (

children.translated_text: up to: from this as cause, distresses cease. Therein, this dark-side occasion should not be tolerated; it should be abandoned, should be purified. The bright side, when unarisen, should be made to arise; and when arisen, its stability, growth, and full development should be brought about." Thus one seeks the [dark and bright] sides.

body.translated_text: How does one seek the [dark and bright] sides? The following occurs to him: "When, by this unattractive appearance, I do not truly understand this unattractiveness as it really is, and generate attachment toward the attractive appearance, whether internal or external — that is nothing but delusion, belonging to the dark side, having the nature of escape, accompanied by suffering, accompanied by harm, accompanied by adversity, accompanied by burning. From this as cause arise in the future: birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, displeasure, and distress. But the contemplation that accords with reality, regarding the nature of unattractiveness in this attractive appearance — this belongs to the bright side; this <s>dharma</s> is without suffering, without harm,

body.text: kathaṃ kālaṃ paryeṣate | tasyaivaṃ bhavati | yeyamadhyātmaṃ [a]śubhā varṇanibhā seyamvarttamānamadhvānamupādāya yā punariyaṃ bahirdhā aśubhā varṇanibhā iyamapi vartamāna (tā)mevādhvānamupādāya | atītaṃ punaradhvānamupādāya | śubhā babhūva | saiṣā tāvadatītamadhvānamupādāya śubhā satī tadyathā me etarhi | vartamānamadhvānamupādāya | evamānupūrvyā etarhi vartamānamupādāya aśubhā saṃvṛttā, sā me iyaṃ [a]śubhā varṇanibhā varttamānamadhvānamupādāyāśubhā satī | anāgate [a]dhvanyaśubhā na bhaviṣyatīti | nedaṃ sthānaṃ vidyate | tadyathaiṣā bāhyā eva[ṃ] vartamānamadhvānamupādāya | iti hyatītānāgatapratyutpanneṣvadhvasu ayamapi me kāya evaṃbhāvī, evaṃbhūta, etāṃ ca dharmatāmanatīta ityevaṃ kālaṃ samanveṣate |
body.translated_text: How does one seek the time? The following occurs to him: "This internal unattractive appearance — it is with reference to the present time-period. And this external unattractive appearance — it too is with reference to the present time-period. But with reference to the past time-period, it was attractive. So it was attractive with reference to the past, just as I am now [attractive] with reference to the present. And in this sequence, now with reference to the present it has become unattractive. So this unattractive appearance of mine, being unattractive with reference to the present, that it will not be unattractive in the future — there is no such possibility. Just as this external one [has transformed] with reference to the present." Thus, in the past, future, and present time-periods, "this body of mine too will be of such a nature, will become such, and this <s>dharmatā</s> (nature of things) it has not transcended" — thus one seeks the time.

body.text: tasyāsya mṛtasya kālagatasyānupūrveṇa vipariṇatā imā avasthāḥ prajñāyante | yaduta vinīlakamitivā yāvadasthiśaṃkalikāyā vā ayamapi me kāyaḥ | pūrvakarmakleśaviddhaḥ | mātāpitryaśucisaṃbhūta odanaka(ku)lmāṣopacitaḥ | yena hetunā, yena nidānena iyaṃ tāvatkālikī śubhā varṇanibhā | prajñāyate | antaḥkāyaḥ punarnityaṃ nityakālamadhyātmaṃ ca bahirdhā cāśubhā evaṃ saṃvṛtiparamārthanidānataḥ | apekṣāyuktiṃ paryeṣate | tasyaivaṃ bhavatīyamaśubhatā | evamāsevitā bhāvitā bahulīkṛtā kāmarāgaprahāṇāya samvartate | kāmarāgaśca prahātavyaḥ | evaṃ kāryakāraṇayuktyā samanveṣate | tasyaivaṃ bhavatyuktaṃ hi bhagavatā | aśubhā āsevitā bhāvitā bahulīkṛtā kāmarāgaprahāṇāya samvarttata ityayaṃ tāvanme āptāgamaḥ | pratyātmamapi me jñānadarśanaṃ pravarttate | ahamasmi yathā yathā aśubhatāṃ bhāvayāmi, manasi karomi | tathā kāmarāgaparyavasthānaṃ anutpannaṃ ca notpadyate | utpannaṃ ca prativigacchati | ānulomikopyeṣa vidhirasti | (

children.text: ) kathamidānīmvipakṣaṃ dharmaṃ manasikurvataḥ | tadvipakṣālambanena kleśa utpadyate | evamupapattisādhanayuktyā paryeṣate | tasyaivaṃ bhavati | prasiddhā dharmatā khalveṣā acintyadharmatā | yadaśubhā bhāvanā kāmarāgasya prahāṇapratipakṣa iti | sā ca cintayitavyā | na vikalpayitavyā | adhimoktavyā | evaṃ dharmatāyuktyā aśubhatāmparyeṣate | iyaṃ tāvadaśubhāprayuktasya trimukhī ṣaḍvastuprabhedālambanā vipaśyanā |
children.translated_text: "How then, when one attends to the antidotal <s>dharma</s>, does the defilement that is its opposite arise through the opposite object?" Thus one seeks by the reasoning of proof by evidence (<s>upapattisādhanayukti</s>). The following occurs to him: "This is indeed a well-established <s>dharmatā</s> (nature of things), an inconceivable <s>dharmatā</s> — that the meditation on unattractiveness is the antidote for the abandonment of sensual desire. And it should be contemplated, not speculated about; it should be accepted with conviction." Thus, by the reasoning of the nature of things (<s>dharmatāyukti</s>), one seeks [to understand] unattractiveness. This, then, is the <s>vipaśyanā</s> (insight) of one engaged in <s>aśubhā</s> (unattractiveness), with three approaches and sixfold object-analysis.

body.translated_text: And for this one who has died, who has passed away, these stages of transformation are recognized in sequence — namely, the discolored and so on up to the bone-chain. "This body of mine too, afflicted by past <s>karma</s> and <s>kleśas</s> (defilements), born from the impurity of mother and father, nourished by rice and grain — for this very reason, this attractive appearance is [merely] temporary and is recognized. But the interior of the body is always, at all times, both internally and externally, unattractive." Thus, from the standpoint of conventional and ultimate causation, one seeks the reasoning of dependence (<s>apekṣāyukti</s>). The following occurs to him: "This unattractiveness, when cultivated, practiced, and made abundant, leads to the abandonment of sensual desire (<s>kāmarāga</s>). And sensual desire should be abandoned." Thus one seeks by the reasoning of cause and effect (<s>kāryakāraṇayukti</s>). The following occurs to him: "For the <s>Bhagavān</s> has said: 'The meditation on unattractiveness, when cultivated, practiced, and made abundant, leads to the abandonment of sensual desire.' This then is the authoritative testimony (<s>āptāgama</s>) for me. And my own knowledge and vision also operates: as I cultivate and attend to unattractiveness, the envelopment of sensual desire, when unarisen, does not arise, and when arisen, it recedes. And this is the concordant method."

body.text: kathaṃ maitrīprayukto vipaśyanṣaḍvastūni paryeṣate | maitryadhipateyaṃ dharmamadhipatiṃ kṛtvā hitasukhādhyāśayagatasya sarveṣu sukhopasaṃhārādhimokṣalakṣaṇā maitrītyetamarthapratisamvedyarthaṃ paryeṣate | sa evamarthapratisaṃvedī punarvicinotītyayaṃ mitrapakṣoyamamitrapakṣoyamudāsīnapakṣaḥ | sarva ete pakṣāḥ parasantānapatitatvādvāhyaṃ vastvityadhimucyate | mitrapakṣaṃ vā adhyātmamamitrodāsīnapakṣaṃ bahirdhā evaṃ ca vastuni maitrīṃ samanveṣate |
body.translated_text: How does one engaged in <s>maitrī</s> (loving-kindness) seek the six objects through <s>vipaśyanā</s>? Making loving-kindness predominant, making this <s>dharma</s> the governing factor, for one whose intention is directed toward benefit and happiness for all, one seeks the meaning to be realized of <s>maitrī</s> — which has the characteristic of resolving upon the conveyance of happiness for all. Being thus a realizer of meaning, one further investigates: "This is the category of friends, this is the category of enemies, this is the category of the neutral." All these categories, since they fall within the continua of others, are resolved upon as external objects. Or, taking the friend-category as internal and the enemy and neutral categories as external, thus one seeks [to apply] <s>maitrī</s> with respect to the object.

body.translated_text: One further investigates: "Regarding the friend-category, the enemy-category, and the neutral-category — I should maintain equal-mindedness, even-mindedness toward them. For what reason? Regarding the friend-category, the conveyance of happiness is not difficult for me. Regarding the neutral-category too, it is not very difficult for me. But regarding the enemy-category, it is very difficult. It is precisely there that I should bring about the conveyance of happiness. How much more so, then, for the friend-category or the neutral-category! For what reason? There is no one here who insults or is insulted, who angers or is angered, who quarrels or is quarreled with, who strikes or is struck. Apart from these, it is merely syllables that resound, merely sound, merely a small matter. And moreover, this body, being material, gross, and composed of the four great elements, is such that while I dwell [in it], contacts of such a form come to me — namely, contacts of sound, or

body.text: api coktaṃ bhagavatā | nāhaṃ taṃ sulabharūpaṃ samanupaśyāmi | yonena dīrghasyādhvanotyayānmātā vā bhū[t] pitā vā, bhrātā vā, bhaginī vā, ācāryo vā, upādhyāyo vā, gururvā, gurusthānīyo veti | tadanenāpi paryāyeṇāmitrapakṣa eva[ṃ] me [a]mitrapakṣaḥ | na cātra kasyacit pariniṣpattiḥ, mitrābhitrabhāvo, mitropi (tramapi) ca kālāntareṇāmitro (traṃ) bhavati | amitro (trama)pi mitrībhavati | tasmānna sarvasattveṣu samacittatā | samatādṛṣṭiḥ karaṇīyā | tulyaśca hitāśayaḥ, sukhādhyāśayaḥ, sukhopasaṃhāraḥ | sukhopasaṃhārādhimokṣa iti | evaṃ sāmānyalakṣaṇena maitrīṃ samanveṣate |
body.translated_text: Moreover, the <s>Bhagavān</s> has said: 'I do not see any being who, through the long course of time, has not been a mother, a father, a brother, a sister, a teacher (<s>ācārya</s>), a preceptor (<s>upādhyāya</s>), a <s>guru</s>, or one who occupies the position of a <s>guru</s>.' By this reasoning too, the enemy faction is [in truth] not my enemy faction. And here there is no fixed determination of anyone [as] friend or foe — even a friend in time becomes a foe, and a foe becomes a friend. Therefore, toward all beings, equanimity of mind, the view of equality, equal intent for their welfare, aspiration for their happiness, the bringing about of their happiness, and the conviction to bring about their happiness [should be cultivated]. Thus one investigates <s>maitrī</s> (loving-kindness) by its general characteristic.

body.text: sa punaḥ pravicinoti | ye tāvadatītamadhvānamupādāya sukhakāmāḥ sattvāḥ te atītāḥ, teṣāṃ kiṃ punaḥ sukhopasaṃhāraṃ kariṣyāmaḥ | ye punarvarttamānāḥ sattvāste varttamānamadhvānamupādāya | yāvadanāgatādadhvano nityakālaṃ sukhino bhavanti (ntī) tyevaṃ maitryā(ḥ)kālaṃ paryeṣate |
body.translated_text: He further reflects: 'Those beings who desired happiness in the past — they are past. What happiness can we now bring to them? body.translated_text: He further reflects: 'There is no self or being whatsoever who desires happiness or to whom happiness is brought. Rather, this is merely aggregates, merely formations, regarding which there is this designation, concept, and convention.' Those formations, moreover, are caused by <s>karma</s> (action) and <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions). Thus one investigates <s>maitrī</s> through the reasoning of dependency. 'It is indeed a well-established nature — an inconceivable nature — that the cultivation of <s>maitrī</s> leads to the abandonment of ill-will.' Thus one investigates <s>maitrī</s> through the reasoning of natural law (<s>dharmatā</s>).

body.translated_text: Therein, how does one investigate the purpose connected with <s>vipaśyanā</s> (insight) meditation whose object is conditionality (<s>pratyayatā</s>) as dependent origination (<s>pratītyasamutpāda</s>)? Making the predominant and governing <s>dharma</s> the object of reflection: 'From the arising of those particular <s>dharmas</s>, these <s>dharmas</s> arise; from the cessation of those particular <s>dharmas</s>, these <s>dharmas</s> cease. There is no agent (<s>dharmī</s>), no lord (<s>īśvara</s>), no creator, no fashioner, no producer of <s>dharmas</s>; there is no <s>prakṛti</s> (primordial nature), no other <s>puruṣa</s> (person) that sets <s>dharmas</s> in motion.' — thus perceiving the meaning, one investigates the meaning.

body.translated_text: He further reflects: 'There is action (<s>karma</s>), there is the fruit (<s>vipāka</s>); but no agent is found — neither a doer nor an experiencer — apart from the mere convention of <s>dharmas</s>.' Among those very formations conditioned by <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance),

body.text: api ca dvividhametatphalaṃ | dvividho heturātmabhāvaphalaṃ ca, viṣayopabhogaphalaṃ ca | ākṣepakaśca heturabhinirvarttakaśca [|] tatrātmabhāvaphalaṃ yadetadvipākajaṃ ṣaḍāyatanaṃ viṣayopabhogaphalaṃ yo (yā) iṣṭāniṣṭakarmādhipateyā ṣaṭsparśasaṃbhavā vedanā [|]
body.translated_text: Moreover, this fruit is of two kinds, and the cause is of two kinds: the fruit that is one's personal existence (<s>ātmabhāvaphala</s>) and the fruit that is the enjoyment of objects (<s>viṣayopabhogaphala</s>); and the projecting cause (<s>ākṣepakahetu</s>) and the completing cause (<s>abhinirvarttakahetu</s>). Therein, the fruit of personal existence is the six sense-bases (<s>ṣaḍāyatana</s>) born of ripening (<s>vipākaja</s>). The fruit of object-enjoyment is the feeling that arises from the six contacts, governed by [the distinction of] desirable and undesirable <s>karma</s>.

body.text: tatrākṣepako heturdvividhe phale sammohāsammohapūrvakāśca puṇyāpuṇyāniṃjyāḥ, saṃskāraparigṛhītaṃ ca (|) punarbhavavijñānāṃkuraprādurbhāvāya tadbījaṃ, vijñānaparigṛhītaṃ paunarbhavikanāmarūpabījaṃ ṣaḍāyatanabījaṃ sparśavedanābījamiti | ya evamāyatyāṃ jātisaṃjñakānāṃ vijñā[na]nāmarūpaṣaḍāyatanasparśavedanānāmutpattaye | ānupūrvyā pūrvaṃmeva bījaparigrahaḥ | ayamākṣepa [ko] hetuḥ |
body.translated_text: Therein, the projecting cause [operates] with respect to the two kinds of fruit, preceded by confusion or non-confusion — the meritorious, demeritorious, and imperturbable formations — and the seed, comprised in those formations, for the manifestation of the sprout of consciousness (<s>vijñāna</s>) [in] renewed existence; the seed of name-and-form comprised in consciousness; the seed of the six sense-bases; the seed of contact and feeling. That which, for the arising in the future of what are designated as 'birth' — consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense-bases, contact, and feeling — is the prior grasping of the seed in sequence — this is the projecting cause.

body.text: yatpunaravidyāsaṃsparśajāṃvedanā vedayamānastadālambanayā tṛṣṇayā paunarbhavikīṃ tṝṣṇāmutpādayati | tṛṣṇāpakṣyaṃ mohapakṣyaṃ copādānaṃ | parigṛhṇāti | yadbalena yatsāṃmukhyena tatkarma vipākadānadāna samarthaṃ bhavatyayamabhinirvṛttihetuḥ | imaṃ ca dvividhaṃ hetumadhipatiṃ kṛtvā evaṃ asya trividhaḥ duḥkhatānupakṣasya kevalasyāsya duḥkhaskandhasya samudayo bhavatīti | evamapekṣāyuktiṃ paryeṣate |
body.translated_text: When, however, experiencing a feeling born of contact with <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance), one generates, with <s>tṛṣṇā</s> (craving) directed at that object, a craving for renewed existence; and grasps with <s>upādāna</s> (clinging), which belongs to the side of craving and the side of delusion — by the force and presence of which that <s>karma</s> becomes capable of yielding its fruition — this is the completing cause (<s>abhinirvarttakahetu</s>). Making this twofold cause the governing condition, 'thus arises the origination of this entire mass of suffering, which has the three aspects of the nature of suffering' — thus one investigates the reasoning of dependency.

body.text: idaṃ pratyayatā pratītyasamutpādaḥ | āsevito bhāvito mohaprahāṇāya samvartate | āptāgamopyeṣa pratyātmika ānumānikopyeṣa vidhiḥ | prasiddhadharmatāpyeṣa te (ṣeti) evaṃ kāryakāraṇayuktimupapattisādhanayuktiṃ dharmatāyuktiñca paryeṣate ||
body.translated_text: This is conditionality (<s>pratyayatā</s>) as dependent origination (<s>pratītyasamutpāda</s>). When practiced and cultivated, it leads to the abandonment of delusion (<s>moha</s>). It is also a trustworthy tradition (<s>āptāgama</s>); it is also a method based on personal inferential knowledge (<s>ānumānika</s>); it is also a well-established natural law (<s>prasiddhadharmatā</s>). Thus one investigates the reasoning of cause and effect (<s>kāryakāraṇayukti</s>), the reasoning of logical proof (<s>upapattisādhanayukti</s>), and the reasoning of natural law (<s>dharmatāyukti</s>).

children.text: ) paryeṣate | kharalakṣaṇā pṛthivī | yāvatsamudīraṇalakṣaṇo vāyuḥ vijānanalakṣaṇaṃ vijñānaṃ | sauṣiryalakṣaṇārūpagatāsphuṭālakṣaṇaścākāśadhāturityevaṃ svalakṣaṇaṃ paryeṣate | sarva ete dhātavaḥ | anityatayā samasamāḥ | yāvannirātmatayetyevaṃ sāmānyalakṣaṇaṃ paryeṣate | iti yaḥ piṇḍasaṃjñino dhātunānātvaṃ ajānānasyā[ne]na kāyena nānādhātukena unnatirmanya (nvā) nā maraṇa eṣa dharmaḥ kṛṣṇapakṣyaḥ viparyayācchuklapakṣya ityeva[ṃ] pakṣaṃ paryeṣate |
children.translated_text: The earth [element] has the characteristic of hardness; and so on, up to: wind has the characteristic of setting in motion; consciousness (<s>vijñāna</s>) has the characteristic of cognizing; the space-element (<s>ākāśadhātu</s>) has the characteristic of hollowness, belonging to the formless, and of unmanifested characteristic. Thus one investigates their specific characteristics. All these elements are equal in their impermanence, and so on up to their being without self — thus one investigates their general characteristic. For one who has the perception of a compact mass, who does not know the diversity of elements, who is proud regarding this body of diverse elements — confusion is a <s>dharma</s> belonging to the dark side; the reverse belongs to the bright side. Thus one investigates the [dark and bright] sides.

body.translated_text: Therein, how does one investigate the purpose connected with <s>vipaśyanā</s> (insight) whose object is the analysis of elements (<s>dhātuprabheda</s>)? The meaning of lineage (<s>gotra</s>), the meaning of element (<s>dhātu</s>), the meaning of designation (<s>saṃjñā</s>), the meaning of cause (<s>hetu</s>), the meaning of nature (<s>prakṛti</s>) — thus perceiving the meaning, one investigates the meaning. Reflecting upon the six elements — earth and the rest — internally and externally, and applying conviction, one investigates the object-thing.

body.text: atītānāgatapratyutpanneṣvadhvasu ṣaḍdhātūnpratītya mātuḥ kukṣau garbhasyāvakrāntirbhavati | evaṃ kālaṃ paryeṣate |
body.translated_text: Dependent on the six elements in the past, future, and present, there is the descent of the embryo into the mother's womb. Thus one investigates the temporal [dimension].

children.translated_text: It is also a trustworthy tradition; it is also a method based on personal inferential knowledge; it is also a well-established nature, an inconceivable nature. Thus one investigates the reasoning of cause and effect, the reasoning of logical proof, and the reasoning of natural law.

body.translated_text: Just as, dependent on grass, wood, and space being enclosed, a house comes to be designated as 'a house' — just so, dependent on the six elements, and on bones, sinews, skin, flesh, and blood, enclosed in space, there comes to be the designation, concept, and convention: 'body, body.' And the former <s>karma</s> and <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions), together with their own seed, are the cause of these [elements]. Thus one investigates the reasoning of dependency. The analysis of elements (<s>dhātuprabheda</s>), when practiced and cultivated, leads to the abandonment of torpor (<s>styāna</s>).

body.text: kathamānāpānasmṛtyālambananicayaprayuktārthaṃ paryeṣate | āśvāsapraśvāsālambanopanibaddhā cittasyāsaṃpramoṣobhilapanatā | ānāpānasmṛtirityevaṃ paryeṣate | adhyātmamupalabhyate | āśvāsapraśvasāḥ kāyapratibaddhatvādbāhyāyaṃtanasaṃgṛhītāścetyevaṃ vastu paryeṣate | dvāvāśvāsau yaśca vāyuḥ praviśati | ya (sa) āśvāso [yaśca] niṣkrāmati | sa ni[ḥ]śvāsaḥ [|] amī dīrghā āśvāsapraśvāsā, amī hrasvā imānsarvakāyena pratisaṃvedayāmi | imānni(ni)tyevaṃ svalakṣaṇaṃ paryeṣate | niruddhe āśvāsepraśvāsa utpadyate | niruddhe āśvāse (praśvāse) āśvāsaḥ | āśvāsapraśvāsapravṛddhipratisambaddhaṃ ca (||) jīvitendriyamayaṃ ca kāyaḥ savijñānaka ityanityā āśvāsapraśvāsā mahāśravaṇetyevaṃ (ṇā ityevaṃ) sāmānyalakṣaṇaṃ paryeṣate | evamāśvāsapraśvāseṣvanupasthitasmṛteḥ yo vitarkakṛtaḥ saṃkṣobhaścetasaḥ maraṇa(dharma) eṣadharmaḥ kṛṣṇapakṣyaḥ | viparyayācchuklapakṣya (

children.translated_text: and so on in detail. Thus one investigates the [dark and bright] sides.

body.translated_text: How does one investigate the purpose connected with accumulating [merit through] the object of <s>ānāpānasmṛti</s> (mindfulness of breathing)? '<s>Ānāpānasmṛti</s> is the non-forgetfulness and intimate awareness of the mind, which is bound to the object of inhalation and exhalation' — thus one investigates. [Breathing] is observed internally; inhalations and exhalations are bound to the body, and are comprised in what is external and moving — thus one investigates the object-thing. 'There are two [kinds of] breathing: the wind that enters — that is inhalation; and the [wind] that exits — that is exhalation. These inhalations and exhalations are long; these are short; I shall experience all these with the entire body; these are impermanent' — thus one investigates their specific characteristics. 'When the inhalation ceases, the exhalation arises; when the exhalation ceases, the inhalation [arises]. And the life-faculty is connected with the increase of inhalation and exhalation, and this body is endowed with consciousness — therefore inhalations and exhalations are impermanent, of great flux' — thus one investigates their general characteristics. 'For one whose <s>smṛti</s> (mindfulness) is not established on the inhalation and exhalation, the mental disturbance caused by discursive thought (<s>vitarka</s>) — this is a <s>dharma</s> [leading to death], belonging to the dark side; the reverse belongs to the bright side,'

body.text: atītānāgata pratyutpanneṣvadhvasvā [śvāsapra]śvāsapratibaddhaḥ kāyaḥ kāyacitta (ḥ) pratibaddhāścāśvāsapraśvāsā ityevaṃ kālaṃ paryeṣate | nānyatra kaścidya āśvasiti praśvasiti vā asya caite āśvāsapraśvāsāḥ | api tu hetusamutpanneṣu, pratītyasamutpanneṣu saṃskāreṣviyaṃ saṃjñā | prajñaptirvyavahāraḥ ityevamapekṣāyuktiṃ paryeṣate | ānāpānasmṛtirāsevitā bhāvitā vitarkopacchedāya saṃvarttate | āptāgamo 'pyeṣa, pratyātmajñānānusāriko 'pyeṣa vidhiḥ | prasiddhadharmatācintya dharmatetyevaṃ kāryakāraṇayuktimupapattisādhanayuktiṃ dharmatāyuktimparyeṣate |
body.translated_text: 'In the past, future, and present, the body is bound to inhalation and exhalation; and inhalations and exhalations are bound to the body and mind' — thus one investigates the temporal [dimension]. 'There is no one apart [from the formations] who inhales or exhales, and these are his inhalations and exhalations. Rather, among formations arisen from causes and arisen dependently, this is the designation, concept, and convention' — thus one investigates the reasoning of dependency. '<s>Ānāpānasmṛti</s> (mindfulness of breathing), when practiced and cultivated, leads to the cutting off of discursive thought (<s>vitarka</s>).' It is also a trustworthy tradition; it is also a method following personal knowledge through inference; it is also a well-established nature, an inconceivable nature. Thus one investigates the reasoning of cause and effect, the reasoning of logical proof, and the reasoning of natural law.

body.text: evaṃ caritaviśodhanenālambanena ṣaḍvastūni paryeṣya, adhyātmaṃ cittaṃ punaḥ punaḥ śamayataḥ (yan), punaḥ punaretadeva yathāparyeṣitaṃ | vipaśyanākāraiḥ paryeṣate |tasya śamathaṃ niśritya vipaśyanā viśudhyate | vipaśyanāṃ niśritya śamatho vaipulyatāṃ(vipulatāṃ) gacchati | kauśalyālambane ca | kleśāviśodhane ca yā vipaśyanā [|]
body.translated_text: Thus, having investigated the six objects for purifying temperament (<s>caritaviśodhana</s>), while repeatedly calming the mind internally, one investigates this very [content] as previously investigated through the modes of <s>vipaśyanā</s> (insight). For him, relying on <s>śamatha</s> (calm abiding), <s>vipaśyanā</s> is purified; relying on <s>vipaśyanā</s>, <s>śamatha</s> reaches fullness. And the <s>vipaśyanā</s> [concerned with] the object of skill (<s>kauśalyālambana</s>) and the object for purifying defilements (<s>kleśaviśodhana</s>)

body.text: ṣaḍvastukarmitāṃ paścādvakṣmāmi svasthāne |
body.translated_text: I shall explain later, in their proper place, the six-fold practice [of these objects].

children.text: ) ca nava vidhaḥ kṛṣṇapakṣasaṃgṛhīto yoginā veditavyaḥ | tadyathā [a]nurūpaprayogatā, abhyastaprayogatā, aviparītaprayogatā | aśithilaprayogatā | kālaprayogatā | upalakṣaṇaprayogatā | asaṃtuṣṭaprayogatā | avidhuraprayogatā | samyakprayogatā ca | anayā navavidhayā śuklapakṣasaṃgṛhītayā tvaritatvaritaṃ cittaṃ samādhīyate | viśeṣāya ca samādheḥ paraiti | yāvatī cānena bhūmirgantavyā bhavatyanuprāptavyā tāṃ laghu laghvevāgantā bhavatyadhandhāyamānaḥ | kṛṣṇapakṣasaṃgṛhītābhirnavavidhābhiḥ prayogatābhirna tvaritatvarita[ṃ] cittaṃ samādhīyate | nāpi samādhiviśeṣāya paraiti | yāvatī cānena bhūmirgantavyā bhavatyanuprāptavyā | tatra dhandhāyate gamanāya |
children.translated_text: And the ninefold [practice-mode] belonging to the dark side (<s>kṛṣṇapakṣa</s>) should be understood by the <s>yogī</s> (practitioner). They are: practice suited [to one's temperament] (<s>anurūpaprayogatā</s>), practiced application (<s>abhyastaprayogatā</s>), non-erroneous application (<s>aviparītaprayogatā</s>), unrelaxed application (<s>aśithilaprayogatā</s>), timely application (<s>kālaprayogatā</s>), observant application (<s>upalakṣaṇaprayogatā</s>), unsatisfied application (<s>asaṃtuṣṭaprayogatā</s>), unfaltering application (<s>avidhuraprayogatā</s>), and correct application (<s>samyakprayogatā</s>). Through this ninefold [practice] belonging to the bright side (<s>śuklapakṣa</s>), the mind is rapidly and swiftly concentrated, and it proceeds toward the excellence of <s>samādhi</s> (concentration). Whatever stage must be reached and attained by him, he reaches it quickly and lightly without delay. Through the ninefold applications belonging to the dark side, the mind is not rapidly concentrated, nor does it proceed toward the excellence of <s>samādhi</s>. And whatever stage must be reached and attained by him, he is delayed in reaching it.

body.translated_text: Therein, the ninefold practice comprised in the bright [side] — and by its opposite,

body.text: katamānurūpaprayogatā (ca) | sa cedrāgacarito 'śubhāyāṃ cittamupanibaghnāti | dveṣacarito maitryāṃ, yāvadvitarkacarita ānāpānasmṛtau, samabhāgacaritaḥ mandarajaskaḥ punaḥ yatrālambane priyārohatā bhavati | tena prayujyate | iyamanurūpaprayogatā [|]
body.translated_text: What is practice suited [to one's temperament] (<s>anurūpaprayogatā</s>)? If he is of passionate temperament, he binds the mind to the meditation on the unattractive (<s>aśubhā</s>). If of hateful temperament, to <s>maitrī</s> (loving-kindness); up to: if of discursive temperament, to <s>ānāpānasmṛti</s> (mindfulness of breathing). If of balanced temperament with little defilement, he applies himself to whatever object he finds agreeable. This is practice suited [to one's temperament].

children.translated_text: he is not in every way a complete beginner. For a beginner, even when not applying himself to an appropriate object, the hindrances do not frequently arise, nor does bodily and mental rigidity (<s>kāyacittadauṣṭhulya</s>). Whereby his mind becomes concentrated. This is practiced application. Therein, what is unrelaxed application (<s>aśithilaprayogatā</s>)? He practices continuously (<s>sātatyaprayogī</s>) and earnestly (<s>satkṛtyaprayogī</s>). If he rises from <s>samādhi</s> for the purpose of alms-round, or for attending upon a teacher with respect, or for attending the sick, or for performing proper duties, or for some other matter of a similar kind — for whatever purpose, he does everything with a mind inclined toward it, directed toward it, and weighted toward it. Having done it quickly and lightly, having completed it, he again applies himself, restraining himself for seclusion. If he meets with assemblies of monks, nuns, laypeople, <s>Kṣatriyas</s>, or <s>Brāhmaṇas</s>, he does not pass a long time in socializing. He speaks little and does not start lengthy conversations. He does not let himself be drawn elsewhere. And he has aroused vigor thus: 'May I this very day attain what is to be attained!' For what reason? 'Many are the conditions for my death — wind may disturb me, bile may, phlegm may, food may be improperly digested causing cholera to settle in the body; a snake may bite me, or a scorpion, or a centipede; there is also danger from humans.' These ever-present possibilities

body.translated_text: What is practiced application (<s>abhyastaprayogatā</s>)? He has done practice such that even at the very least

body.translated_text: Therein, what is non-erroneous application (<s>aviparītaprayogatā</s>)? From time to time he cultivates the sign of calm (<s>śamathanimittā</s>), the sign of exertion (<s>pragrahanimittā</s>), and the sign of equanimity (<s>upekṣānimittā</s>).
