[He knows] exertion (<s>pragraha</s>), the sign of exertion, and the time for exertion. [He knows] equanimity (<s>upekṣā</s>), the sign of equanimity, and the time for equanimity.

body.text: tatra śamathaḥ navākārā cittasthitiḥ | nirnimittañca taccittaṃ tatra bhavati, nirvikalpaṃ, śānta praśāntaṃ, śamathasthitaṃ, niṣkevalaṃ, tenocyate śamatha iti | tatra śamathanimittaṃ dvividhamālambananimittaṃ, (

children.text: ) nidānanimittañca | jñeyavastusabhāgaṃ pratibimbamālambananimittaṃ | yenālambanena taccittaṃ śamayati, śamathaparibhāvite cetasi uttaratra śamathasya pāriśuddhaye | yo vipaśyanā prayoga idaṃ nidānaṃ (na)nimittaṃ [|] śamathakālaḥ katamaḥ | āha | uddhate citte ūrdhvamvābhiśaṃkini śamathasya kālo bhāvanāyai | tathā vipaśyanāparibhāvite citte iti karaṇīyavyākṣepopahate śamathakālo bhāvanāyai | tatra vipaśyanā caturākārātrimukhī ṣaḍvastuprabhedālambanavyavacārā ||
children.translated_text: and the causal sign (<s>nidānanimittā</s>). The reflected image (<s>pratibimba</s>) similar to the knowable object is the object-sign — the object by which the mind is calmed. When the mind has been thoroughly cultivated by <s>śamatha</s>, for the further purification of <s>śamatha</s>, whatever practice of <s>vipaśyanā</s> (insight) [is undertaken] — this is the causal sign. What is the time for <s>śamatha</s>? He says: When the mind is agitated or when one suspects agitation above, it is the time for cultivating <s>śamatha</s>. Likewise, when the mind has been thoroughly cultivated by <s>vipaśyanā</s>, [i.e., when] it is impaired by the scattering of activities that need to be done, it is the time for cultivating <s>śamatha</s>. Therein, <s>vipaśyanā</s> has four aspects, three approaches, and operates with six categories of objects.

body.translated_text: Therein, <s>śamatha</s> (calm) is the nine-aspected mental stability (<s>navākārā cittasthiti</s>). That mind therein is without a sign (<s>nirnimitta</s>), without conceptual elaboration (<s>nirvikalpa</s>), peaceful, deeply peaceful, established in calm, free from turbidity — therefore it is called <s>śamatha</s>. The sign of <s>śamatha</s> is twofold: the object-sign (<s>ālambananimittā</s>),

body.text: tatra vipaśyanānimittaṃ dvividhamālambananimitta[ṃ] nidānanimittañca | tatrālambananimittaṃ vipaśyanānimittaṃ [śamatha]pakṣyaṃ jñeyavastusabhāgaṃ pratibimbamālambananimittaṃ yenālambanena prajñāṃ vyavacārayati | tatra nidānanimittaṃ vipaśyanāparibhāvite cetasi uttaratra vipaśyanāpariśuddhaye cetaḥ śamathabimbayogaḥ [|]
body.translated_text: The sign of <s>vipaśyanā</s> is also twofold: the object-sign and the causal sign. The object-sign of <s>vipaśyanā</s> belonging to the <s>śamatha</s>-side is the reflected image similar to the knowable object — the object by which one conducts wisdom (<s>prajñā</s>). The causal sign: when the mind has been thoroughly cultivated by <s>vipaśyanā</s>, for the further purification of <s>vipaśyanā</s>, the practice of mental calm (<s>cetaḥśamatha</s>) upon the object [is undertaken].

body.text: tatra vipaśyanākālaḥ śamathaparibhāvite cetasi ādita eva cājñeyavastuyathābhūtāvabodhāya vipaśyanāyāḥ kālo bhāvanāyai |
body.translated_text: Therein, the time for <s>vipaśyanā</s>: when the mind has been thoroughly cultivated by <s>śamatha</s>, and initially, for the understanding of the knowable object as it truly is, it is the time for cultivating <s>vipaśyanā</s>.

body.text: tatra pragrahaḥ katamaḥ | yānyatamānyatamena prasadanīyenālambanenodgṛhītena (

children.text: ) cittasaṃharṣaṇā saṃdarśanā samādāpanā [|] tatra pragrahanimittaṃ yena ca prasadanīyenālambanena nimittena cittaṃ pragṛhṇāti | yasya vīryārambhaḥ tadānulomikastatra pragrahakālaḥ līnaṃ cittaṃ līnatvābhiśaṃkini pragrahasya kālo bhāvanāyai |
children.translated_text: is the gladdening, displaying, and encouraging of the mind. The sign of exertion: the inspiring object-sign by which one uplifts the mind. The initial arousal of effort that accords with it. The time for exertion: when the mind is sluggish or when one suspects sluggishness, it is the time for cultivating exertion.

body.translated_text: Therein, what is exertion (<s>pragraha</s>)? That which, through any inspiring object (<s>prasadanīyālambana</s>) that has been taken up,

body.text: tatropekṣākatamā | yā ālambane asaṃkliṣṭacetasaḥ cittasamatā śamathavipaśyanāpakṣe | prasa(śa)ṭhasvarasaṃvāhitā | karmaṇyacittasya ca karmaṇyatā, cittasyānupradānamanābhogakriyā | tatropekṣānimittaṃ | yena cālambanena cittamadhyupekṣate | yā ca tasminnevālambane vīryodrekāpratikāyatā | tatropekṣākālaḥ śamathavipaśyanā pakṣālayau (lau)ddhatyavinirmukte cetasi (

children.translated_text: it is the time for cultivating equanimity. This is timely application (<s>kālaprayogatā</s>).

body.translated_text: Therein, what is equanimity (<s>upekṣā</s>)? That which is the mental evenness (<s>cittasamatā</s>) of a mind unafflicted toward the object, belonging to the side of <s>śamatha</s> and <s>vipaśyanā</s>, flowing naturally, the workability of a workable mind, the letting go of the mind, and effortless activity. The sign of equanimity: the object by which one maintains equanimity toward the mind, and the non-resistance to the excess of effort regarding that very object. The time for equanimity: when the mind is freed from sluggishness and restlessness, both on the side of <s>śamatha</s> and <s>vipaśyanā</s>,

body.text: tatra katamā upekṣā lakṣaṇā (upalakṣaṇa)prayogatā [|] tānyeva nimittāni sugṛhītāni bhavanti | susaṃlakṣitāni yeṣāṃ sūdgṛhītatvāt | yadā ākāṃkṣate | tadā vyuttiṣṭhate samādhigocaraṃ (|) pratibimbamutsṛjya samāhitabhūmikāprākṛtālambanamanasikāreṇa [|] iyamupalakṣaṇāprayogatā |
body.translated_text: Therein, what is observant application (<s>upalakṣaṇaprayogatā</s>)? Those very signs have been well-grasped, well-observed; because they are well-grasped, whenever he wishes, he rises from the domain of <s>samādhi</s>, releasing the reflected image (<s>pratibimba</s>), and [returns to] the mental attention of the ordinary object belonging to the concentrated plane. This is observant application.

body.text: tatra katamā asaṃtuṣṭaprayogatā | asaṃtuṣṭo bhavati kuśalai-kuśalairdhamaiḥ | aprativā (bhā)ṇi(ṇī) ca | prahāsairuttaraṃ praṇītataraṃ sthānamabhiprārthayamānorupī bahulaṃ viharatīti | nālpamātrakenā (ṇā)varamātrakenā(ṇā)ntarā viṣādamāpadyate | atyuttare karaṇīye | iyamasaṃtuṣṭaprayogatā |
body.translated_text: Therein, what is unsatisfied application (<s>asaṃtuṣṭaprayogatā</s>)? He is unsatisfied with wholesome <s>dharmas</s>, and is not complacent. Aspiring to what is higher and more excellent, abandoning what is lower, he dwells abundantly. He does not fall into discouragement in the middle, on account of a small or inferior [achievement], when there is something still higher to be accomplished. This is unsatisfied application.

body.text: tatra katamā avidhuraprayogatā | śikṣāpadasamādānamvā na khaṇḍīkaroti, na chi(cchi)drīkaroti | na ca śiśumudāravarṇaṃ raṃjanīyaṃ mātṛgrāmaṃ dṛṣṭvā nimittagrāhī bhavatyanuvyaṃjanagrāhī, bhojane ca samakārī bhavati | jāgarikānuyuktaścālpārtholpakṛtyolpavyāsakaḥ | cirakṛtacirabhāṣitamanusmarttā bhavatyanusmārayitā | ityevaṃbhāgīyā dharmā avidhuraprayogatetyucyate | anukūlā ete dharmāścittaikāgratāyāḥ | avidūrā, na ca cittakṣepāya samvarttante | tena bahirdhā vyāsaṃgāya, nādhyātmacittākarmaṇyatāyai | (
body.translated_text: Therein, what is unfaltering application (<s>avidhuraprayogatā</s>)? He does not break or puncture the undertaking of the training rules. He does not, upon seeing a young woman of fine complexion, charming, grasp at the sign or at the secondary characteristics. He is moderate in food. He is devoted to wakefulness and is one of few needs, few tasks, and few concerns. He remembers and recollects what was done and said long ago. Such and similar <s>dharmas</s> are called unfaltering application. These <s>dharmas</s> are favorable to one-pointedness of mind, are close [to concentration], and do not conduce to the scattering of the mind — that is, to external engagement or to the internal unwieldiness of the mind.

body.text: tatra samyakprayogatā katamā | adhimucyādhimucyālambanasya vibhāvanayā samyakprayoga ityucyate | sa cedaśubhāprayukto bhavatyaśubhāṃ cāśubhākārairmanasikaroti | nimittamātrānusāriṇyā vipaśyanayā [|] tena manasikārastadālambano muhurmuhurvibhāvayitavyo, muhurmuhuḥ saṃmukhīkartavyaḥ |
body.translated_text: Therein, what is correct application (<s>samyakprayogatā</s>)? By intensifying, again and again, the vivification of the object through conviction (<s>adhimukti</s>), it is called correct application. If he is applied to the meditation on the unattractive (<s>aśubhā</s>), he attends to the unattractive with the aspects of unattractiveness, through <s>vipaśyanā</s> (insight) that follows the mere sign. By that mental attention, the object should be vivified again and again, made present again and again.

body.text: vibhāvanā punaḥ pañcavidhā adhyātmacittābhisaṃkṣepataḥ | asmṛtyamanasikārataḥ | tadanyamanasikārataḥ | pratipakṣamanasikārataḥ | ānimittadhātumanasikārataśca | tatra navākāracittasthityā vipaśyanā pūrvaṃgamayā adhyātmaṃ cittābhisaṃkṣepataḥ | sarvanimittavaipulyena āditaḥ | avikṣepāyopa nibadhnato 'smṛtyamanasikārataḥ | samāhitabhūmikādālambanālambanāntaraṃ samāhitabhūmikameva manasikurvatastadanyamanasikārataḥ | śubhatāpratipakṣeṇāśubhāṃtā (bhatāṃ) yāvadvitarkapratipakṣeṇa ānāpānasmṛtiṃ | rūpapratipakṣeṇākāśadhātu[ṃ] manasi kurvataḥ pratipakṣamanasikārataḥ | sarvanimittānāmamanasikārādānimittasya ca dhātormanasikārādāninimittadhātumanasikārataḥ | api ca | vyāpya tadālambanaṃ vibhāvanālakṣaṇaṃ vyavasthāpitamasmiṃstvarthe adhyātmaṃ nimittābhisaṃkṣepataḥ | asmṛtyamanasikārataścābhipretā | (

children.text: ) tatrādikarmike(ṇa) tatprathamakalpiko (karmikeṇa) ādita eva cittaṃ na kañci(kvaci)dālambane upanibandhitavyaṃ | aśubhāyāmvā, tadasminvā, nānyatra vikṣepāyaiva | kaccinme cittaṃ nirnimittaṃ, nirvikalpaṃ śāntaṃ, praśāntamavicalamavikampyamanutsukaṃ, nirvyāpāpāramadhyātmamabhiramata iti | tathā prayukta utpannotpanneṣu sarvabāhyanimitteṣu asmṛtyamanasikāraṃ karoti | iyamasyāsmṛtyamanasikāreṇālambanavibhāvanā [|]
children.translated_text: Therein, at first, the beginner (<s>ādikarmika</s>) should not bind his mind to any particular object whatsoever — whether to the unattractive or to anything else — so as not to cause distraction. [He should think:] 'Is my mind without a sign, without conceptual elaboration, peaceful, deeply peaceful, unmoving, unshaking, free from eagerness, free from busyness, delighting internally?' While thus engaged, regarding all external signs as they arise, he performs non-attention and non-mindfulness. This is his vivification of the object through non-attention and non-mindfulness.

body.translated_text: Vivification (<s>vibhāvanā</s>) is fivefold: through internal mental contraction (<s>adhyātmacittābhisaṃkṣepa</s>), through non-attention and non-mindfulness (<s>asmṛtyamanasikāra</s>), through attention to something other (<s>tadanyamanasikāra</s>), through antidotal attention (<s>pratipakṣamanasikāra</s>), and through attention to the signless element (<s>ānimittadhātumanasikāra</s>). Therein, through the nine-aspected mental stability preceded by <s>vipaśyanā</s>, internally through mental contraction — from the very beginning, through the fullness of all signs, binding [the mind] for the sake of non-distraction, through non-attention and non-mindfulness. Making mental attention from one object to another within the concentrated plane, through attention to something other. Attending to the unattractive as the antidote to the attractive, up to attending to <s>ānāpānasmṛti</s> (mindfulness of breathing) as the antidote to discursive thought, and attending to the space-element as the antidote to form — through antidotal attention. Through the non-attention to all signs and the attention to the signless element — through attention to the signless element. Moreover, pervading that object, the characteristic of vivification is established in this sense: through internal contraction upon the sign; and through non-attention and non-mindfulness as intended.

body.text: sa tatra yogaṃ kurvan pratigṛhṇāti, sa nirmimitte cālambane savikalpamaśubhādike carati | kathaṃ ca punaścarati | nimittamātrānusāriṇyā vipaśyanayā paryeṣaṇāpratyavekṣaṇānucāriṇyā [|] na caikāṃśena vipaśyanāprayukto bhavati | punareva vipaśyanānimittaṃ (|) pratyudāvartya tadevālambanaṃ śamathākāreṇa manasi karoti | tena tadālambanaṃ tasminsamaye muktaṃ bhavati, nodgṛhītaṃ | yasmāttadālambanaḥ śamatho vartate | tasmānna muktaḥ | yasmānna nimittīkaroti | na vikalpayati | tasmānnodgṛhītamevamadhyātmamabhisaṃkṣepataḥ | ālambanaṃ vibhāvayati | (

children.text: ) tatra vipaśyanānimittamudgṛhītavataḥ | punarjñeyavastunimittālambanaṃ sa cedayamekāṃśenālambanamadhimucyate | na punaḥ punarvibhāvayet | nāsyādhimokṣa uttarottaraḥ | pariśuddhaḥ, paryavadātaḥ | pravartate | yāvaj jñeyavastupratyakṣopagamāya | yataśca punaḥ punaradhimucyate | punaḥ punarvibhāvayati | tatosyottarottarodhimokṣaḥ | pariśuddhataraḥ, pariśuddhatamaḥ pravartate | yāvajjñeyavastupratyakṣopagamāya | tadyathā citrakaraścitrakarāntevāsī vā tatprathamaścitrakarmaṇi prayuktaḥ syāt | sa ācāryasyāntikācchikṣāpūrvagamaṃ rūpakamādāya dṛṣṭvā dṛṣṭavā pratirūpakaṃ karoti | kṛtvā kṛtvā vibhāvayati, vināśayati | punareva ca karoti | ya yathā yathā bhaṅktyā bhaṅktyā karoti | tathā tathāsyottaraṃ rūpakaṃ pariśuddhataraṃ paryavadātataraṃ khyāti | evaṃ hi samyakprayuktaḥ kālāntareṇācāryasamatāṃ gacchati | tatprativiśiṣṭatāmvā [|] sacetpunarabhaṃ(narbhaṃ?) ktyā tadrūpakaṃ tasyaivopariṣṭātpaunaḥpunyena kuryāt | na janvandhasya tadrūpakapariśuddhiṃ nigacchedevamihāpi nayo veditavyaḥ | tatra yāvadālambanamadhimucyate | tāvadvibhāvayati | na tvavaśyaṃ yāvadvibhāvayati | tāvadadhimucyate | parīttamadhimucyate, parīttameva vibhāvayati | evaṃ yāvanmahadgatapramāṇaṃ | parīttaṃ punarvibhāvayitvā (bhāvya) (
children.translated_text: Therein, for one who has grasped the sign of <s>vipaśyanā</s> (insight), the knowable object becomes the sign-object. If this person resolves upon the object in only one way and does not repeatedly refine it, then his resolution does not progress as ever more purified and cleansed — up to the direct approach to the knowable object. But when one repeatedly resolves and repeatedly refines, then one's resolution becomes progressively more purified and more cleansed — up to the direct approach to the knowable object. Just as a painter or a painter's apprentice who has first engaged in the work of painting, having taken a model image from the teacher, views it again and again, makes a copy, and having made it, refines it, discards it, and makes it again. The more times one remakes it, the more the resulting image appears progressively more purified and more cleansed. Thus, one who is properly engaged, in the course of time, reaches equality with the teacher — or even superiority. But if one were to keep remaking that image over and over on top of the same [surface] without discarding it, one would never arrive at the purity of that image, just as a person born blind [could never do so]. The same principle should be understood here. Therein, to the extent that one resolves upon the object, to that extent one refines it; but it is not necessarily the case that to the extent one refines, to that extent one resolves. One resolves upon a limited [scope] and refines just that limited [scope]. Likewise up to the great and immeasurable. And having refined the limited,

children.text: ) kadācitparīttamevādhimucyate | kadācinmahadgatameva | pramāṇamevaṃ mahadgate | pramāṇe veditavyaṃ | tatra rūpiṇāṃ dharmāṇāṃ yannimittaṃ pratibimbaṃ, pratibhāsaṃ(saḥ) tadaudārikaṃ nirmāṇasadṛśamarūpiṇāmvā punardharmāṇāṃ nāmasaṃketapūrvakaṃ yathānubhāvādhipateyaṃ | pratibhāsamiyamucyate | samyakprayogatā | saiṣā navavidhā śuklapakṣyā śamathavipaśyanānulomā prayogatā veditavyā | evaṃ paryāyeṇa navākāraiva vilomatā | sa eṣa kṛṣṇaśuklapakṣavyavasthānenāṣṭādaśavidhaprayogo bhavatīyamucyate ekāgratā ||
children.translated_text: sometimes one resolves upon just the limited, sometimes upon the great. The same should be understood for the immeasurable. Therein, the sign — the reflected image (<s>pratibimba</s>), the appearance (<s>pratibhāsa</s>) — of material <s>dharmas</s> is gross, similar to a magical creation (<s>nirmāṇa</s>). But for immaterial <s>dharmas</s>, preceded by name-conventions, according to the predominance of one's experience — this is the appearance. This is called proper practice. These nine [kinds of] proper practice should be understood as the bright-side practice in conformity with <s>śamatha</s> (calm abiding) and <s>vipaśyanā</s> (insight). Likewise, by way of reversal, the nine aspects constitute adverse practice. This practice, through the arrangement of the dark and bright sides, becomes eighteen-fold — this is called one-pointedness (<s>ekāgratā</s>).

body.translated_text: While practicing yoga there, he grasps [the object]; he moves in a sign-less object and with conceptualization in the unattractive and other [meditations]. And how does he move? Through <s>vipaśyanā</s> (insight) that follows the mere sign, through investigation, examination, and following. He is not exclusively applied to <s>vipaśyanā</s>. Then again, turning back from the sign of <s>vipaśyanā</s>, he attends to that very object in the mode of <s>śamatha</s> (calm). Therefore, at that time, that object is released, not grasped. Since <s>śamatha</s> with that as its object is operative, therefore it is not released. Since he does not make a sign, does not conceptualize — therefore it is not grasped. In this way, internally through contraction, he vivifies the object.

body.text: tatrāvaraṇaviśuddhiḥ katamā | āha | caturbhiḥ kāraṇairevaṃ samyakprayukto yogī āvaraṇe svañcittaṃ pariśodhayati | svabhāvaparijñānena, nidānenādīnavaparijñānena, pratipakṣabhāvanayā ca |
body.translated_text: Therein, what is the purification from obstacles (<s>āvaraṇaviśuddhi</s>)? He says: through four causes, the <s>yogī</s> who is properly engaged purifies the mind from obstacles — through understanding their essential nature (<s>svabhāva</s>), through understanding their cause (<s>nidāna</s>), through understanding their danger (<s>ādīnava</s>), and through cultivating their antidote (<s>pratipakṣa</s>).

body.text: tatra katama āvaraṇasvabhāvaḥ | āha | catvāryāvaraṇāni | paritamanā, nivaraṇaṃ, vitarkaḥ | (

children.text: ) ātmasaṃpragrahaśceti | tatra paritamanā yā naiṣkramyaprāvivekyaprayuktasya kliṣṭā utkaṇṭhā, aratiḥ | spṛhaṇā, daurmanasyamupāyāsaḥ | tatra nivaraṇaṃ kāmacchandādīni pañcanivaraṇāni | tatra vitarkaḥ kāmavitarkādayaḥ | kliṣṭā vitarkāḥ | tatrātmasaṃpragraho yadaṇumātrekā (ṇā)varamātrekena (ṇa) jñānadarśanasparśamātrakenā(ṇā)tmānaṃ saṃpragṛhṇāti | ahamasmi lābhī, anye ca na tatheti | pūrvavadvistareṇa veditavyamayamāvaraṇasvabhāvaḥ |
children.translated_text: and <s>ātmasaṃpragraha</s> (self-conceit). Therein, <s>paritamanā</s> (distress) is the afflicted longing, discontent, craving, mental anguish, and vexation of one engaged in renunciation and seclusion. Therein, the hindrances (<s>nīvaraṇa</s>) are the five hindrances beginning with sensual desire (<s>kāmacchanda</s>). Therein, discursive thoughts (<s>vitarka</s>) are the afflicted thoughts beginning with thoughts of sensuality (<s>kāmavitarka</s>). Therein, self-conceit (<s>ātmasaṃpragraha</s>) is when, upon the slightest or merest contact with knowledge and vision, one grasps at the self, [thinking:] 'I am an attainer; others are not like this' — and so forth in detail as before. This is the essential nature of obstacles.

body.translated_text: Therein, what is the essential nature of the obstacles? He says: there are four obstacles — <s>paritamanā</s> (distress),  <s>nīvaraṇa</s> (hindrance), <s>vitarka</s> (discursive thought),

body.text: tatra paritamanā yāvatṣaṇnidānāni | tadyathā pūrvakarmādhipatyā, vyādhiparikleśādvā āśrayadaurbalyaṃ | atiprayogaḥ | ardhaprayogaḥ | ādiprayogaḥ | kleśapracuratā | vivekānabhyāsaśca nivaraṇasya, vitarkāṇāmātmasaṃpragrahasya nivaraṇasthānīye, avitarkasthānīye, svātmasaṃpragrahasthānīyeṣu dharmeṣvayoniśomanasikāro bahulīkāranivaraṇavitarkasaṃpragrahāṇāṃ nidānaṃ (

children.text: ) yadaśubhatāmamanasi kṛtya śubhatāṃ manasikarotyayamatrāyoniśaḥ | evaṃ maitrīṃ [ṃ] manasikṛtya, prahāya naimitta (tti) [kī]mālokasaṃjñā[ṃ] manasikṛtyāndhakāranimittaṃ śamathamamanasikṛtya, jñātijānapadāmaravitarkaṃ paurāṇakrīḍitahasitarasitaparicāritaṃ | iyaṃ (daṃ) pratyayatā pratītyasamutpādamamanasikṛtya, traiyaghvikeṣvahamiti vā, mameti vā, ayogavihitāṃ saṃjñāṃ manasi karotyayamatrāyoniśasta(śaḥ) |
children.translated_text: When, disregarding the unattractive (<s>aśubha</s>), one attends to the attractive — this is the improper [attention] here. Likewise, disregarding <s>maitrī</s> (loving-kindness) [and attending to malice]; disregarding the perception of light and attending to the sign of darkness; disregarding <s>śamatha</s> (calm abiding) [and attending to] thoughts about relatives, countryfolk, and the immortals, reminiscences of former amusements, laughter, jests, and pastimes; disregarding conditionality and <s>pratītyasamutpāda</s> (dependent origination) [and attending to] 'I' or 'mine' — inappropriately formed perceptions regarding the three time-periods — this is the improper [attention] here.

body.translated_text: Therein, <s>paritamanā</s> (distress) has up to six causes (<s>nidāna</s>). Namely: bodily weakness due to the predominance of past <s>karma</s> or from the affliction of disease; excessive effort; half-hearted effort; initial effort [only]; prevalence of defilements; and unfamiliarity with seclusion. For the hindrances, discursive thoughts, and self-conceit — improper mental attention (<s>ayoniśomanasikāra</s>) to <s>dharmas</s> that stand in the position of hindrances, discursive thoughts, and self-conceit, and its habitual repetition, is the cause of hindrances, discursive thoughts, and self-conceit.

body.text:
tatrādīnavaḥ katamaḥ | asminnāvaraṇe sati saṃvidyamāne caturvidhepyanadhigataṃ nādhigatāt parihīyate | yogaprayogādbhraśyate | saṃkliṣṭavihārī ca bhavati, duḥkhavihārī ca bhavatyātmā caitamavavadati | parataścāvavādaṃlabhate | kāyasya ca bhedāt paraṃ maraṇādapāyeṣūpapadyate | ayamatrādīnavaḥ |
tatra pratipakṣaḥ katamaḥ | tatra paritamanā yā samāsato 'nusmṛtayaḥ | pratipakṣaḥ anusmṛtimanasikāreṇāyaṃ cittaṃ saṃhaṣayitvā (saṃharṣya) utpannāṃ paritamanāṃ prativinodayatyu(tyanu)tpannāṃ ca notpādayati | tatra yacca kāyadaurbalyaṃ, yaścāpratiyogo, yaścādiprayogaḥ | tatra vīryasamatā pratiṣe(ve)dhaḥ | pratipannaḥ yordhaprayogaḥ [|] tatra śuśrūṣā, paripṛcchā pratipakṣaḥ | yā kleśapracuratā tasyā (

children.text: ) yathāyogamaśubhādyālambanaprayogaḥ | pratipakṣaḥ | yo 'nabhyāsastasyaivaṃvidhaṃ pratisaṃkhyānaṃ pratipakṣaḥ | pūrvaṃ me (mayā)vivekābhyāso na kṛto, yena me etarhi vivekaprayuktasya paritamanā utpadyate [|] sa cedetarhi na kariṣyāmyabhyāsaḥ (saṃ) evamāyati[ḥ] punarbhava evaṃrūpo bhaviṣyati | pratisaṃkhyāya mayā aratistyaktavyā | ratiḥ karaṇīyetyevamiṣṭānāṃ nivaraṇādīnāmayoniśomanasikāraviparyaryeṇa yoniśomanasikārabhāvanā pratipakṣo veditavyaḥ |
children.translated_text: the application of an appropriate object such as <s>aśubhā</s> (the unattractive) and the like is the antidote. For unfamiliarity [with seclusion], the antidote is analytical reflection of this kind: 'Previously I did not cultivate familiarity with seclusion; therefore distress arises in me now when engaged in seclusion. If I do not practice now, in future existences I shall be of the same kind.' Having so reflected: 'I must abandon discontent and cultivate delight.' Thus, for the stated hindrances and the rest, the antidote should be understood as the cultivation of proper mental attention (<s>yoniśomanasikāra</s>), the reversal of improper mental attention.

body.translated_text: Therein, what is the danger (<s>ādīnava</s>)? When this obstacle is present, one does not attain the four [fruits that are] unattained, nor does one not decline from what has been attained. One falls away from the application of <s>yoga</s>. One becomes a dweller in defilement and a dweller in suffering. And one's own self reproaches one, and from others one receives reproach. And after the breakup of the body, after death, one is reborn in the lower realms. This is the danger here. Therein, what is the antidote? For <s>paritamanā</s> (distress), in summary, the <s>anusmṛtis</s> (recollections) are the antidote. Through the mental attention of recollection, one gladdening the mind removes arisen distress and prevents unarisen [distress] from arising. For bodily weakness, lack of counter-effort, and initial-only effort — the antidote is the equalization of vigor (<s>vīryasamatā</s>). For excessive effort — reverence and questioning are the antidote. For prevalence of defilements,

body.text: tatra svabhāvaṃ parijñāya āvaraṇataḥ, saṃkleśataḥ, tāvacchamathabāhulyaṃ [|] sā khalveṣā vipaśyanā jñeyā (

children.text: ) kṛṣṇapakṣataḥ | parivarjanīyametaditi | nidānaparivarjanācca punarasya parivarjaneti | nidānaṃ paryeṣate | aparivarjanācca punarasya parivarjanīyasya ko doṣa ityata ādīnavaṃ paryeṣate | parivarjitasya cāyatyāṃ kathamanutpādo bhavatītyataḥ pratipakṣaṃ bhāvayatyevamanenāvaraṇebhyaścittaṃ pariśodhitaṃ bhavati |
children.translated_text: from the dark side [perspective]: 'This is to be avoided.' And from avoiding its cause, there is the avoidance of this [obstacle]. One investigates the cause. 'And if this, which is to be avoided, is not avoided, what is the fault?' — thus one investigates the danger. 'And how does the non-arising of the avoided [obstacle] come about in the future?' — for this purpose one cultivates the antidote. Thus, by this [method], one's mind becomes purified from the obstacles.

body.translated_text: Therein, having understood the essential nature of the obstacle — [understanding it] as an obstacle, as a source of defilement — to that extent [there is] predominance of <s>śamatha</s>. This very insight (<s>vipaśyanā</s>) should be understood

body.text: sa tatra yāvaddeśanābāhulyaṃ vipaśyanānulomikaṃ tāvadvipaśyanābāhulyaṃ, yāvadvivapaśyanā bāhulyaṃ nānyādanantā veditavyā | yaduta ebhireva tribhirmukhaiḥ ṣaṇṇāṃ vastūnāmekaikaśyā (syā a)nantākārapraveśanayena, yathā ca yathā vipaśyanā samyakprayuktasya pṛthuvṛddhivaipulyatāṃ (vipulatāṃ) gacchatyabhyāsapāriśuddhibalamadhipatiṃ kṛtvā, tathā, tathā, śamathapakṣasyāpi kāyacittapraśrabdhijanakasya pṛthuvṛddhivaipulyatā (vipulatā) veditavyā | tasya yathā yathā kāyaḥ praśrabhyate, cittaṃ ca, tathā tathālambanacittaikāgratāyāśca yadutāśraya[ṃ] vivarddhayate | yathā cittaikāgratā vivardhate tathā tathā kāyaḥ praśrabhyate, cittaṃ ca, ityetau dvau dharmāvanyonyaṃ nirvṛtāvanyonyaṃ pratibaddhoyaduta cittaikāgratā, pratyakṣajñānotpattiḥ |
body.translated_text: Therein, to the extent that there is predominance of teaching [i.e., analytical investigation] in conformity with <s>vipaśyanā</s>, to that extent there is predominance of <s>vipaśyanā</s>; to the extent that there is predominance of <s>vipaśyanā</s>, there is nothing else beyond it to be known — namely, through precisely these three methods, by entering each of the six objects through infinite aspects. And just as <s>vipaśyanā</s> grows, develops, and expands for one who is properly engaged, by making the power of purification through practice predominant — so too should the growth, development, and expansion of the <s>śamatha</s> (calm) side, which generates pliancy of body and mind (<s>kāyacittapraśrabdhi</s>), be understood. As the body becomes pliant and the mind [becomes pliant], the one-pointedness of mind on the object develops in its support. As one-pointedness of mind develops, the body becomes pliant and the mind [becomes pliant]. Thus, these two <s>dharmas</s> are mutually productive and mutually dependent — namely, one-pointedness of mind and the arising of direct perceptual knowledge.

body.text: tatra kiyatā aśubhā pratilabdho(dhā) bhavati | kiyatā yāvadānāpānasmṛtiḥ pratilabdhā bhavatīti | (

children.text: ) peyālaṃ ataścāsya yoginaḥ aśubhāprayogasyāsevanānvayāt bhāvanānvayādbahulīkārānvayāccarato vā, viharato vā, viṣayasaṃmukhībhāve [a]pi nimittapratyavekṣaṇayāpi prakṛtyaivānabhisaṃskāreṇa bahutarāśubhatāsaṃprakhyānaṃ | yathāpi tatsubhāvitatvādaśubhāyāḥ kāmarāgasthānīyeṣu dharmeṣu cittaṃ [na] praskandati | na prasīdati | nādhimucyate | upekṣā saṃtiṣṭhate | nirvitpratikūlatā veditavyaṃ(yā) | yoginānuprāpto (ptaṃ)me, aśubhāprāptaṃ me, bhāvanāphalamiyatā aśubhā pratilabdhā bhavati | viparyayeṇa [a]pratilabdhā veditavyā | yathā aśubhā evaṃ maitrī, idaṃpratyayatāpratītyasamutpādaḥ | dhātuprabhedaḥ | ānāpānasmṛtiśca veditavyā | tatrāyaṃ viśeṣaḥ bahutaraṃ maitracittatā khyāti | na pratighanimittaṃ | vyāpādasthānīyeṣu dharmeṣu cittaṃ na praskandatīti vistaraḥ | bahutaramanityatā, duḥkhatā, nairātmyaṃ khyāti, na nityasukhasattvāya dṛṣṭisahagataṃ sammohanimittaṃ mohaparyavasthānīyeṣu dharmeṣu | cittaṃ (na)praskandatīti (
children.translated_text: And so forth in brief. Consequently, for this <s>yogī</s>, through the course of repeated practice, cultivation, and frequent engagement in the application of <s>aśubhā</s>, whether going about or dwelling, even when face-to-face with the object, through the examination of the sign, naturally and spontaneously, a more abundant appearance of unattractiveness [manifests]. When, through the well-cultivatedness of <s>aśubhā</s>, the mind does not rush toward <s>dharmas</s> that stand in the position of sensual desire (<s>kāmarāga</s>), does not delight in them, does not resolve upon them, and equanimity is established — without revulsion — this should be known [as the sign of attainment]. [The <s>yogī</s> reflects:] 'It has been attained by me; the fruit of meditation of <s>aśubhā</s> has been attained by me.' To this extent, <s>aśubhā</s> is attained. In the opposite case, it should be known as not attained. As with <s>aśubhā</s>, so too <s>maitrī</s> (loving-kindness), conditionality and <s>pratītyasamutpāda</s> (dependent origination), analysis of the <s>dhātus</s> (elements), and <s>ānāpānasmṛti</s> (mindfulness of breathing) should be understood. Therein, the distinction is: a more abundant appearance of loving-minded state manifests; the sign of hostility does not [appear]; the mind does not rush toward <s>dharmas</s> standing in the position of malice (<s>vyāpāda</s>) — and so forth in detail. A more abundant appearance of impermanence, suffering, and non-self manifests; the sign of delusion accompanied by views of permanence, happiness, and self does not [appear]; the mind does not rush toward <s>dharmas</s> standing in the position of delusion (<s>moha</s>) —

children.text: ) vistaraḥ | bahutaraṃ nānādhātukatā [ta]dekadhātukatā kāyapi(ci)ttaprabhedasaṃjñā khyāti | na tveva pi (ci)ttasaṃjñā, mānaparyavasthānīyeṣu dharmeṣu cittaṃ na praskandatīti vistaraḥ | bahutarā adhyātmamupaśamasaṃjñā | śamathasaṃjñā | khyāti | na tveva prapañcasaṃjñā vitarkaparyavasthānīyeṣu dharmeṣu cittaṃ na praskandatīti vistaraḥ |
children.translated_text: and so forth in detail. A more abundant perception of the multiplicity of <s>dhātus</s> (elements), their singularity, and the distinction of body and mind manifests; the perception of [a unified] self does not [appear]; the mind does not rush toward <s>dharmas</s> standing in the position of conceit (<s>māna</s>) — and so forth in detail. A more abundant internal perception of pacification and perception of calm manifests; the perception of conceptual proliferation does not [appear]; the mind does not rush toward <s>dharmas</s> standing in the position of discursive thought (<s>vitarka</s>) — and so forth in detail.

body.translated_text: Therein, to what extent is <s>aśubhā</s> (the unattractive) attained? To what extent up to <s>ānāpānasmṛti</s> (mindfulness of breathing) attained?

body.text: tatra niyatā(taṃ)śamathaśca vipaśyanā cobhe mitrībhūte samayugamvarttete | yena yuganaddhavāhīmārga ityucyate | āha | yo lābhī bhavati navākārāyāṃ (

children.text: ) cittasthitau navamasyākārasya yaduta samāhitatāyāḥ [|] sa ca taṃ pariniṣpannaṃ | samādhiṃ niśritya adhiprajñaṃ dharmavipaśyanāyāṃ prayujyate | tasya tasminsamaye dharmānvipaśyataḥ [|] svarasavāhana eva mārgo bhavatyanābhogavāhanaḥ | anabhisaṃskāreṇa vipaśyanā pariśuddhā, paryavadātā, śamathānuyoga(tā) kalpa(lpi)tā parigṛhītā pravarttate | yathaiva śamathamāsate [te] nocyate śamathaścāsyavipaśyanā cobhe mitrībhūte samayugamvarttete | śamathavipaśyanāyuganaddhavāhī ca mārgo bhavatīti || anantaroddānaṃ ||
children.translated_text: mental stability (<s>cittasthiti</s>), namely, the state of being collected (<s>samāhitatā</s>) — relying on that perfected <s>samādhi</s> (concentration), one engages in the <s>dharma</s>-insight of higher wisdom (<s>adhiprajña</s>). For that person, at that time, while contemplating <s>dharmas</s>, the path proceeds by its own momentum, without deliberate effort, spontaneously. <s>Vipaśyanā</s>, purified and cleansed, proceeds as conjoined with the practice of <s>śamatha</s>, as if designed and adopted [for it]. Just as when one practices <s>śamatha</s>, one is not [merely practicing] <s>śamatha</s>; rather, both <s>śamatha</s> and <s>vipaśyanā</s>, having become friends, proceed together in union. And the path becomes one of yoked <s>śamatha</s> and <s>vipaśyanā</s>. The immediately following summary verse (<s>uddāna</s>):

body.translated_text: Therein, when both <s>śamatha</s> (calm abiding) and <s>vipaśyanā</s> (insight) are definitely joined as friends and proceed together in union, it is called the path of yoked practice (<s>yuganaddhavāhī mārga</s>). He says: one who has attained the ninth of the nine aspects of

children.translated_text: Grasping the sign, the search, the examination following the methods,

children.text: arthatastu lakṣaṇauḥ pacchaiḥ (pakṣaiḥ) kālaiśca saha yuktibhiḥ ||
children.translated_text: but in terms of meaning, with characteristics, sides, times, and reasonings,
appropriate practice, and [its] relaxation, the reversal,
the temporal indication, contentment, non-deviation, and the mode of practice,

children.text: samyak prayogatā caiva navādhārā dvidhā matā |
children.translated_text: proper practice itself — nine foundations, considered as twofold,
from essential nature, from cause, and likewise from seeing the danger,

body.text: pratibhāvitā caiva śuddhirāvaraṇasya hi ||
body.translated_text: and from cultivation of the antidote — indeed the purification from obstacles.

body.text: tatra manaskārabhāvanā katamā [|] āhādikarmikastatprathamakarmika evaṃ vyāpini lakṣaṇe vyavasthāpite ekāgratāyāmā (ā)varaṇaviśuddheśca mithyāprayogaṃ ca (

children.text: ) varjayati | samyakprayoge ca śikṣate | sa tatprathamata ekāgratāṃ prahāṇābhiratiṃ cādhigamiṣyāmīti caturbhirmanaskāraiḥ prayujyate | katamaiścacaturbhiścittasantā panīyena manaskāreṇa, cittābhiṣyandanīyena, praśrabdhijanakena, jñānadarśanaviśodhakena ca manaskāreṇa [|]
children.translated_text: And trains in right practice. He, [thinking] 'I shall first attain one-pointedness and delight in abandonment,' applies himself with four kinds of mental attention. Which four? The mental attention that causes remorse in the mind (<s>cittasantāpanīya</s>), the mental attention that causes the mind to flow (<s>cittābhiṣyandanīya</s>), that which generates tranquility (<s>praśrabdhijanaka</s>), and that which purifies knowledge and vision (<s>jñānadarśanaviśodhaka</s>).

body.translated_text: Therein, what is the cultivation of mental attention (<s>manaskārabhāvanā</s>)? A beginner, a first-timer, having established the pervading characteristic, avoids wrong practice regarding one-pointedness and the purification of obstructions,

body.text: tatra cittasantāpano manaskāraḥ katamaḥ [ḥ] [|] āha | yenāyaṃ manaskāreṇa | saṃvejanīyeṣu dharmeṣu cittaṃ samvejayatyayaṃ cittasantāpano manaskāraḥ |
body.translated_text: Therein, what is the mental attention that causes remorse in the mind? He says: That mental attention by which one arouses a sense of urgency (<s>saṃvega</s>) in the mind regarding objects that are cause for urgency — this is the mental attention that causes remorse in the mind.

body.text: tatra katamaścittābhiṣyandano manaskāraḥ | yenāyaṃ prasadanīyena manaskāreṇa cittamabhipramodayatyayaṃ (|) cittābhiṣyandano manaskāraḥ |
body.translated_text: Therein, what is the mental attention that causes the mind to flow? That mental attention by which, through an attention that inspires faith, one causes the mind to rejoice — this is the mental attention that causes the mind to flow.

body.text: tatra katamaḥ praśrabdhijanako manaskāraḥ | āha | yenāyaṃ manaskāreṇa kālena kālaṃ cittaṃ samvejanīyeṣu dharmeṣu saṃvejayitvā (saṃvejya) kālena kālamabhipramodanīyeṣu dharmeṣu cittamabhipramodayitvā (modyādhyātmaṃ śamathayati | nirnimittāyāṃ | nirvikalpakatāyāmevaṃ sthāpayatyekāgrāṃ smṛtiṃ pravarttayati yenāsya hetunā, (

children.text: ) yena pratyayena kāyacittadauṣṭhulyapratipakṣeṇa kāyacittahlādanakarī kāyapraśrabdhiścittapraśrabdhiścotpadyate | ayamucyate praśrabdhijanako manaskāraḥ |
children.translated_text: By which condition, as the antidote to bodily and mental dysfunction (<s>dauṣṭhulya</s>), bodily tranquility (<s>kāyapraśrabdhi</s>) and mental tranquility (<s>cittapraśrabdhi</s>) that refresh body and mind arise — this is called the mental attention that generates tranquility.

body.translated_text: Therein, what is the mental attention that generates tranquility? He says: That mental attention by which, from time to time, having aroused urgency in the mind regarding objects that are cause for urgency, and from time to time, having caused the mind to rejoice regarding objects that inspire rejoicing, one internally calms [the mind], establishes it in the signless, in the non-conceptual state, and sets in motion unified mindfulness — by which cause,

body.text: tatra jñānadarśana viśodhano manaskāraḥ katamaḥ | yena manaskāreṇa kālena kālaṃ cittena tathādhyātmaṃ saṃśayamiti (saṃśamayati) tena punaḥ punarabhīkṣṇaṃ adhiprajñaṃ dharmavipaśyanāyāṃ yogaṃ karoti | yaduta tamevādhyātmaṃ cetaḥśamathaṃ niśritya [|] ayamucyate jñānadarśanaviśodhano manaskāraḥ |
body.translated_text: Therein, what is the mental attention that purifies knowledge and vision? That mental attention by which, from time to time, one thus internally calms the mind, and then again and again, repeatedly, applies oneself to <s>vipaśyanā</s> (insight) into <s>dharmas</s> with higher wisdom — that is, relying upon that very internal <s>cetaḥśamatha</s> (mental calm) — this is called the mental attention that purifies knowledge and vision.

body.text: katamaḥ kālena kālaṃ saṃvejanīyeṣu dharmeṣu cittaṃ samvejayatyevamasya taccittaṃ taptaṃ bhavati | santaptamudvignaṃ saṃvignaṃ yadutāsravasthānīyeṣu ca dharmeṣu | sarvasaṃvejanīyāni sthānāni | katamāni | āha [|] catvāri | tadyathā ātmavipattiḥ, paravipattiśca, vartamāne samavahite saṃmukhībhūte yoniśo manasikārānvayātsamvejanīyaṃ sthānaṃ bhavati | tatrātmasampattiḥ | parasampattiśca | abhyatīte kṣaṇe niruddhe vigate vipariṇate yoniśo manasikārānvayātsamvejanīyaṃ (

children.text: ) sthānaṃ bhavati | sa kālena kālamabhipramodanīyeṣu dharmeṣu cittamabhipramodayati | tasyābhipramodayataḥ | evamasya taccittaṃ snigdhaṃ bhavatyārdraṃ ca, dravañcācchaṃ ca, prasannaṃ ca |
children.translated_text: From time to time one causes the mind to rejoice regarding objects that inspire rejoicing. As one causes it to rejoice, thus that mind becomes soft, moist, fluid, clear, and serene.

body.translated_text: How does one, from time to time, arouse a sense of urgency in the mind regarding objects that are cause for urgency? Thus his mind becomes heated, scorched, distressed, and agitated with regard to objects that are bases for the <s>āsravas</s> (outflows). What are all the bases for arousing urgency? He says: There are four — namely: one's own misfortune (<s>ātmavipatti</s>) and the misfortune of others (<s>paravipatti</s>), which, when present, encountered, and come face to face, through proper attention (<s>yoniśo manasikāra</s>), become bases for urgency. And one's own good fortune (<s>ātmasampattiḥ</s>) and the good fortune of others (<s>parasampattiḥ</s>), which, when past, ceased, gone, and transformed, through proper attention, become bases for urgency.

body.text: tatrābhipramodanīyāḥ dharmāḥ katame || āha | trividhā[ḥ] a (catvāro 'bhipramonādhiṣṭhānaṃ, ratnāni, śikṣāpadapāriśuddhiḥ | ātmani ca | viśeṣādhigamasaṃbhāvanājātasya cetaso [a]saṃkocaḥ | sa evaṃ ratnānyanusaraṃścittamabhipramodayati lābhā me sulabdhāḥ | yasya me śāstā tathāgatorhan samyaksaṃbuddhaḥ | lābhā me sulabdhā yo (a)haṃ svākhyāte dharmavinaye pravrajitaḥ | lābhā me sulabdhāḥ | yasya me sabrahmacāriṇaḥ śīlavanto guṇavantaḥ peśalāḥ | kalyāṇadharmāṇaḥ | bhadrakaṃ me maraṇaṃ bhaviṣyati | bhadrikā kālakriyā, bhadrako [a]bhisaṃparāyaḥ | evaṃ catvāryanusmaraṃścittamabhipramodayati |
body.translated_text: Therein, what are the objects that inspire rejoicing? He says: There are four bases for rejoicing: the [Three] Jewels, the purity of the training-rules (<s>śikṣāpadapāriśuddhi</s>), [confidence in] oneself, and the non-contraction of mind born from estimating one's own [capacity for] higher attainment. Thus, recollecting the Jewels, one causes the mind to rejoice: 'It is a gain for me, well-gained, that my teacher is the <s>Tathāgata</s>, <s>Arhat</s>, <s>Samyaksaṃbuddha</s> (Perfectly Awakened One). It is a gain for me, well-gained, that I have gone forth in the well-proclaimed <s>Dharma</s> and <s>Vinaya</s>. It is a gain for me, well-gained, that my fellow practitioners in the holy life are virtuous, endowed with good qualities, amiable, of wholesome character. My death will be blessed, my passing will be blessed, my future destiny will be blessed.' Thus, recollecting these four [jewels], one causes the mind to rejoice.

body.text: kathaṃ śikṣāpadapāriśuddhiṃ śīlapāriśuddhiṃ anusmarata(raṃ)ścittamabhipramodayati | lābhā me sulabdhā[ḥ] so [a]haṃ śāstari tathāgate [a]rhati samyaksaṃbuddhe, tasya ca svākhyāte dharmavinaye, tatra ca supratipanne śrāvakasaṃghe, ahamebhiḥ sabrahmacāribhiḥ śīlasāmānyagataḥ | śikṣāsāmānyagato, maitrakāyavāṅmanaskarmāntaḥ, dṛṣṭisāmānyagataḥ | sādhāraṇaparibhogī [|] evaṃ śikṣāpadapāriśuddhiṃ, (

children.translated_text: The purity of morality, one causes the mind to rejoice — namely, with the joy that is preceded by freedom from remorse.

body.translated_text: How does one cause the mind to rejoice by recollecting the purity of the training-rules and the purity of morality? 'It is a gain for me, well-gained, that regarding the Teacher, the <s>Tathāgata</s>, <s>Arhat</s>, <s>Samyaksaṃbuddha</s>, and regarding the well-proclaimed <s>Dharma</s> and <s>Vinaya</s>, and regarding the well-practicing community of <s>Śrāvakas</s> (hearers) — I, with these fellow practitioners in the holy life, have reached commonality in morality, commonality in training, with actions of body, speech, and mind that are friendly, have reached commonality in view, and share in the use [of requisites].' Thus recollecting the purity of the training-rules,

body.text: tatra kathamātmanaḥ adhigamasaṃbhāvanāmadhiṣṭhāya bhavyo [a]hamasmyeva[ṃ] pariśuddhaśīlaḥ | pratibalaśca bhājanabhūtaśca | ebhiḥ sabrahmacāribhiḥ śīlasāmānyagato, dṛṣṭisāmānyagataḥ, sadbhiḥ sāmānyagataiḥ (samyaggataiḥ) satpuruṣaiḥ, bhavyo [a]hamasmyevaṃbhūta, evaṃ pratipanno, dṛṣṭa eva dharme aprāptasya prāptaye, anadhigatasyādhigamāya, āsākṣātkṛtasya sākṣātkriyāyai | iti prāmodyamutpādayatyevamātmano [a]dhigamasaṃbhāvanādhiṣṭhānena cittamabhipramodayati |
body.translated_text: Therein, how does one, based on the estimation of one's own attainment, [think:] 'I am indeed capable, being of such pure morality, and I am competent and a fit vessel. Having reached commonality in morality and commonality in view with these fellow practitioners in the holy life — with good persons who have rightly gone, with true persons — I, being of such nature, thus practicing, am capable in this very life of attaining what has not been attained, of reaching what has not been reached, of directly realizing what has not been directly realized.' Thus one generates joy, and by this, through the basis of estimating one's own attainment, one causes the mind to rejoice.

body.text: api ca | yadanena pūrveṇāparamārabdhavīryeṇa viharatā viśeṣādhigamaḥ kṛto bhavati | tadanusmarannuttari ca viśeṣādhigamamabhiśraddhyādadhaṃ ścittamabhipramodayatyayamaparaḥ | saṃvejanīyeṣu dharmeṣu cittamabhisaṃtāpayannāsravamāsravasthānīyebhyo dharmebhyaścittaṃ vimukhī karoti | viguṇī karoti | prātimukhyenāvasthāpayati | viśleṣayatyabhipramodanīyeṣu dharmeṣvabhipramodayannamiṣyandayannaiṣkramyapravivekajeṣu dharmeṣu sasnehaṃ cittamabhimukhīkarotyupaśleṣayati | ramayati | saṃyojayatyevamasya taccitte(ttaṃ) yābhyāṃ dvābhyāṃ dharmābhyāṃ | sarvakṛṣṇapakṣavimukhaṃ sarvakṛṣṇa(śukla)pakṣābhimukhaṃ ca (

children.text: ) pravarttate | yaduta saṃvegapraharṣābhyāṃ yataścittamevaṃ kṛṣṇapakṣa vimukhaṃ ca | kṛtvā cittasantāpanīyena manaskāreṇa śuklapakṣābhimukhaṃ kṛtvā, abhiṣyandanīyena manaskāreṇa kālena kālamadhyātmaṃ ca pradadhāti | yaduta cetaḥśamathena praśrabdhijanakena manaskāreṇa kālena kālaṃ dharmānvicinoti | pravicinoti | parivitarkayati | parimīmānsa(māṃsā)māpadyate | jñānadarśanaviśodhake(ne)na manaskāreṇa [|] evamasya taccittaṃ kālena kālaṃ śamathavipaśyanāparigṛhītaṃ | sarvākārasarvaguṇahetūpakṛtaḥ (taṃ) teṣāṃ teṣāṃ rātridivasānāmatyayāt | kṣaṇalavamuhūrttānāṃ (ṇāṃ) [|] viśeṣāya paraiti |
children.translated_text: Namely, by urgency and joy. Since the mind is thus turned away from the dark side through the mental attention that causes remorse, and turned toward the bright side through the mental attention that causes it to flow — from time to time one settles [the mind] internally, namely through <s>cetaḥśamatha</s> (mental calm), by the mental attention that generates tranquility. From time to time one investigates, thoroughly investigates, deliberates upon, and examines <s>dharmas</s> — by the mental attention that purifies knowledge and vision. Thus that mind, from time to time encompassed by <s>śamatha</s> (calm) and <s>vipaśyanā</s> (insight), furnished with the causes of all qualities in every aspect, progresses toward distinction with the passing of those days and nights, moments, instants, and hours.

body.translated_text: Moreover, whatever special attainment has been achieved by this person while dwelling with previously aroused energy — recollecting that and having confidence in further special attainment, one causes the mind to rejoice. This is another [basis]. While arousing urgency regarding objects that cause urgency, one turns the mind away from the <s>āsravas</s> (outflows) and from objects that are bases for the outflows, makes it averse, sets it facing the opposite direction, separates it. While causing the mind to rejoice regarding objects that inspire rejoicing, causing it to flow, one makes the mind affectionately inclined toward <s>dharmas</s> born of renunciation and seclusion (<s>naiṣkramyapraviveka</s>), brings it close, delights it, and conjoins it. Thus, by these two <s>dharmas</s>, that mind turns away from the entire dark side and turns toward the entire bright side,

body.text: tadyathā jātarūparajataṃ dakṣeṇa karmāreṇa vā, karmā[rā]ntevāsinā vā kālena kālaṃ yadā saṃtāpitaṃ ca bhavati | vigatamalakaṣāye bhāve nābhiṣyanditaṃ ca bhavati | tatra tatrālaṃkārakarmaṇā mṛdukarmaṇyatāyogenābhimukhīkṛtaṃ bhavati | tamenaṃ dakṣaḥ karmāro vā, karmā[rā]ntevāsī vā tadupamena śilpajñānena karmāntavastunā yatreṣṭā(ma)laṃkāravikṛtistatra pariṇamayatyena (va)meva yoginā yadā taccittamabhidhyādimalakaṣāye vimukhībhāvenodvejitaṃ ca bhavati | kliṣṭadaurmanasyavimukhībhāvena cābhipramoditaṃ bhavati | (

children.text: ) tamenaṃ yogī yatra yatra niyojayati | śamathapakṣe vā vipaśyanāpakṣe vā tatra tatra sūpaśliṣṭaṃ ca bhavati | sulagnaṃ cāvikalaṃ cāvikampyaṃ ca | yathābhipretārthasampattaye ca paraiti |
children.translated_text: The <s>yogin</s>, wherever he directs [that mind] — whether to the <s>śamatha</s> (calm) side or to the <s>vipaśyanā</s> (insight) side — there it becomes well-attached, well-adhered, complete, and unshakeable, and it proceeds toward the accomplishment of whatever purpose is intended.

body.translated_text: Just as gold and silver, [worked] by a skilled goldsmith or a goldsmith's apprentice, when heated from time to time, when in a state free from the impurity of dross it is caused to flow, and when made supple through the craft of ornamentation with softness and workability — that skilled goldsmith or goldsmith's apprentice, with his craft-knowledge, transforms it into whatever ornamental form is desired. In the same way, by the <s>yogin</s>, when that mind has been made averse to the defilement of covetousness and the like through turning away, and when it has been caused to rejoice through turning away from afflicted unpleasant states,

body.text: tatra kathamādikarmikaḥ tatprathamakarmiko manaskārabhāvanāyāṃ viniyujyate | yathāyaṃ viniyujyamānaḥ pratipadyamānaśca spṛśati | tatprathamataḥ prahāṇābhiratiṃ cittasyaikāgratāṃ | iha yogajño yogaprayukte nādikarmi(tamādikarmi)kaḥ (kaṃ) | tatprathamata evamavavadate | ehi, tvaṃ, bhadramukha, trīṇi nimittodgrāhakāni (ṇi) kāraṇāni niśritya yaduta dṛṣṭamvā śrutamvā, cintānumānādhipateyaṃ vā | parikalpaṃ pañca nimittānyudgṛhṇīṣva [|] samvejanīyaṃ, prasadanīyamādīnavanimittamālokanimittaṃ vasturūpaṇānimittañca [|] sa cetsa yogaprayukta ādikarmiko rāgacarito bhavatyaśubhāvineyaḥ kathaṃ sa pañcānāṃ nimittānāmudgrahaṇāyā[va]bodhyate | evama[va]bodhyate | ehi, tvaṃ, bhadramukha | yaṃ yameva grāmamvā nigamamvopaniśritya viharasi | sa cedanyatra grāme, nigame vānyatamaṃ puruṣamvā, striyamvā ābādhikaṃ śrṛṇoṣi | duḥkhitambāḍhaglānaṃ, mṛtamvā kālagataṃ, puruṣamvā striyamvā [|] api tu tasya puruṣasya vā, striyā vānyatamānyatamaṃ mitrāmātyajñātisālohitaṃ, (

children.text: ) paracakrakṛtamvā tadgrāmaparyāpannasya janakāyasya bhojanavyasanamagnidāhakṛtamvā, udakāpaharaṇakṛtamvā, kuvihitapraviṇāśakṛtamvā, kuprayuktakarmāntapralujyanākṛtamvā, apriyadāyādādhigamakṛtamvā, kulāṃgāra vipraṇāśakṛtamvā [|] no cecchṛṇoṣi | apitu pratyakṣaṃ paśyasi | no vānyasmiṃ (smin) grāmanigame, no ca tasminneva grāmanigame, na pareṣāma (raira)pi tvātmanaiva spṛṣṭo bhavasi | śārīrikābhirvedanābhirduḥkhābhistīvrābhiriti vistareṇa pūrvavat |
children.translated_text: Or that the community belonging to that village has been afflicted by an enemy army, or by the calamity of famine, fire, flood, or poorly secured destruction, or by the failure of poorly managed enterprises, or by the coming of unwanted heirs, or by the ruin caused by a family-destroyer — or if you do not hear [such things] but rather see them directly; or [it happens] not in another village or town, but in that very village or town; or not to others but you yourself are touched by bodily feelings that are painful, intense,' and so on in detail as before.

body.translated_text: Therein, how is a beginner, a first-timer, engaged in the cultivation of mental attention? How, when so engaged and practicing, does he first touch delight in abandonment and one-pointedness of mind? Here, the <s>yoga</s>-knower, [addressing] the beginner who is engaged in <s>yoga</s> practice, first instructs him thus: 'Come, O fortunate one! Relying on three causes for grasping signs — namely, what has been seen, what has been heard, or what is governed by thought and inference — undertake to grasp five signs: the sign that arouses urgency, the sign that inspires faith, the sign of danger, the sign of light, and the sign of the reality of the object.' If that beginner who is engaged in <s>yoga</s> practice is of passionate temperament, to be trained through <s>aśubhā</s> (the unattractive) meditation, how is he instructed for the grasping of the five signs? He is instructed thus: 'Come, O fortunate one! Whatever village or town you dwell near — if in another village or town you hear that some man or woman is sick, suffering, severely ill, or has died and passed away — whether [that person] or any one of their friends, ministers, relatives, or kinsmen,

body.text: sarvaṃ dṛṣṭvā śrutvā caivaṃ cittaṃ saṃvejaya | duḥkho batāyaṃ saṃsāraḥ, kṛcchra ātmabhāvapratilabdho yatremā evaṃ rūpātmamaśca (rūpā ātmanaśca) pareṣāñca vipattaya upalabhyante | yadutārogyavipattirapi, jātivipattirapi, bhogavipattirapi, vyādhirvyādhidharmatā ca | maraṇaṃ, maraṇadharmatā ca | api caikeṣāṃ śīlavipattirapi, dṛṣṭivipattirapi yato nidānaṃ sattvā dṛṣṭe ca dharme duḥkhavihāriṇo bhavanti | samparāye ca durgatigāminaḥ | yāśca sampattayo dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihārāya, abhisamparāye ca, sugatigamanāya tā apyanityā[ḥ], tāsāmapi anityatā prajñāyate | vipattiścet saṃmukhībhūtā, vimukhībhūtā tasminsamaye sampattiḥ | asaṃmukhībhūtāyāmapi vipattau durlabhā sampattirvināśadharmiṇī ca, evaṃ ca punaścittamudvejayitvā(jya) sādhu ca, (

children.text: ) suṣṭhu ca, yoniśaḥ pradadhatsva | anāśvāsyametatsthānamaviśvāsyaṃ | yatsaṃsāre me saṃsarataḥ, aparinirvṛtasyāvimuktacetasaḥ etā vipattisampattayo, na me saṃmukhībhāvaṃ, vimukhībhāvaṃ ca gaccheyuḥ | na vā atonidānaṃ me duḥkhamutpadyate (dyeta) | tīvraṃ, kharaṃ, kaṭukamanālāpamalabhyametatsthānaṃ tasmādetatsarvārthamadhipatiṃ kṛtvā prahāṇaratiratena me bhavitavyamapramattena, evaṃ bahulavihāriṇo me apyevāsyānarthasyākriyā syādityevaṃ yoniśaḥ pradadhatsva, evaṃ tvaṃ saṃvejanīyaṃ nimittamudgṛhya, punaḥ prasadanīyaṃ nimittamudgṛhṇīṣva [|] evaṃ ca punarudgṛhṇīṣva [|] ātmanaḥ śīlāni pratyavekṣasva | kiṃ pariśuddhāni me śīlānyapariśuddhāni [vā], yā (yo) me smṛtisaṃpramoṣādvā, anādarādvā kleśapracuratayā vā, avyutpannato vāsti kaścicchikṣāvyatikramaḥ | vyatikrānte vā, me (mayā) śikṣā[ṃ] yathādharmaṃ pratikṛtyādhyāśayena ca punarakaraṇāya cittamutpāditaṃ | kaści(kacci)nme kartavyaṃ kṛtamakarttavyañca (vyaṃ vā) | na kṛtaṃ samāsataḥ | kaccidadhyāśayasampanno [a]smi prayogasampannaśca | yaduta | śikṣāpadeṣu | evaṃ na te pratyavekṣamāṇena | sa cetpariśuddhaḥ śīlaskandhaḥ, na punaste cetanā karaṇīyā | kaccinmevipratisāḥ ra utpadyetāpi tu dharmaṃtaiveyaṃ | yadevaṃ viśuddhaśīlasyāvipratisāra (
children.translated_text: ) Well and truly, attend properly! This station [of saṃsāra] is unreliable, not to be trusted — for while I am wandering in <s>saṃsāra</s>, not yet having attained <s>parinirvāṇa</s>, with mind not yet liberated, these misfortunes and fortunes should not come face to face with me and turn away from me, nor should suffering arise for me on that account — intense, harsh, bitter, unpleasant, unobtainable is this station [of liberation]. Therefore, making this purpose of all purposes the governing principle, I must become one who delights in abandonment, heedful. 'If I dwell abundantly thus, perhaps the non-occurrence of this harm will come about.' Attend properly thus! Thus, having grasped the sign that arouses urgency, then grasp the sign that inspires confidence. And grasp it thus: examine your own moral conduct — 'Are my moral precepts purified or unpurified? Have I committed any transgression of the training through loss of mindfulness, or through carelessness, or through the abundance of afflictions, or through lack of learning? And if I have transgressed the training, have I properly confessed it according to the <s>Dharma</s> and generated the intention not to do it again? Have I done what should be done and not done what should not be done?' In brief: 'Am I accomplished in intention and accomplished in practice — that is, with regard to the training rules?' Examining thus — if your aggregate of moral conduct is purified, then no further effort need be made by you: 'May no remorse arise in me!' For this is simply the natural law — that for one of purified morality, non-remorse (<s>avipratisāra</s>)

children.text: ) utpadyate | evaṃ cāvipratisāriṇā na cetanā karaṇīyā, kaccinme prāmodyaṃ utpadyeta | api tu dharmataiveyaṃ yadavipratisāriṇaḥ prāmodyamutpadyate | anena tāvadekena prāmodyādhiṣṭhānena dvayāvipratisārapūrvakaṃ prāmodyamutpādayitavyaḥ (m) | utpādya pareṇa saṃpraharṣādhiṣṭhānena mānasaṃ saṃpraharṣaya | sa cet punarbhavasi pūrveṇāparaṃ parīttasyāpi viśeṣādhigame prītirjanayitavyā, bhavyohamasmi, pratibalaḥ | evaṃ pariśuddhaśīlo bhagavataḥ śikṣāsu supratiṣṭhitaḥ | dṛṣṭe dharme prāptasya prāptaye, anadhigatasyādhigamāya | asākṣātkṛtasya sākṣātkriyāyai | anenāpyadhiṣṭhānena mānasaṃ saṃpraharṣaya || sa cetpunarlābhī bhavati pūrveṇāparaṃ paracittasyāpi viśeṣādhigamasya [|] sa tvaṃ tamadhipatiṃ kṛtvā pareṣāṃ ca paripūrṇe viśeṣādhigame yaduta tathāgate, tathāgataśrāvakeṣu vā, ātmanaścottariviśeṣādhigamasaṃpratyayajāto mānasaṃ saṃpraharṣaya iti (|) ya ebhirākārairmanasaste sa praharṣa iti | ya ebhirākāraiḥ sa pūrvapramuditasyaitarhi prītimanaskatetyucyate |
children.translated_text: ) arises. And for one free from remorse, no further effort need be made: 'May gladness arise in me!' For this is simply the natural law — that for one free from remorse, gladness arises. By this first basis of gladness, the twofold gladness preceded by non-remorse is to be generated. Having generated it, by the next basis of joy, gladden the mind. If, furthermore, you have previously [succeeded], then regarding even a small attainment of distinction, delight should be generated [thinking]: 'I am capable, I am competent!' — thus, with morality purified, well-established in the <s>Bhagavān's</s> training, regarding what is to be attained in this very life: for the attainment of what has not been attained, for the realization of what has not been realized, for the direct witnessing of what has not been directly witnessed — by this basis too, gladden the mind. If, furthermore, you become one who obtains, previously [having progressed], direct knowledge even of another's mind — making that the governing principle, and in the complete attainment of distinction by others — namely, in the <s>Tathāgata</s> and in the disciples of the <s>Tathāgata</s> — with the confidence born of one's own further attainment of distinction, gladden the mind. Whatever mental joy arises through these modes — that is the joy. Whatever arises through these modes for one who was previously glad — that is called the present-time joy and mental delight.

body.translated_text: Having seen and heard all this, arouse urgency in the mind thus: 'Painful indeed is this <s>saṃsāra</s> (cycle of existence), hard-won is the attainment of a personal existence, in which such misfortunes of oneself and others are observed — namely, loss of health, loss of birth [status], loss of wealth, disease and the liability to disease, death and the liability to death; and furthermore, for some, loss of morality and loss of [right] view, on account of which beings become dwellers in suffering in the present life and are destined for unfortunate rebirths in the future. And those good fortunes that serve for pleasant dwelling in the present life and for going to fortunate rebirths — these too are impermanent, their impermanence is perceived. If misfortune has come face to face, then at that time good fortune has turned away. Even when misfortune has not come face to face, good fortune is rare and subject to destruction.' And having thus aroused urgency in the mind, well and

body.text: evaṃ prasadanīyaṃ nimittamudgrāhayatyudgrāhayitvā (hya) punassamanuśāsti | ehi, tvaṃ, bhadramukha, saṃvejanīyena nimittena saṃtāpitacittaḥ, prasadanīyena cittenābhiṣyanditacittaḥ prahāyābhidhyādaurmanasyaṃ (sye) loke bahulaṃ vihariṣyasi | yatra ca yatrālambane prayokṣyase || (

children.text: ) śamathapakṣe, vipaśyanāpakṣe vā, tatra tatrālambane cittaṃ sthitaṃ bhaviṣyati | adhyātmaṃ susaṃsthitaṃ, kāyacittapraśrabdhicittaikāgratāśca pratilapsyase [|] evaṃ kṛṣṇapakṣavimukhībhūtaḥ śuklapakṣābhimukhībhūtasya yaduta saṃvegābhiṣyandanatayā sarvaṃ punarasyādīnavanimittamudgṛhṇīṣva yaduta nimittebhyo vipakṣebhyabhyaścopakleśebhyaśca [|]
children.translated_text: ) whether in the side of <s>śamatha</s> (calm abiding) or in the side of <s>vipaśyanā</s> (insight) — with whatever object, the mind will become settled. Internally well-settled, you will obtain bodily and mental tranquility (<s>praśrabdhi</s>) and one-pointedness of mind. Thus, having turned away from the dark side and turned toward the bright side — namely, through the moistening of urgency — again grasp the sign of danger regarding all [hindrances]: namely, regarding signs, regarding opposing [thoughts], and regarding secondary afflictions.'

body.translated_text: Thus he causes [the student] to grasp the sign that inspires confidence. Having caused him to grasp it, he then further instructs: 'Come, good-faced one! With a mind heated by the sign that arouses urgency, with a mind moistened by the sign that inspires confidence, having abandoned covetousness and mental distress regarding the world, you shall dwell abundantly. And with whatever object you shall engage —'
