children.translated_text: ) and in pacification — the perception of non-burning, contentment, and unattractiveness. Having grasped this sign, furthermore grasp the sign of light — namely, having grasped the sign from a lamp, or from the radiance of a mass of fire, or from the disc of the sun, or from the disc of the moon; then, going to a cemetery, grasp the sign from a blue-discolored [corpse], up to a bone or a chain of bones; or if not from a cemetery, then from a painting or from a wooden [model of a] cemetery. Having grasped [the sign], approach your lodging. Having approached — gone to the forest, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty dwelling — sit on a bed, or a seat, or a grass mat; having crossed the legs, having washed the feet, holding the body upright, establishing mindfulness face-to-face; having sat down, first, for one-pointedness and non-distraction of the mind, apply yourself with mindfulness bound [to the object]. And therein, [apply] the six perceptions: the perception of non-conceptuality, the perception of pacification, the perception of non-disturbance, the perception of non-anxiety and non-agitation, and the perception of non-burning, contentment, and unattractiveness. And therein, let the discriminative attention regarding distraction and non-distraction be present in you — by which discriminative attention regarding distraction and non-distraction, you should fully know the distraction in signs, thoughts, and secondary afflictions, and the non-distraction in one-pointedness accompanied by the cultivation of the six perceptions. And therein, regarding distraction and non-distraction, be so attentive that your entire mental continuum, your mental stream, bound to one-pointedness, internally bound to mental calm (<s>śamatha</s>), should proceed in succession

children.text: ) nirnimittā pravarteta | nirvikalpā upaśāntā [|] sa cetpunaḥ saṃpramoṣā[t]smṛtisaṃpramoṣāttathā śamathaprāpte cetasi nimittavitarkopakleśānabhyāsadoṣādābhāsamāgacchanti | sukhamādarśayanti | ālambanīkurvanti | teṣūtpannotpanneṣu smṛtyamanasikāraḥ kartavyaḥ | yaduta pūrvadṛṣṭamevamadhipatiṃ kṛtvā evaṃ tadālambanama[nu]smṛtyamanasikāreṇa vibhāvitaṃ | viśvastamanābhāsagatāyāmavasthāpitaṃ bhaviṣyati | taccaitad, bhadramukha, sūkṣmamālambanaṃ | duḥpra(duṣpra)tividhyamasya te prativi(ve)dhāya tīvra[c]chandaśca vyāyāmaśca karaṇīya[ḥ |]
children.translated_text: ) as signless, non-conceptual, and pacified, by the power of vigor, without interruption, in continuous succession. If, however, through loss of mindfulness, when the mind has thus attained calm, the signs, thoughts, and secondary afflictions — due to the fault of habitual tendency — come into appearance, display themselves pleasantly, and make themselves objects [of attention] — then, as they arise one by one, mindful attention should be applied, namely: making what was previously seen the governing principle, by recollecting and attending to that object, it will have been developed, made trustworthy, and established in the state free from appearances. And this, good-faced one, is a subtle object, difficult to penetrate — for its penetration, intense desire and effort must be applied by you.

body.translated_text: Therein, the signs are the ten beginning with the sign of form; the [discursive] thoughts are the eight beginning with thoughts of sensual desire; the secondary afflictions are the five beginning with sensual desire [as a hindrance]. And grasp the danger regarding them thus: 'These signs are agents of disturbance for the mind; these thoughts are agents of agitation and disturbance of the mind; these secondary afflictions are agents of non-pacification of the mind. And the disturbance of the mind caused by signs, the agitation caused by thoughts, and the affliction caused by secondary afflictions — this is the painful dwelling of the mind. Therefore these signs, thoughts, and secondary afflictions are painful, ignoble, connected with harm, and productive of distraction and disturbance of the mind.' Having grasped the sign of danger thus, for the sake of one-pointedness, the settling of the mind, and non-distraction of the mind, grasp the sign through six modes: namely, through the perception of signs and signlessness — the perception of non-disturbance; through the perception of non-conceptuality, and in non-conceptuality — the perception of non-anxiety and non-disturbance; through the perception of pacification;

body.text: idaṃ cālambanaṃ sandhāyoktaṃ bhagavatā | janapadakalyāṇī janapadakalyāṇīti bhikṣavo mahājanakāyaḥ sannipateta | atha puruṣa āgacchedabālajātīyaḥ | taṃ kaścideva[ṃ] vadedidaṃ te bhoḥ, puruṣa, tailapātrapūrṇaṃ samatittikamanabhiṣekyamantarā ca janakāyaḥ sannipateta | sā khalu janapadakalyāṇīma(a)ntarā ca (

children.text: ) mahāsamājaṃ | pariharttavyamayaṃ ca te utkṣiptāsiko vadhakapuruṣaḥ pṛṣṭhataḥ pṛṣṭhataḥ samanubaddhaḥ | sa cettvamasmāttailapātrādekabindumapi pṛthivyāṃ nipātayiṣyasi tataste utkṣiptāsiko badhakapuruṣa ucchinnamūlaṃ śiraḥ prapātayiṣyati | kiṃ manyadhve bhikṣavaḥ api nu sa puruṣaḥ amanasikṛtvā tailapātramamanasikṛtvā tailapātramamanasikṛtvā utkṣiptāsikaṃ badhakapuruṣaṃ janapadakalyāṇī[ṃ] manasi kuryānmahājanasamājamno, no, bhadanta, tatkasya hetostathā hi tena puruṣeṇo[tkṣi]ptāsiko vadhakapuruṣaḥ pṛṣṭhataḥ pṛṣṭhataḥ samanubaddho dṛṣṭaḥ | tasyaivaṃ syāt [|] sa cedahamasmāttailapātrādekabindumapi pṛthivyāṃ pātayiṣyāmi | ato me utkṣiptāsiko badhakapuruṣaḥ ucchinnamūlaṃ śiraḥ prapātayiṣyati | nānyatra sa puruṣaḥ amanasikṛtya(tvā) janapadakalyāṇī[ṃ] mahāsamājamvā | tadeva tailapātraṃ sarvacetasā samanvāhṛtya samyageva pariharedevameva bhikṣavaḥ | ye keciccatvāri smṛtyupasthānāni satkṛtya bhāvayanti | gurukṛtya sarvacetasā samanvāhṛtyate me (ta ime) śrāvakā iti [|] tatra janapadakalyāṇīti kāya[c]chandādyupakleśaparyavasthānīyānāndharmāṇāmetadadhivacanaṃ | paramapradhānā nṛttagītavādita iti vitarkaprapañcasaṃkṣobhasthānīyānāṃ dharmāṇāmetadadhivacanaṃ | mahāsamāja iti | rūpanimittādīnāṃ daśānāṃ nimittānāmetadadhivacanaṃ | (
children.translated_text: ) the great assembly, you must carry it. And this man with a drawn sword, an executioner, is following close behind you. If you let even one drop from this oil-bowl fall upon the ground, that man with a drawn sword, the executioner, will strike off your head at the root." What do you think, <s>bhikṣus</s>? Would that man, disregarding the oil-bowl, disregarding the man with the drawn sword — the executioner — attend to the beauty queen of the land or the great assembly?' 'No, venerable sir.' 'For what reason? Because the man with the drawn sword, the executioner, has been seen following close behind him. He would think: "If I let even one drop from this oil-bowl fall upon the ground, the man with the drawn sword, the executioner, will strike off my head at the root." Without attending to the beauty queen or the great assembly, he would carry that very oil-bowl with his whole mind, carefully and properly. Even so, <s>bhikṣus</s>, whoever cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness (<s>smṛtyupasthāna</s>) with reverence, with diligence, with whole-minded attention — they are my [true] disciples.' Therein, 'beauty queen of the land' — this is a designation for the qualities that are the domain of secondary afflictions, such as desire for the body and so on. 'The foremost [performers of] dance, song, and music' — this is a designation for the qualities that are the basis of agitation caused by the proliferation of discursive thought. 'Great assembly' — this is a designation for the ten signs beginning with the sign of form.

children.text: ) abālabhāgīyaḥ puruṣa iti | yogācārasyādhivacanaṃ | tailapātramiti | śamathopanibaddhasya cittasya etadadhivacanaṃ | kāyacittapraśrabdhisnehanārthena utkṣiptāsiko badhakapuruṣa itinimittavitarkopakleśeṣu pūrvodgṛhītasyādīnasyaitadadhivacanaṃ [|] satkṛtya viharati | na caikabindumapi pṛthivyāṃ pātayatīti vikṣepāvikṣepaparijñānāvadhānaparigṛhītasya śamathamārgasyaitadadhivacanaṃ | yenāyaṃ sarvo (sarvāṃ) cittasantatiṃ cittadhārāṃ nirmimittāṃ nirvikalpāmupaśāntāṃ vīryabalena nirantarāṃ paurvāpayeṇa pravarttayati | na caikacittamutpādayati | nimittālambanamvā vitarkopakleśālambanamvā ||
children.translated_text: ) 'The man who is not of the nature of a simpleton' — this is a designation for the <s>yogācāra</s> (meditation practitioner). 'The oil-bowl' — this is a designation for the mind bound to <s>śamatha</s> (calm abiding), for the purpose of the unctuous application of bodily and mental tranquility. 'The man with drawn sword, the executioner' — this is a designation for the danger previously grasped regarding signs, thoughts, and secondary afflictions. 'He dwells with reverence and does not let even one drop fall upon the ground' — this is a designation for the path of calm abiding that is encompassed by the discriminative attention regarding distraction and non-distraction, by which one sets in motion the entire mental continuum, the mental stream — signless, non-conceptual, pacified — without interruption, in continuous succession, by the power of vigor, and does not generate even a single thought with signs as its object or with thoughts and secondary afflictions as its object.

body.translated_text: And with reference to this object, the <s>Bhagavān</s> said: '<s>Bhikṣus</s>, suppose a great crowd of people were to gather [to see] a beauty queen of the land. And suppose a man were to come, of the nature of a simpleton. Someone might say to him: "Sir, this oil-bowl is full to the brim, not to be spilled. Between here and the crowd that has gathered — and that beauty queen of the land — between here and

body.text: tamenamevaṃ śamathaprayuktamādikarmikaṃ yogī samanuśāsti | yāvatte, bhadramukha, evaṃ śamathamārgaprayuktasya evamupāyaparigṛhītaṃ smṛtisaṃprajanyasahagataṃ sābhirāmaṃ cittaṃ bhavati | tāvatte śamathamārga eva bhāvayitavyaḥ | sa cetpunaranabhyāsamoṣānna ramate sopāyaṃ ca tadālamba tasmānnirvikalpādālambanād vyutthāya savikalpa ālambane smṛtyupanibaddhaṃ kurute | yadeva te pūrvodgṛhītamaśubhanimittaṃ tadeva manasi kuru tatprathamato nimittamātrānusāriṇyā vipaśyanayā yaduta vinīlakamvā, vipūyakamvā, yāvadasthiśaṃkalikāmvā || tathā prayuktaśca tatprathamava(ta) ekaṃ vinīlakamadhimucyasva, (

children.text: ) yāvadekāmasthiśaṃkalikāṃ yataścātra kṛtaparicayo bhavasi | prabhāsvaraśca tedhimokṣaḥ pravartate | tadālambanandvau tadā dvau, trīṇi, catvāri, paṃca, daśa, viṃśa, triṃśaccatvāriṃśat | pañcāśadvinīlakaśataṃvinīlakasahasraṃ, yāvatsarvā diśo vidiśaśca | pramāṇākāreṇa pūrvā[ṃ] nirantarā[ma]dhimucyasva | yeṣāṃ na syādavakāśaḥ antato daṇḍaviṣṭambhanakoṭīmātramapi [|] yathāvinīlakānāmevaṃ yāvada sthiśaṃkalikānāṃ sarvamevamadhimuktimanaskāraṃ niśritya bhūtamanaskāramavatara, evaṃ ca punaravatara, yāvantyetāni vinīlakāni mayādhimuktāni yāvadasthiśaṃkalikā ato [a]pramāṇavarāṇi me pūrvāntabhārabhya, tatra tatra bhavagaticyutyupapādeṣu, mṛtasya kālagatasya yāni vinīlakāni nirvṛttāni, yāvadasthiśaṃkalikānirvṛtyāṃ | yeṣāṃ pūrvā koṭirna prajñāyate, nivartamānānāṃ, tāḥ sa cetkaścit saṃharet saṃhṛtāśca na vinaśyeyuḥ, na ca pūtībhaveyuḥ | nāsti sa pṛthivīpradeśo yatra teṣāmavakāśaḥ syāt | ekakalpikā nāmapi, tāvadyāvadasthiśaṃkalikānāṃ sa cetkaścitsaṃhārako bhavet | tāsāṃ syāt saṃhṛtānāṃ vipulapārśvaparvatasamā rāśiḥ | yathā pūrvasyāntara (pūrvānta)mārabhyaivama parāntamapi yāvat (|) duḥkhasyāntaṃ na (
children.translated_text: ) and so on up to one skeleton. And when you have become practiced in this, and your resolution proceeds with clarity, then [resolve upon] two, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred discolored [corpses], a thousand, and so on, filling all the directions and intermediate directions — resolve upon them continuously, without gaps, in the manner of measurement, so that there would not be space even for the tip of a stick. As with the discolored corpses, so too with the skeletons and all the rest — relying on this resolution-based mental attention (<s>adhimuktimanaskāra</s>), descend into reality-based mental attention (<s>bhūtamanaskāra</s>). And descend thus: "However many discolored corpses up to skeletons I have resolved upon — more immeasurably numerous than these are those that, beginning from my beginningless past, in the various existences and destinies, in the passings and rebirths, have been produced as my discolored corpses up to skeletons after death and the making of time — whose beginning cannot be discerned. If someone were to collect the bones of the deceased, and once collected they did not decay and did not putrefy — there would be no spot of earth where there would be room for them. Even those from a single <s>kalpa</s> (eon) alone — if there were someone to collect those skeletons, the heap of those collected would be equal to the broad Pārśva mountain." As from the beginningless past, so too toward the endless future — [thinking:] "I shall not make an end of suffering" — thus you should apply yourself (

children.text: ) kariṣyāmyevaṃ hi tvamabhiyukṣi (yuṃkṣva) | manaskāraṃ niśritya bhūtamanaskāramavatīrṇo bhaviṣyasi (bhava) | na caitāni vinīlakāni yāvadasthiśaṃkalikā [yā] vipaśyanāprayuktena sakṛdvipaśyitavyā[ni], nānyatraikaṃ vinīlakamadhimucya punaścittaṃ śamayitavyaṃ tāvacca tadvinīkamadhimoktavyaḥ (vyaṃ) yāvattasmenā (sminnā)lambane sābhirāmaprabhāsvaraṃ nopāyāsena paryavanahyate | na tāvātkālakaraṇīyaṃ bhavati | tasmin samaye adhyātmaṃ sā(saṃ?) śamayitavyaṃ yathā vinīlakamevaṃ yāvadasthiśaṃkalikaikā evaṃ yāvadapramāṇā anenaiva nayena veditavyā[ḥ] | cittamadhyātmaṃ saṃśamayitvā (saṃśamya) vimoktavyāstataḥ sarvapaścādapramāṇāni vinīlakānyapramāṇā yāvadasthiśaṃkalikā adhyātmaṃ cittābhisaṃkṣepeṇa vibhāvayatyanābhāsagatāyāṃ sthāpayati | na ca tāni nimittānyutsṛjati || savikalpāni nāpi ca kalpayati | nānyatra tadālambanameva nirnimittaṃ nirvikalpamupaśāntaṃ cittamavasthāpayati |
children.translated_text: ). Relying on [resolution-based] mental attention, you shall have descended into reality-based mental attention. And these discolored corpses up to skeletons should not be viewed just once by one engaged in <s>vipaśyanā</s>; nor, after resolving upon one discolored corpse, should the mind be calmed and then again resolve upon that corpse — one should resolve upon that discolored corpse until the mind, with delight and clarity upon that object, is not overwhelmed with distress — and not at that time should the work [of the next stage] be done. At that point, one should calm the mind internally. As with one discolored corpse, so up to one skeleton — and likewise up to immeasurable [corpses] — all should be understood by this same method. Having calmed the mind internally, one should release them; and then [resolve upon] all the immeasurable discolored corpses, up to the immeasurable skeletons — by the compression of the mind internally, one makes them fade and establishes [the mind] in the state of non-appearance. One does not abandon those signs; they are conceptual, but one does not conceptualize [further]. One does not place [the mind] on anything else — rather, one establishes the mind upon that very object: signless, non-conceptual, and peaceful.

body.translated_text: The <s>yogī</s> then further instructs that beginner engaged in <s>śamatha</s> (calm abiding): 'So long, O fortunate one, as your mind, while engaged in the path of <s>śamatha</s>, remains thus — sustained by skillful means, accompanied by mindfulness and clear comprehension, and delightful — so long should the path of <s>śamatha</s> alone be cultivated. But if, due to lack of practice, one does not delight [in that], even though it is sustained by skillful means and has that object, then one should rise from the non-conceptual object and, on a conceptual object, bind mindfulness. That very sign of unattractiveness (<s>aśubhanimitta</s>) which was previously grasped — attend to that, beginning first with <s>vipaśyanā</s> (insight) that follows mere signs; namely, the discolored corpse, the festering corpse, and so on up to the skeleton. And while thus engaged, first resolve upon one discolored corpse (

body.text: sa punaścopadiśyate, yatte bhadramukha, pūrvamevālokanimittamudgṛhītaṃ, tattvaṃ śamathapakṣaprayoge [a]pi manasi kuru, vipaśyanāpakṣaprayoge [a]pi, ālokasahagatena (

children.text: ) cittena, saprabhāsasahagatena, prabhāsvareṇānandhakāreṇa śamathavipaśyanāṃ bhāvaya | evaṃ ca te śamathavipaśyanāmārge ālokasaṃjñāṃ bhāvayataḥ | sa ce dādita eva avispaṣṭodhivimokṣo bhaviṣyatyālambane samya[gā]bhāsaḥ | sa tena hetunā, tena pratyayena, bhāvanābhāsādviśiṣṭatā bhaviṣyati | pracurābhāsa(ga)tā ca | sa cetpunarādita eva vispaṣṭo bhaviṣyati | pracurābhāsaḥ | sa bhūyasyā mātrayā vispaṣṭataratāṃ pracurābhāsataratāñca gamiṣyati | sa tvametatsamveganimittena sūdgṛhītena, prasadanīyanimittena, śamathanimittena, vipaśyanānimittena, lokanimittena, sūdgṛhītena kālamadhyātmaṃ cittaṃ saṃśayamayankālena kālaṃ dharmānvicinvanti(cinvan), nimittamātrānusāriṇyā vipaśyanayā smṛtyupasthāneṣvavatara | yadutāśubhāprayogamevādhipatiṃ kṛtvā, evaṃ ca punarvicinvan bahirdhā ṣaṭtriṃśato (t)dravyāṇi kāyāt keśādi prasāvaparyantā (ntaṃ) nimittamudgṛhya adhyātmametāni sarvāṇi aśucidravyāṇyadhimucyādhyātmaṃcittaṃ saṃśamaya (sva), idaṃ te bhaviṣyatyadhyātmaṃ kāyena kāyānupaśyanāyāḥ yadutātmano 'ntaḥ kāyamārabhya, sa tvaṃ punarapi bahirdhā aśubhānimittenodgṛhītena vinīlakaṃ cādhimucyasva, yāvadasthi vā śaṃkalikāmvā, (
children.translated_text: ) with a mind accompanied by light, accompanied by radiance, luminous and free from darkness — cultivate <s>śamatha</s> and <s>vipaśyanā</s>. And when, while cultivating the perception of light on the path of <s>śamatha-vipaśyanā</s>, if from the beginning your resolution upon the object is unclear and the illumination is not correct — by that cause, by that condition, through cultivation the illumination will become superior and more abundant. But if from the beginning it is clear and the illumination is abundant — it will become even clearer and more abundantly luminous. You, with this well-grasped sign of spiritual urgency, with this sign of faith, sign of <s>śamatha</s>, sign of <s>vipaśyanā</s>, and sign of light — well-grasped — from time to time calm the mind internally, and from time to time investigate the <s>dharmas</s>; by <s>vipaśyanā</s> that follows mere signs, descend into the <s>smṛtyupasthānas</s> (foundations of mindfulness). Namely, making the practice of unattractiveness (<s>aśubhāprayoga</s>) the predominant factor — and while thus investigating, externally examining the thirty-six substances of the body from hair to excretions, having grasped the sign, internally resolve upon all these impure substances, and calm the mind internally. This will become for you the internal contemplation of the body in the body (<s>kāye kāyānupaśyanā</s>) — namely, beginning with your own inner body. And you should further, with the externally grasped sign of unattractiveness, resolve upon the discolored corpse up to the bone or skeleton (

children.text: ) parīttena vādhimokṣeṇa, mahadgatena vā [a]pramāṇena vādhimucyādhimucyādhyātmaṃ cittaṃ saṃśamaya, idaṃ te bhaviṣyati | bahirdhā kāyena kāyānupaśyanāyā, yaduta parasāntatikaṃ bahiḥkāyamārabhya, sa tvaṃ punarapyātmanaḥ antaḥkāye 'śubhatāparibhāvitena cetasāścāśubhatāparibhāvitena cetasā parakāye cāntarbahiścāśubhatāparibhāvitena cetasātmānaṃ ghri(mri)yamāṇamadhimucyasva, mṛtamvā punaḥ śmaśāne [a]bhinirhriyamāṇamabhinirhṛtamvā, śmaśāne cchoritaṃ | choritamvā vinīlakāvasthaṃ, vipūyakāvasthaṃ, yāvadasthiśaṃkālikāvasthamadhimucyasva, idaṃ te bhaviṣyatyadhyātmabahirdhā kāye kāyānupaśyanāyāḥ sa[t]tvaṃ, punarapi catvāro 'rūpiṇaḥ skandhāḥ śrutacintādhipateyena parikalpanimittagrāheṇa triṣu bhāgeṣvadhimucyasva śamathapakṣye, vikṣepapakṣye, vipaśyanāpakṣye ca | yadādhyātmaṃ cittamabhisaṃkṣipasi tatra nirmimittanirvikalpopaśamākārā nirvyāpārānutsukāsaṃkṣobhaniḥparidāha nairvṛtyasukhasaṃjñākārā avikṣepālambanā vedanādayaścatvāro [a]rūpiṇaḥ skandhāḥ | pratikṣaṇaṃ pratikṣaṇamanyo 'nyatayā navanavaniṣpurāṇatayā pravartanta ityadhimucyasva, idaṃ te bhaviṣyatyadhyātmabahirdhā vedanāsu, citte, dharmeṣu, dharmānupaśyanāyāḥ sattvaṃ | ye pūrvaṃ viṣayopādānā, viṣayālambanā asamāhitabhūmipatitā abhyapatitāḥ (
children.translated_text: ) — with limited resolution, or with extensive resolution, or with immeasurable resolution — resolving again and again, calm the mind internally. This will become for you the external contemplation of the body in the body — namely, beginning with the bodies of others in their continuum. And you should further, with a mind pervaded by the [perception of] unattractiveness regarding your own inner body, and with a mind pervaded by the unattractiveness of others' bodies, and with a mind pervaded by the unattractiveness of both inner and outer — resolve upon yourself as dying, or as dead, or as being carried to the cremation ground, or as having been carried there, or as thrown down at the cremation ground. Having been thrown down, resolve upon the state of discoloration, the state of festering, up to the state of a skeleton. This will become for you the internal-external contemplation of the body in the body. And you should further resolve upon the four formless aggregates — by the sign-grasping of conceptual construction under the predominance of learning and reflection — in three aspects: the <s>śamatha</s> side, the distraction side, and the <s>vipaśyanā</s> side. When you compress the mind internally, therein the feelings and the other three formless aggregates — [having] the aspects of signlessness, non-conceptuality, peace, non-activity, non-eagerness, non-disturbance, non-burning, and the perception of <s>nirvṛti</s>-happiness — with objects of non-distraction, moment by moment proceeding in the manner of otherness, newness, and becoming obsolete — thus resolve. This will become for you the internal-external contemplation of feelings, of mind, and of <s>dharmas</s> in <s>dharmas</s>. Those which were previously the appropriations of sense-objects, with sense-objects as their basis, fallen into the unconcentrated level, that had occurred (

children.text: ) kṣīṇā, ye caitarhi smṛtisaṃpramoṣāccittakṣepe satyutpadyante nimittavitarkopakleśālambanādhipateyā vedanādayaścatvāro [a]rūpiṇaḥ skandhāsteṣāmā(yā)pāyikatāṃ tāvatkālikatāmitvarapratyupasthāyitāṃ, sādīnavatāṃ, sadhruvatāmanāśvāsikatāmaparimucyasva | idaṃ te bhaviṣyati | bahirdhā vedanācittadharmānupaśyanāyāḥ sattvaṃ, punarapi vipaśyanānimittamudgṛhya sanimitte saṃkalpe manaskāre sthitaḥ | ye savikalpasanimittālambanādhipateyā adhyātmamutpadyante | vedanādayacatvāro [a]rūpiṇaḥ skandhāsteṣāṃ pratikṣaṇaṃ navanavatāṃ niṣpurāṇatāmanyo 'nyatāṃ pūrvavadadhimucyasva | idaṃ te bhaviṣyati bahirdhā vedanāyāṃ, citte, dharmeṣu dharmānupaśyanāyāḥ [sattvaṃ] | evaṃ hi tvamaśubhāprayogamadhipatiṃ kṛtvā catvāri smṛtyupasthānānyavatīrṇo bhaviṣyasi | smṛtyupasthāne, prayoge [a]pi ca | te kālena kālaṃ śamathavipaśyanāyāṃ prayoktavyaṃ | sa tvamevamupasthitayā smṛtyā caturṣu smṛtyupasthāneṣu yaṃ yameva grāmaṃ vā, nigamaṃ bopaniśritya viharasi, sa tvaṃ tameva grāmaṃ vā, nigamaṃ vā | tannityena cittena, tatpravaṇena, tatprābho(bhā)reṇa ālambanamālambananimittamutsṛjatā piṇḍāya praviśa | caṇḍasya hastinaścaṇḍasyāśvasya, caṇḍasya goścaṇḍasya kurarasya, ahiśvabhrasthāṇukaṇṭakapalvalaprapātasyandikagūthakaṭhallapāpike yā caryā śayanāsanaparivarjanā [|] (
children.translated_text: ) and are exhausted — and those which even now arise when the mind is distracted through loss of mindfulness, under the predominance of signs, discursive thought, and affliction-objects — the feelings and the other three formless aggregates — resolve upon their transitoriness, their momentariness, their quick arising, their nature as defective, their nature as ephemeral, their unreliable nature. This will become for you the external contemplation of feelings, mind, and <s>dharmas</s> in <s>dharmas</s>. And further, having grasped the sign of <s>vipaśyanā</s>, established in mental attention that has signs and conceptions, those feelings and the other three formless aggregates that arise internally under the predominance of conceptual and sign-bearing objects — resolve upon their moment-by-moment newness, obsolescence, and otherness, as before. This will become for you the external contemplation of feelings, mind, and <s>dharmas</s> in <s>dharmas</s>. Thus, making the practice of unattractiveness the predominant factor, you will have descended into the four <s>smṛtyupasthānas</s> (foundations of mindfulness). And in the practice of the foundations of mindfulness too, from time to time you should engage in <s>śamatha-vipaśyanā</s>. And you, with mindfulness thus established in the four foundations of mindfulness, whatever village or town you dwell near — you should enter that very village or town for alms with a mind that is constantly [directed to practice], inclined toward it, weighed down by it, releasing the object and its sign. [Beware of] fierce elephants, fierce horses, fierce bulls, fierce hawks, snakes, precipices, stakes, thorns, swamps, cataracts, excrement, mud, and filth — and the harmful conduct of [avoiding dangerous] beds and seats. (

) arakṣitaste ātmā bhavati | yeṣu ca te viṣayanimitteṣvindriyāṇi prerayitavyāni teṣvanābhogatayā asaṃvṛtānīndriyāṇi bhavantu | yeṣu vā punarnimitteṣvindriyāṇi prerayitavyāni | teṣu teṣūpasthitā
smṛtiḥ | bhavatu, yaduta kleśāsamudācārāya | sa tvamevaṃ surakṣitena kāyena, susaṃvṛtairindriyaiḥ, sūpasthitayāsmṛtyā, tadgatena mānasena mātrayā piṇḍapātaṃ paribhuṃkṣva | mitabhāgī(ṇī) ca bhava, sārdhaṃ gṛhasthapravrajitairyuktakā(bhā)ṇī, kālabhāṇī, ārjavabhāṇī | praśāntabhāṇī | adharmyā ca te [tvayā] kathā sarveṇa sarvaṃ parivarjayitavyā | dharmyāmapi te [tvayā] kathā[ṃ] kathayatā na vigṛhya kathā karaṇīyā | tatkasya hetoḥ [|] vigṛhya kathāsaṃrambhānuyogamanuyuktasya puruṣapudgalasya viharataḥ kathābāhulye cittaṃ santiṣṭhate | tathā bāhulye satyauddhatyamauddhatye satyavyupaśamaḥ | avyupaśāntacittasyārāccittaṃ samādherbhavati | na tvamevaṃcārī tvaritatvaritamanutsṛṣṭenālambanena me [a]dyaśamathavipaśyanāyāṃ yathodgṛhītenaiva nimittena pratanukāritayāvā, antakāritayā ca | yogaṃ kuru, te (sa tvam) agnimathanaprayogeṇa ca sātatyasatkṛtyaprayogatayā pratatakārī bhava, evaṃ tu punaścitaṃ praṇidhatsva | sa cedyāvadāyurjambūdvīpe sarveṣāṃ jaṃbūdvīpakānāṃ manuṣyāṇāmabhūttatsarvamabhisamastaṃ mamaikasyaitarhi (
children.translated_text: ) Your self will be unguarded. Regarding those sense-object signs toward which the sense-faculties should not be directed, let the sense-faculties remain unguarded through non-engagement. But regarding those signs toward which the faculties should be directed, let mindfulness be established — namely, for the non-arising of <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions). And you, with a well-guarded body, with well-restrained sense-faculties, with well-established mindfulness, with a mind directed [to the practice] — eat your alms in moderation. Be one who eats sparingly. In conversation with householders and renunciants, be one who speaks what is fitting, speaks at the right time, speaks honestly, speaks peacefully. All un-<s>Dharmic</s> conversation should be entirely abandoned by you. And even when engaged in <s>Dharmic</s> conversation, you should not engage in debate. Why? For a person engaged in the pursuit of contentious debate, the mind settles into the abundance of talk; when there is abundance, there is restlessness; when there is restlessness, there is no calm; and for one whose mind is not calm, the mind is far from <s>samādhi</s>. And you, conducting yourself thus, swiftly and without releasing the object — engage in <s>śamatha-vipaśyanā</s> practice today with the very sign as grasped, either by making it subtle or by bringing it to an end. Practice <s>yoga</s>! And like the practice of fire-kindling by friction, with constant and respectful application, be a persistent practitioner. And further, resolve your mind thus: "If all the lifespans of all the humans in <s>Jambudvīpa</s> that ever existed were gathered together and were now mine alone (

children.text: ) syāt | so [a]haṃ tāvadapramāṇenāyuṣā pramāṇayogaprayogeṇa ca sātatyasatkṛtyaprayogatayā pratatakārī bhavā[mi] [|] evaṃ ca punaścittaṃ praṇidhatsva | sa cedyāvadāyurjabūdvīpe manasikāre śamathavipaśyanāyāṃ yogaṃ na riṃcayaṃ(yan) yadutāsyaiva yogaprayogasya mahāphalatāṃ mahānuśaṃsatāṃ ca viditvā prāgevāsmin pari(praṇi)dhatte [|] āyuṣītvare jīvite dūramapigatvā varṣaśati(ta)ke parigaṇyamānamauntike [|]
children.translated_text: ) — I, with such immeasurable lifespan and with measured application of <s>yoga</s>, with constant and respectful application, would be a persistent practitioner." And further, resolve your mind thus: "If I were not to relent in the mental attention and <s>yoga</s> of <s>śamatha-vipaśyanā</s> for as long as the lifespan in <s>Jambudvīpa</s> [lasts]" — namely, knowing the great fruitfulness and great benefit of this very <s>yoga</s> practice, one resolves even beforehand. Life being brief and existence fleeting, even if one were to go far [in years], a hundred years, when reckoned, is trifling.

body.translated_text: One is further instructed: 'That sign of light (<s>ālokanimittam</s>) which you previously grasped, O fortunate one — attend to that in the practice of the <s>śamatha</s> side as well, and in the practice of the <s>vipaśyanā</s> side as well, (

body.text: evaṃ hi tvaṃ yathānuśiṣṭaḥ pratatakārī vātyantakārī ca | yasyārthe prahāṇamupagatastasyārthasyābādhako bhaviṣyasi | tatprathamata[sta]mpra[kṣya]si | mṛdukāṃ kāyapraśrabdhiṃ cittaikāgratāṃ tataścottari vipulālaukikalokottarāṃ sampadamārāgayiṣyati(si) |
body.translated_text: For thus, you who are instructed, acting continuously and acting to the utmost, will be unobstructed with regard to the purpose for which you undertook the effort of abandonment. First you will experience a gentle bodily tranquility (<s>kāyapraśrabdhi</s>) and one-pointedness of mind; and then, beyond that, you will attain a vast, supramundane and transcendent accomplishment.

body.text: evamayamādikarmikastatprathamakarmikaḥ | aśubhāprayukto yogajñenācāryeṇa codyamānaḥ samyaga(k) codito bhavatyevaṃ ca pratipadyamānaḥ | samyakpratipanno bhavati | yathā [a]śubhāvineyo [a]śubhāyāṃ, tathā maitryavineyādayo [a]pi ānāpānasmṛtiparyavasānāya yathāyogaṃ veditavyāstatrāyaṃ viśeṣaḥ | tadanyeṣvavataraṇamukheṣu taṃ vibhāvayiṣyāmi | tatra maitrībhāvanāprayuktenādikarmikā(ṇa)bahirdhā mitrapakṣādudāsīnapakṣācca (

children.text: ) nimittamudgṛhya pratirūpaśayanāsanagato hi sukhādhyāśayagatena manaskāreṇa samāhitabhūmikena pūrvamekaṃ mitramadhimoktavyamekamamitramekamu(ka u)dāsī naṃ (naḥ), teṣu ca tri[ṣu] pakṣeṣu tulyaṃ hitasukhādhyāśayagatena manaskāreṇopasaṃhāraśca karaṇīyaḥ | sukhitā bhavantyete sukhakāyāḥ sattvā yadutānavadyakāmasukhena, anavadyasaprītikasukhena, anavadyaniṣprītikasukhena | tataḥ paścād dve mitrāṇi, trīṇi, catvāri, pañca, daśa, viṃśa, triṃśatpūrvavadyāvatsarvā diśo vidiśaśca mitrāmitra (traiḥ) pūrṇā adhimucyante | nirantarā yatra nāstyantaramantato daṇḍakoṭīviṣkambhanamātramapi yathā mitrapakṣeṇaivamamitrodāsīnapakṣeṇa veditavyaṃ | sa ca maitrīprayogaṃ ca na jahāti | nānyatra bhāvayanneva maitrīṃ smṛtyupasthāneṣvavatarati | kathaṃ punaravataratyadhimucyamāno [a]vatarati | yathāhamapyanyeṣāṃ mitrasammato [a]mitrasammataścodāsīnasammataśca [|] ahamapi sukhakāmo duḥkhapratikūlaḥ | idamasyādhyātmaṃ kāye kāyānupaśyanāyāḥ [sattvam] | ete [a]pi sattvāḥ pareṣāṃ mitrabhūtā, amitrabhūtā, udāsīnabhūtāśca, yathā me te [a]pi sukhakāmāḥ duḥkhapratikūlā idamasya bahirdhā kāyānupaśyanāyāḥ [sattvaṃ], yathāhaṃ tathaite sattvā, yathā me ātmanaḥ sukhameṣaṇīyaṃ sattvānāmātmasamatayātmatulyatayā (
children.translated_text: having gone to a suitable lodging, with mental attention belonging to the concentrated level directed toward the wish for happiness — first one should resolve upon one friend, one enemy, and one neutral person. And with respect to these three classes, one should apply equally a mental attention directed toward the wish for their welfare and happiness: 'May these beings be happy, those beings of happy bodies — namely, through blameless sensual happiness, through blameless happiness accompanied by rapture, and through blameless happiness free from rapture.' Then afterwards, two friends, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty — as before, up to all directions and intermediate directions being filled with friends — one resolves upon them as uninterrupted, where there is no gap even to the extent of the tip of a stick. Just as with the class of friends, so too should it be understood with the class of enemies and the class of neutral persons. And one does not abandon the practice of <s>maitrī</s>; nor does one cultivate <s>maitrī</s> separately — rather, while cultivating <s>maitrī</s> itself, one descends into the <s>smṛtyupasthānas</s> (foundations of mindfulness). And how does one descend? One descends through resolution: 'Just as I too am reckoned by others as a friend, an enemy, or a neutral person, and I too desire happiness and am averse to suffering — this is the internal contemplation of the body in the body. These beings too are friends, enemies, and neutral persons to others, and like me, they too desire happiness and are averse to suffering — this is the external contemplation of the body in the body. Just as I am, so are these beings; just as happiness is to be sought for myself, so by the equality and likeness of self [and others],

children.text: ) eṣāṃ sattvānāṃ mayābhihitasukhopasaṃhārakaraṇāya itīdamasyādhyātmabahirdhā kāye kāyānupaśyanāyāḥ [sattvam] | catvāri caitāni smṛtyupasthānāni, saṃbhinnaskandhālambanatayā saṃbhinnālambanaṃ smṛtyupasthānaṃ bhavati | rūpanimittantu yogī udgṛhya varṇasaṃsthānanimittaṃ, vijñaptinimittaṃ ca mitrāmitrodāsīnapakṣād(kṣebhyo) 'dhimucyate | tenedaṃ kāyasmṛtyupasthānameva vyāvasthāpyate | so 'dhimuktimanaskāraṃ niśritya, bhūtamanaskāramasyāvataratyevaṃ ca punaradhimucyamāno [a]vatarati | yāvadapramāṇāḥ sattvā ete mayā (a)dhimuktā | hitasukhagatenādhyāśayena | ato [a]pramāṇatarāḥ sattvā ye mamapūrvāntamārabhya mitrāmitrodāsīnapakṣatayā [a]bhyatītā ye mama mitratāṃ gatvā amitratāmupagatā, amitratāṃ gatvā mitratāṃ codāsīnatāṃ topa(copa)gatāstadanena paryāyeṇa sarva eva sattvāssamasamā, nāstyatra kācinmitratā vā, amitratā vodāsīnatā vā, pariniṣpannetyanenaiva paryāyeṇa tulyahitasukhopasaṃhāratā ca karaṇīyā | yathā pūrvāntamārabhya evamaparāntamapyāramya, satyāṃ saṃsṛtau saṃsāre yepi ca mayā sattvāḥ pūrvāntamārabhya tanmaitreṇa cittenānukampitāḥ | kiṃ (
children.translated_text: I should make the effort to bring about the aforesaid happiness for these beings' — this is the internal-and-external contemplation of the body in the body. And these four foundations of mindfulness, by virtue of having a combined aggregate-object, become the foundation of mindfulness with a combined object. The <s>yogī</s>, having grasped the form-sign — the sign of color, shape, and gesture — from the classes of friends, enemies, and neutral persons, resolves upon it. Therefore this is established as the contemplation of body (<s>kāyasmṛtyupasthāna</s>) alone. Relying on the mental attention of resolution, one descends into the mental attention of reality. And descending further through resolution: 'However many beings I have resolved upon with a mental attitude directed toward their welfare and happiness — far more numerous than these are the beings who, from beginningless time, have passed through the classes of friend, enemy, and neutral toward me; who, having been friends, became enemies; who, having been enemies, became friends or neutral. By this reasoning, all beings are absolutely equal — there is here no such thing as friendship, enmity, or neutrality in an ultimate sense.' And by this very reasoning, equal application of welfare and happiness should be practiced. Just as from the beginningless past, so too regarding the future — as long as there is the round of <s>saṃsāra</s>. And whatever beings I have, from the beginningless past, shown compassion to with a mind of <s>maitrī</s> —

children.text: ) cāpi te [a]bhyatītā apitu tānetarhyanukampe yaduta cittaniṣkāluṣya(kaluṣa)tāmavyāpannatāmupādāya | sukhitā bata te sattvā, bhūtā bhaviṣyan (abhūvan), ye, [a]pi ca na bhūtā anāgate [a]dhvani sukhitā bhavantu | evaṃ bhūtamanaskārānupratiṣṭhasya maitrīvihāriṇaḥ yaḥ puṇyābhiṣyandaḥ kuśalābhiṣyandaḥ | tasyādhimokṣikamaitrīvihāragataḥ puṇyaskandhaḥ | śatimāmapi kalāṃ naupeti | sahasrimāmapi | saṃkhyāmapi, kalāmapi | gaṇanāmapyupaniṣadamapi nopaiti [|] śeṣaṃ pūrvat ||
children.translated_text: not only have those [beings] passed away, but I should show compassion to these present ones too — namely, for the sake of the purity and freedom from ill-will of the mind. 'May those beings who have been happy, who were [once happy], and those who have never been happy — may they be happy in the future!' Thus, for one who is established in the mental attention of reality, dwelling in <s>maitrī</s>, the overflow of merit and the overflow of wholesomeness — the aggregate of merit pertaining to the dwelling in <s>maitrī</s> through resolution — does not approach even a hundredth part, not even a thousandth, not even a calculable fraction, a measure, an enumeration, or a comparison. The rest is as before.

body.translated_text: Thus, this beginner — that is, one practicing for the first time — who is engaged in the contemplation of unattractiveness (<s>aśubhā</s>), being exhorted by a teacher skilled in <s>yoga</s>, is correctly exhorted, and practicing in this manner, is one who practices correctly. Just as it is for one to be trained through unattractiveness, so too for those to be trained through <s>maitrī</s> (loving-kindness) and so on, up to <s>ānāpānasmṛti</s> (mindfulness of breathing) — this should be understood as appropriate. Here is the distinction: I shall explain the entry-points for the other [practices]. Therein, the beginner engaged in the cultivation of <s>maitrī</s>, having grasped the sign externally from the class of friends and from the class of neutral persons,

body.text: tatredaṃpratyayatāpratītyasamutpāda ādikarmikaḥ śrutacintādhipateyena parikalpitaṃ na nimittamudgṛhṇātyanyeṣāṃ sattvānāmajñānaṃ | sammoho yeneme pratyakṣamanityaṃ nityato [a]vagacchanti pratyakṣamaśuci śucitaḥ, duḥkhaṃ sukhataḥ, nirātmakatāmātmataḥ | viparyastā ete sattvā viparyāsa hetordṛṣṭe dharme, vedanāsu samparāye cātmabhāvābhirnivṛttau, tṛṣyanti, tṛṣitāśca jātimūlakāni karmāṇi kṛtvā evamāyatyāṃ karmakleśahetu [............] kevalaṃ saṃduḥkhamabhinirvartayantyevaṃ nimittamudgṛhyādhyātmamadhimucyate | ayamapi kevalo duḥkhaskandha evameva saṃbhūta iti | ye cātmabhāvā nānantā[ḥ] paryantāḥ pūrvāntamārabhya yeṣāmādireva na prajñāyate | (

children.text: ) te 'pyevaṃbhūtā, eṣāmapi sattvānāmatītānāgatapratyutpannāḥ sarva evātmabhāvā duḥkhaskandhasaṃgṛhītā evamevābhinirvṛttāḥ | āyatyāṃ notpadyante | sa khalvayamiyaṃ(daṃ)pratyayatāpratītyasamutpādamanaskāraḥ sarvabhūtamanaskāra eva nāstyādhimokṣikaḥ | yadi na punarātmano vartamānān skandhān pratītyasamutpannān manasikaroti | tadādhyātmaṃ kāye yāvaddharmeṣu dharmānudarśī viharati | yadā ca punaḥ pareṣāṃ vartamānānskandhān pratītyasamutpannānmanasi karoti | tadādhyātmabahirdhā kāye yāvaddharmeṣu dharmānudarśī viharati | yadātmanaśca pareṣāṃ cātītānāgatān [skandhān] pratītyasamutpannānmanasi karoti | tadādhyātmabahirdhā kāye yāvaddharmeṣu dharmānudarśī viharati | śeṣaṃ pūrvat |
children.translated_text: these too are of this very nature. For these beings too, all existences — past, future, and present — are included within the aggregate of suffering, produced in just this way; and in the future, they will not arise [if the conditions are removed]. This mental attention of conditionality and dependent origination is entirely the mental attention of reality — there is nothing of resolution in it. When one mentally attends to one's own present aggregates as dependently arisen, then one dwells internally contemplating the body in the body, and up to contemplating <s>dharmas</s> in <s>dharmas</s>. When one mentally attends to others' present aggregates as dependently arisen, then one dwells externally. When one mentally attends to one's own and others' past and future aggregates as dependently arisen, then one dwells internally-and-externally contemplating the body in the body, up to contemplating <s>dharmas</s> in <s>dharmas</s>. The rest is as before.

body.translated_text: Therein, the beginner engaged in the practice of conditionality and dependent origination (<s>idaṃpratyayatāpratītyasamutpāda</s>): through the dominance of learning and reflection, having grasped the conceptually constructed sign — [namely,] the ignorance and delusion of other beings by which they apprehend what is directly perceived as impermanent to be permanent, what is directly perceived as impure to be pure, suffering to be happiness, and what is devoid of self to be a self — 'These beings are perverted, and due to the cause of perversion, in this very life and in future lives, with regard to feelings and with regard to the obtaining of [new] existences, they crave; and craving, they perform actions rooted in birth; and thus, in the future, through the cause of <s>karma</s> and <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions) [...] they bring about a mass of nothing but suffering.' Having thus grasped the sign, one internally resolves: 'This too is nothing but a mass of suffering, produced in just this way.' And the existences that are not endless but limited — from the beginningless past, whose beginning is simply not discernible —

body.text: tatra dhātuprabhedaprayogaprayukta ādikarmiko bahirdhāpṛthivīkāṭhinyanimittamudgrahya, tadyathā bhūparvatatṛṇavanaśarkarakaṭhillamaṇimuktivaiḍūryaśilāpravālādikebhyaścādhyātmaṃ kāṭhinyamadhimucyate | bahirdhā apsvabdhātornni(rni)mittamudgṛhya, tadyathā nadīprasravaṇataḍāgakūpādibhya[ḥ], tathā mahato [a]gniska ska[ndhasya]bdhau vādityakiraṇasaṃtāpitā bhūrāviṣṭebhyo (

children.text: ) [vā] sarvebhyaḥ | udārāgnisaṃpratāpitebhyo vā praśrayebhyaśca no bahirdhā vāyuskandhātpūrvadakṣiṇapaścimottarebhyo vāyubhyo yāvadvāyumaṇḍalebhyaḥ | ye deśā [astyādestāraṇīyā] vāyugatena sacchidrāḥ, suśirāḥ, sāvakāśāḥ, tasmādākāśadhātornimittamudgṛhṇātyadhyātmamabdhātuṃ, tejo dhātuṃ vāyudhātumākāśadhātumadhimucyati(te) | śrutacintādhipateyena ca parikalpitena [|] evaṃ vijñānadhātornimittamudgṛhṇāti | cakṣurādhyātmikamāyatanamaparibhinnaṃ ced bhavati | rūpamābhāsagataṃ | na ca tajjo manaskāraḥ pratyupasthito bhavati | na tajjasya cakṣurvijñānasya prādurbhāvo bhavati | viparyayādbhavati | evaṃ yāvanmanodharmānmanovijñānaṃ veditavyam |
children.translated_text: or from all [things] greatly heated by fire, and from streams — one [resolves internally]. And regarding the external wind-element — from the eastern, southern, western, and northern winds, up to the wind-circles; those regions that are to be covered by the wind, that have openings, hollows, and spaces — therefore one grasps the sign of the space-element (<s>ākāśadhātu</s>) [as well]. One internally resolves upon the water-element, fire-element, wind-element, and space-element. And through the dominance of learning and reflection, with a conceptually constructed [sign], one likewise grasps the sign of the consciousness-element (<s>vijñānadhātu</s>): if the internal sense-base of the eye is unimpaired, and if a form has come into the range of light, yet the corresponding mental attention has not arisen, then the corresponding eye-consciousness does not manifest; but in the reverse case, it does. Likewise, up to the mind, mental objects, and mind-consciousness should be understood.

body.translated_text: Therein, the beginner engaged in the practice of element-analysis (<s>dhātuprabhedaprayoga</s>): having externally grasped the sign of hardness of the earth-element — such as from land, mountains, grass, forests, pebbles, stones, gems, pearls, lapis lazuli, rocks, coral, and the like — one internally resolves upon [that same] hardness. Having externally grasped the sign of the water-element — such as from rivers, springs, ponds, wells, and the like — and likewise from the great fire of a conflagration, or from the ocean, or from the earth heated by the rays of the sun,

body.text: evaṃ nimittamudgṛhyāpyeṣāṃ sarveṣāṃ vijñānānāmasmin kāye cāturmahābhūtike bījaṃ dhāturgotraṃ prakṛtirityadhimucyate | tānyetāni catvāri mahābhūtāni tatprathamato [a]ṅgapratyaṃgo(gato) [a]rthaṃ vināpyadhimucyate [|] tataḥ paścāt | sūkṣmatarāvayava prabhedānādhimucyate | evaṃ yāvadgatāyanapraviṣṭa[s]tu[ṭi]samatayā, evaṃ yāvacchanaiḥ śanaiḥ paramāṇuśo [a]dhimucyate | sa ekaikamaṃgāvayavapramāṇaparamāṇusañcayasanniviṣṭamadhimucyate | (

children.text: ) kaḥ punarvādaḥ sarvakāyamayaṃ(yam | ayaṃ) dhātuprabhedaprayuktasya cārthaprabhedaparyantaḥ rūpiṇāṃ tābaddhātūnāmākāśadhātoḥ punaḥ | yatpunarasya tasmin prayoge śamathavipaśyanābhāvanāyāṃ vikṣepāvikṣepaparijñāvadhānamidamasya saṃprajanyasya smṛtisamatāyāśca [|] yatpunaḥ saṃveganimittaṃ, prasadanīyaṃ ca nimittaṃ sūdgṛhītaṃ bhavatīdamasyābhidhyādaurmanasya vinayasya, tasyaivamātāpino viharato yāvat (d) dvitīyaloke [a]bhidhyādaurmanasyaṃ pūrvameva samyakprayoga[sa]mārambhakāle | sūkṣmacittapraśrabdhirdurupalabhyā pravarttate | yā tatra śamathamvā bhāvayato, vipaśyanāmvā prasvasthacittatā, prasvasthakāyatā | cittakāya karmaṇyatā | iyamatra kāyacittapraśrabdhiḥ | tasya saiva sūkṣmā cittaikāgratā cittakāyapraśrabdhiścābhivara[ṃ] nī audārikāṃ sūpalakṣyāṃ cittaikāgratāṃ kāyapraśrabdhimāvahati | yaduta hetupāraṃ paryādānayogena, na tasya, na cirasyedānīmaudārikīcittakāyapraśrabdhiścittaikāgratā ca | sūpalakṣyotpatsyatīti | yāvadasyā pūrvanimittaṃ pūrva nirgauravapratibhāsamutpadyate | na caitadvādhalakṣaṇaṃ | tasyānantarotpādādyatprahāṇarativivandhakārī (ri)ṇāṃ kleśānāṃ pakṣyaṃ cittaṃ(tta)dauṣṭhulyaṃ tatprahīyate | tatpratipakṣeṇa ca cittakarmaṇyatā (
children.translated_text: How much more so the entire body! This is the limit of the analysis of meaning for one engaged in element-analysis, with respect to the material elements and the space-element. Now, his awareness of distraction and non-distraction in that practice of cultivating <s>śamatha</s> (calm abiding) and <s>vipaśyanā</s> (insight) — this is his clear comprehension (<s>saṃprajanya</s>) and equanimity of mindfulness. And his firm grasping of the sign of spiritual urgency (<s>saṃvega</s>) and the faith-inspiring sign — this is his removal of covetousness and mental displeasure (<s>abhidhyādaurmanasya</s>). For one thus dwelling with ardent effort — up to the point of [removing] covetousness and mental displeasure in the second [stage] — even at the very time of the initial proper practice, a subtle mental tranquility (<s>cittapraśrabdhi</s>), difficult to discern, operates. This tranquillity that occurs — whether one is cultivating <s>śamatha</s> or <s>vipaśyanā</s> — is comfort of mind, comfort of body, workability of mind and body. This is the tranquility of body and mind here. That very subtle one-pointedness and tranquility of mind and body eventually, with increasing [practice], brings about a coarse, easily discernible one-pointedness and bodily tranquility — namely through the process of bringing [the practice] to the far shore of causation. Before long, the coarse tranquility of mind and body and one-pointedness will arise, easily discernible. Prior to this, a preliminary sign arises — a perception of heaviness that is not of the nature of an obstacle. Immediately after its arising, the mental rigidity (<s>cittadauṣṭhulya</s>) that belongs to the side of the afflictions that obstruct delight in abandonment is removed; and through its antidote, mental workability (<s>cittakarmaṇyatā</s>) and

children.text: ) cittapraśrabdhirutpadyate | tasyotpādāt kāyapraśrabdhyutpādānukūlāni vāyūrdhva [mu]ktāni mahābhūtāni kāye 'vakramanti | teṣāmavakramaṇahetoryatkāyadauṣṭhulyaṃ tadvigacchati | prahāṇaratiriva[daka]rakleśāpakṣyakāyapraśrabdhyā ca tatpratipakṣikayā sarvakāyaḥ pūryate | syādā [............] dhyāti |
children.translated_text: mental tranquility (<s>cittapraśrabdhi</s>) arise. From the arising of that, great elements conducive to the arising of bodily tranquility are released upward and descend into the body. Due to their descending, whatever bodily rigidity (<s>kāyadauṣṭhulya</s>) existed is removed. And bodily tranquility (<s>kāyapraśrabdhi</s>), which is the antidote to the afflictions on the side of [obstructing] delight in abandonment, fills the entire body. One would then meditate [...].

body.translated_text: Having thus grasped the sign, one resolves that the seed, the element, the <s>gotra</s> (nature), and the fundamental nature of all these consciousnesses lies in this body composed of the four great elements (<s>cāturmahābhūtika</s>). First, one resolves upon those four great elements as they are distributed among the limbs and sub-limbs — even apart from their purposes. Then afterwards, one resolves upon ever finer subdivisions of their parts. Thus, gradually, up to equality with the finest atomic particles (<s>paramāṇu</s>), one resolves, step by step, down to the level of individual atoms. One resolves upon each limb and sub-limb as an accumulation of atoms of a certain measure.

body.text: tataḥ prathamopanipāte cittauṣṭhilyaṃ (cittadauṣṭhulyaṃ) cittasumanaskāraprāmodyasahagatālambanasābhirāmatā ca | cittasya tasmin samaye khyāti | tasyordhvaṃ yo 'sau tatprathamopanipātī praśrabdhivegaḥ | sa śanaiḥ śanaiḥ pariślathataro bhavati | chāyevānugatā praśrabdhiḥ kāye ca pravarttate | yacca tadauddhilyaṃ(ddhatyaṃ) cetasastadapyavahīyate | praśāntākāracittasālambane śamatho yastacca(yassa)pravarttate | tata ūrdhvamayaṃ yogī ādikarmikaḥ samanaskāro bhavati | [sa]manaskāra iti ca saṃkhyāṃ gacchati | tatkasya hetoḥ | rūpārthānurodhena samāhitabhūmiko manaskāraḥ parīttastaprathamataḥ pratilabdho bhavati | tenocyate samanaskāra iti |
body.translated_text: Then, at the first [moment of] attainment, the unsuitability of the mind (<s>cittadauṣṭhulya</s>), the mental agreeability, joy, and delight in the object accompanied by gladness — these manifest in the mind at that time. After that, the initial rush of <s>prasrabdhi</s> (pliancy) gradually becomes more relaxed. Like a shadow following, <s>prasrabdhi</s> extends also in the body. And that excitement (<s>auddhatya</s>) of the mind also subsides. <s>Śamatha</s> (calm abiding) with respect to the object in a mind of peaceful aspect operates. From that point onward, this <s>yogī</s>, as a beginner, becomes one who has attained mental attention (<s>samanaskāra</s>), and is reckoned as having attained mental attention. For what reason? Because, in conformity with the purpose of the form-realm, a limited mental attention belonging to the concentrated plane has been attained by him for the first time. Therefore he is called one with mental attention.

body.text: tasyāsya samanaskārasyādikarmikasyemāni liṃgāni bhavanti | parīttamanena rūpāvacaraṃ cittaṃ pratilabdhaṃ bhavati | parīttā kāyapraśrabdhiścittapraśrabdhiścittaikāgratā, bhavyo bhavati pratibalaḥ | kleśaviśodhanālambanaḥ (

children.text: ) prayoge 'sya, stigvā(mā)cāsya cittasantatiḥ pravarttate | śamathopagūḍhāccaritaṃ tadānena viśodhitaṃ bhavati | sa cedraṃjanīye viṣaye carati, na tīvraṃ rāgaparyavasthānamutpādayati | alpamātrekaṇāvaramātrakeṇa ca | pratipakṣasanniśrayeṇābhoga mātrakeṇāśakto [a]tiprativiśoda(dha)yituṃ | yathā raṃjanīye evaṃ dveṣaṇīye, mohanīye mānasthānīye, vitarkasthānīye veditavyam | niṣaṇṇasya cāsya pratisaṃlayane cittaṃ pratidadhatastvaritatvaritaṃ cittaṃ praśrabhyate || kāyaśca [|] kāyadauṣṭhulyāni ca nātyarthaṃ bādhante | na cātyarthaṃ nivaraṇasamudācāro bhavati | na cātyarthamutkaṇṭhā ratiparitamanāsahagatā[ḥ] saṃjñāmanasikārāḥ samudācaranti | vyutthitasyāpi manasa[ś] (vyutthitamanaso 'pi) carataḥ | praśrabdha(bdhi)mātrā kāciccitte, kāye, (citte) cānugatā bhavatītyevaṃ bhāgīyāni [sa]manaskārasya [ādikarmikasya] liṃgāni nimittānyavadātāni veditavyāni ||
children.translated_text: in his practice, his mind-continuum operates with steadiness. And his temperament becomes purified through being embraced by <s>śamatha</s>. If he moves among objects that arouse desire, he does not generate intense envelopment of attachment; and by merely a small or inferior amount, through the support of the antidote, by a mere effort, he is unable to completely purify [the defilement]. As with objects that arouse desire, so too should it be understood for those that arouse aversion, delusion, pride, and discursive thought. And when seated in meditative absorption, as he directs his mind, the mind quickly becomes pliant, and the body also. The bodily unsuitabilities (<s>kāyadauṣṭhulya</s>) do not excessively afflict him. The manifestation of the hindrances (<s>nīvaraṇa</s>) does not excessively occur. Longings and perceptions and mental attentions accompanied by the dissatisfaction of discontent do not excessively arise. Even when the mind has emerged [from absorption] and he is moving about, some degree of <s>prasrabdhi</s> (pliancy) remains following the mind and the body. Such are the signs and marks, the bright indications, of the beginner who has attained mental attention, to be understood.

body.translated_text: For this beginner who has attained mental attention, these are the signs: by this limited [attainment], a form-realm mind has been attained; the bodily <s>prasrabdhi</s> (pliancy), mental <s>prasrabdhi</s>, and one-pointedness of mind are limited; he becomes capable and able for the object of purification from defilements (<s>kleśaviśodhanālambana</s>) —

body.text: | piṇḍoddānam ||
body.translated_text: Summary verse:

children.translated_text: Approaching, and the gladdening, questioning, seeking,
application, guarding, accumulation, seclusion, single-mindedness of existence,

body.text: āvaraṇaśuddhayutkṛṣṭeha manaskārasya bhāvanā ||
body.translated_text: purification from obstacles, and the exalted cultivation of mental attention.

body.text: || yogācārabhūmau śrāvakabhūmisaṃgṛhītāyāṃ tṛtīyaṃ yogasthānaṃ samāptam ||
body.translated_text: In the <s>Yogācārabhūmi</s>, within the <s>Śrāvakabhūmi</s>, the Third Yoga Stage is completed.

body.text: IV. caturthaṃ yogasthānam
body.translated_text: IV. The Fourth Yoga Stage

body.text: tatra labdhamanaskārasya yoginaḥ | evaṃ parīttaprahāṇaratipraviṣṭasya tadūrdhvaṃ dve gatī bhavataḥ | ananye | katame dve tadyathā | laukikī ca lokottarā ca |
body.translated_text: Therein, for the <s>yogī</s> who has attained mental attention, who has thus entered into the limited delight in abandonment — from that point onward, there are two and no other courses: the worldly (<s>laukikī</s>) and the supramundane (<s>lokottarā</s>).

body.text: tatrāyamādikarmiko yogācāraḥ | samanaskāraḥ | laukikayā vā gatyā gamiṣyāmi | lokottarayā veti | tameva manaskāraṃ bahulīkaroti | yathā yathā bahulīkaroti | tathā tathā sā praśrabdhiścittaikāgratā ca | teṣāṃ teṣāṃ rātridivasānāmatyayātpṛthuvṛddhivaipulyatāṃ gacchati | yadā cāsya dṛṣṭisthiraḥ kharaśca manaskāraḥ saṃvṛtto bhavati | pariśrabdhaścālambanādhimokṣaḥ | pravartate | śamathavipaśyanāpakṣyācca nimittānyudgṛhītāni bhavanti | tadā sa laukikena mārgeṇa gantukāmastatra ca prayogamārabhate lokottareṇa vā mārgeṇa [|]
body.translated_text: Therein, this beginner yogic practitioner who has attained mental attention [thinks:] "I shall proceed by the worldly course or by the supramundane." He intensifies that very mental attention. As he intensifies it, that <s>prasrabdhi</s> (pliancy) and one-pointedness of mind, with the passage of successive days and nights, grow broadly, increase, and become extensive. When his mental attention has become firm and stable in its orientation, and his conviction (<s>adhimokṣa</s>) regarding the object has become pliant and operates, and the signs belonging to the side of <s>śamatha</s> and <s>vipaśyanā</s> have been grasped — then, wishing to proceed by the worldly path, he undertakes practice therein, or by the supramundane path.

body.text: tatra kati pudgalāḥ | ye dṛṣṭe dharme laukikenaiva (

children.text: ) mārgeṇa pṛ(ga)cchanti | na lokottareṇa | āha | catvārastadyathā sarva ito bāhyakaḥ | iha dhārmiko 'pi mandaḥ | pūrvaśamathacaritastathā bhūyo 'pyaparipakvakuśalamūlaḥ | bodhisattvasyāyatyāṃ bodhimanuprāptukāmaḥ | no tu dṛṣṭa eva dharme (|) amī catvāraḥ pudgalā dṛṣṭa eva dharme laukikamārgayāni(yi)no bhavanti |
children.translated_text: and not by the supramundane? He says: Four — namely: one entirely belonging to an external [tradition]; one who, even in this <s>Dharma</s>, is dull; one who has previously practiced calm but whose wholesome roots are still not yet ripened; and a <s>Bodhisattva</s> who wishes to attain awakening in the future, but not in this very life. These four types of persons proceed by the worldly path in this very life.

body.translated_text: Therein, how many types of persons are there who, in this very life, proceed by the worldly path alone

body.text: tacca laukikamārgagamanaṃ dvividhaṃ | saka[la]bandhanānāñca pṛthagjanānāṃ, vikalabandhanānāṃ ca | śaikṣāṇāṃ |
body.translated_text: And that proceeding by the worldly path is twofold: that of ordinary persons (<s>pṛthagjana</s>) who have the full set of bonds, and that of trainees (<s>śaikṣa</s>) who have a partial set of bonds.

body.text: tatpunaḥ katamat | kāmānāmaudārikatāṃ paśyataḥ, prathame ca dhyāne samāpattyupapattikleśāntatāṃ paśyatastatkāmavairāgyagamanamevaṃ yāvat | ākiñcanyāyatanavairāgyaṃ veditavyam | tathā asaṃjñisamāpattiḥ | (

children.translated_text: Through the support of the <s>dhyāna</s> attainments, the production of the five [superknowledges] from the six kinds of consciousness.

body.translated_text: What then is that? For one who sees the coarseness of sense-desires and who sees the peace in the attainment of and rebirth in the first <s>dhyāna</s> and the quiescence of defilements therein — proceeding through dispassion from sense-desires, and similarly up to dispassion from the realm of nothingness (<s>ākiñcanyāyatana</s>), should be understood. Likewise, the attainment of non-perception (<s>asaṃjñisamāpatti</s>).

body.text: tatra kāmavairāgyāya prayukto yogī saptabhirmanaskāraiḥ | kāmavairāgyamanuprāpnoti | katame punaste sapta manaskārāḥ | āha | lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī, ādhimokṣikaḥ, prāvivekyo, ratisaṃgrāhakaḥ | mīmānsā(māṃsā)manaskāraḥ | prayoganiṣṭhaḥ, prayoganiṣṭhāphalaśca |
body.translated_text: Therein, the <s>yogī</s> engaged in dispassion from sense-desires attains dispassion from sense-desires through seven mental attentions. What are those seven mental attentions? He says: the mental attention that discerns characteristics (<s>lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedin</s>), the resolving (<s>ādhimokṣika</s>), the secluded (<s>prāvivekya</s>), the delight-gathering (<s>ratisaṃgrāhaka</s>), the investigating (<s>mīmāṃsā</s>), the culmination of practice (<s>prayoganiṣṭha</s>), and the fruit of the culmination of practice (<s>prayoganiṣṭhāphala</s>).

body.text: tatra lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī manaskāraḥ katamaḥ | āha | yena manaskāreṇa kāmānāmaudārikalakṣaṇaṃ pratisaṃvedayate | prathame ca dhyāne śāntalakṣaṇaṃ | kathaṃ ca punaraudārikalakṣaṇaṃ pratisaṃvedayati | āha | kāmānāṃ ṣaḍvastūni paryeṣamāṇaḥ arthanya svūlakṣaṇaṃ (arthaṃ, svalakṣaṇaṃ, sāmānyalakṣaṇaṃ) | pakṣaṃ kālaṃ yuktiñca |
body.translated_text: Therein, what is the mental attention that discerns characteristics? He says: The mental attention by which one discerns the coarse characteristics of sense-desires and the peaceful characteristics of the first <s>dhyāna</s>. And how does one discern the coarse characteristics? He says: Seeking the six objects regarding sense-desires — the meaning, the particular characteristic, the general characteristic, the side, the time, and the reasoning.

body.text: tatraudārikārthaṃ tāvatparyeṣate | itīme kāmāḥ sādīnavā, bahūpadravā, bahvītikā, bahūpasargā iti | yā eṣu kāmeṣu bahvādīnavatā | yāvadbahūpasargatā | ayamaudārikārthaḥ | tatra vastu paryeṣate | astyadhyātmaṃ kāmeṣu kāma(c)chanda iti |
body.translated_text: Therein, one first seeks the meaning of coarseness: "These sense-desires are full of danger, full of adversity, full of calamity, full of misfortune." That which is the manifold dangerousness of these sense-desires, up to the manifold misfortune — this is the meaning of coarseness. Therein, one seeks the object: "There is internally, with respect to sense-desires, the desire for sense-pleasures (<s>kāmacchanda</s>)."

body.text: tatra svalakṣaṇaṃ paryeṣate | amī kleśakāmāḥ | amī vastukāmāḥ | te punaḥ sukhasthānīyā, duḥkhasthānīyā, (

children.text: ) aduḥkhasukhasthānīyāśca | sukhasthānīyāḥ kāmarāgādhiṣṭhānāḥ | saṃjñācittaviparyāsādhiṣṭhānāḥ | duḥkhasthānīyā[ḥ] punardveṣādhiṣṭhānāḥ krodhopanāhādhiṣṭhānāḥ | aduḥkhāsukhasthānīyāḥ mrakṣapradāśamāyāśāṭhyāhrīkyama(kyā)napatrāpyādhiṣṭhānā dṛṣṭiviparyāsādhiṣṭhānāśca | evamamī kāmāḥ praduṣṭavedanānugatāśca, pratyastakleśānugatāścaivaṃ kāmānāṃ svalakṣaṇaṃ paryeṣate |
children.translated_text: and those standing in the position of neither-suffering-nor-pleasure. Those standing in the position of pleasure are based on sensual attachment (<s>kāmarāga</s>), based on the distortion of perception and mind. Those standing in the position of suffering are based on aversion and anger (<s>dveṣa</s>, <s>krodha</s>, <s>upanāha</s>). Those standing in the position of neither-suffering-nor-pleasure are based on hypocrisy, spite, deceit, dissimulation, shamelessness, recklessness, and based on the distortion of views. Thus these sense-desires are accompanied by corrupted feelings and accompanied by underlying defilements. Thus one seeks the particular characteristic of sense-desires.

body.translated_text: Therein, one seeks the particular characteristic: "These are defilement-desires (<s>kleśakāma</s>); these are object-desires (<s>vastukāma</s>)." And they are further [distinguished as] those standing in the position of pleasure, those standing in the position of suffering,

body.text: tatra kathaṃ sāmānya lakṣaṇaṃ (|) paryeṣate | sarva ete kāmā jātiduḥkhatayā, jarāduḥkhatayā (yā)vadicchāvighātaduḥkhatayā samasamamanubaddhāścānuśaktāśca | ye 'pikāmopabhogino mahatyāṃ kāmasampadivarta[n]te | te 'pi jātyādidharmatayā avinirmuktāstāvatkālikī sā teṣāṃ sampat | evaṃ sāmānyalakṣaṇaṃ paryeṣate |
body.translated_text: Therein, how does one seek the general characteristic? All these sense-desires are equally and universally bound by and attached to the suffering of birth, the suffering of old age, up to the suffering of frustrated desire. Even those who enjoy sense-pleasures and live in great sensual prosperity — they too are not free from the nature of birth and so forth. That prosperity of theirs is merely temporary. Thus one seeks the general characteristic.

body.text: kathaṃ pakṣaṃ paryeṣate | kṛṣṇapakṣapatitā ete kāmāḥ | asthikaṃkālopamā, mānsapeśyupamāstṛṇolkopamāḥ | aṃgārakarṣūpamāḥ | āśīviṣopamāḥ | svapnopamāḥ | yācikālaṃkāropamāḥ | tṛṇaphalopamāśca | paryeṣamāṇā api satvāḥ (ttvāḥ) kāmān paryeṣaṇākṛtaṃ (|) duḥkhaṃ pratisaṃvedayanti | ārakṣākṛtaṃ, snehaparibhraṃśakṛtamātṛptikṛtamasvātantryakṛtaṃ, duścaritakṛtaṃ, (

children.text: ) ca duḥkhaṃ pratisaṃvedayanti | pūrvavadeva tāvatsarvaṃ veditavyaṃ |
children.translated_text: they experience suffering. All of this should be understood as stated before.

body.translated_text: How does one seek the [dark and bright] sides? These sense-desires belong to the dark side. They are like a skeleton, like a piece of meat, like a grass-torch, like a pit of burning coals, like a venomous snake, like a dream, like borrowed ornaments, like the fruit of a tree. Even when beings seek sense-desires, they experience suffering caused by the seeking; suffering caused by guarding, caused by the breakdown of affection, caused by insatiability, caused by lack of independence, caused by misconduct,

body.text: tathā kāmānpratiṣevataḥ | paṃcādīnavā uktāḥ | bhagavatā alpāsvādāḥ kāmāḥ bahusu(duḥ)khā, bahvādīnavāḥ [|] kāmānkhalu pratiṣevamāṇasya nāstyalaṃ tāva(t) tṛptitā ca paryāptitā vā, anena paryāyeṇa kāmā vigarhitā buddhaiḥ buddhaśrāvakaiśca sadbhiḥ samyaggataiḥ, satpuruṣaiḥ [|]
body.translated_text: Likewise, for one who indulges in sense-desires, five dangers have been stated by the <s>Bhagavān</s>: sense-desires have little savor, much suffering, many dangers. When one indulges in sense-desires, there is never sufficient satiation or contentment. By this method, sense-desires have been censured by the <s>Buddhas</s>, the disciples of the <s>Buddhas</s>, the good, the rightly-practiced, and the virtuous.

body.text: kāmānkhalu pratiṣevamāṇasya saṃyojanānyupacayaṃ gacchanti | nāsti cāsya kiṃcit pāpakamakuśalaṃ karmākaraṇīyaṃ vadāmi | itīme kāmā atṛptikārakā[ḥ] sādhāraṇā, adharmaviṣamacaryāhetavaḥ | kāmatṛṣṇāvivardhakāḥ, satāṃ vivarjanīyāḥ, kṣipramviṣayagāminaḥ, pratyayādhipā, pramādabhūmayo, riktā, anityāstucchā, mṛṣāmoṣadharmāṇo, māyopamāḥ, bālalāpanāḥ | ye ca dṛṣṭadhārmikāḥ (|) kāmāḥ, ye ca sāṃparāyikāḥ, ye ca divyāḥ, ye ca mānuṣyakāḥ | mā[ra]mārabhyaiṣa gocaro, mārasyaiṣa nivāpo yatreme 'nekavidhāḥ pāpakā akuśalā dharmā mānasāḥ saṃbhavanti | yadutābhidhyā, vyāpādā[ḥ], saṃrambho vā, ye vā punarāntarāyikā bhavantyāryaśrāvakasyāśikṣamāṇasyānekaparyāyeṇa kṛṣṇapakṣapatitā ete kāmā yadbhūyasā [|] evampakṣaṃ paryeṣate |
body.translated_text: When one indulges in sense-desires, the fetters (<s>saṃyojana</s>) increase. And there is no evil, unwholesome action, I declare, that would not be committed. Thus these sense-desires produce insatiability, are common [to all], are causes of unrighteous and wrongful conduct, increase the thirst for sense-pleasures, are to be avoided by the good, quickly lead to [rebirth in lower] destinations, are governed by conditions, are the ground of heedlessness, are empty, impermanent, trifling, of a deceptive and illusory nature, like a magical show, the prattle of fools. And whatever sense-desires pertain to this life, whatever to the next, whatever are divine, whatever are human — all are the domain of <s>Māra</s>, the bait of <s>Māra</s>, inasmuch as manifold evil unwholesome mental <s>dharmas</s> arise — namely, covetousness, malice, hostility, and those that create obstacles for the noble disciple who is in training. In many ways, these sense-desires belong to the dark side. Thus one seeks the [dark and bright] sides.

body.text: atītānāgatapratyutpanneṣvadhvasu anityaṃ nityakālaṃ (ma)dhruvaṃ dhruvakālame te kāmāḥ | evaṃ bahūpadravāḥ, bahūpasargā, bahvādīnavā ityevaṃ kālamparyeṣate |
body.translated_text: In the past, future, and present time-periods, these sense-desires are impermanent at all times, unstable at all times. Thus they are full of adversity, full of misfortune, full of danger. Thus one seeks the time.

body.text: kathaṃ yuktiṃ paryeṣate | mahatā saṃrambheṇa, mahatyā paryeṣṭyā, mahatā pariśrameṇa vividhairvicitraiḥ śilpakarmasthānaiḥ kāmāḥ saṃhriyante | nirvartyante, upacīyante [|] te punaḥ sūpacitā api, sunirvartitā api | yāvadeṣa bahirdhā parigrahavastunaḥ mātā(tṛ)pitṛputradāradāsīdāsakarmakarapauruṣeyamitrāmātyajñātisālohitānāṃ | asya vā punaḥ kāyasyādhyātmikasya rūpiṇa audārikasya cāturmahābhūtikasyaudanakalmāṣopacitasya nityotsadanasnapanapārimardanabhedana(c)chedana vikiraṇavidhvaṃnsa(dhvaṃsa)na dharmeṇa utpannotpannaduḥkhamātrapratīkārāya samvartante | kṣudduḥkhapratīkārāya bhojanaṃ | śītoṣṇaduḥkhapratīghātāya | hrīkopanapraticchādanāya (|) ca vastraṃ [|] nidrāklamaduḥkhapratīghātāya ca śayanāsanaṃ | caṃkramasthānaduḥkhapratighātāya ca | vyādhiduḥkhapratighātāya ca (|) glānabhaiṣajyamiti duḥkhapratīkārabhūtā ete kāmā iti | naite raktena paribhoktavyāḥ | na saktena nānyatra vyādhigrastenaivātureṇa vyādhimātropaśamāya bhaiṣajyamāptāgamo 'pyeṣaḥ | tathaite kāmāḥ evaṃ caivaṃ caudārikāḥ | pratyātmamapi me jñānadarśanaṃ (

children.text: ) pravarteta | ānumāniko 'pyeṣa vidhiḥ | prakṛtiścaiṣā kāmānāṃ anādikālikā prasiddhadharmatā acitta (-cintya?)dharmatā | sā na cintayitavyā(ḥ) | na vikalpayate (yitavye)tyevaṃ yuktimparyeṣate |
children.translated_text: also operates [accordingly]. And this method is also inferential. And this is the primordial, beginningless, well-established <s>dharmatā</s> (nature of things), the inconceivable <s>dharmatā</s> of sense-desires. It is not to be speculated about, not to be conceptualized — thus one seeks the reasoning.

body.translated_text: How does one seek the reasoning? With great effort, great seeking, great exertion, through various and diverse crafts and occupations, sense-desires are gathered, produced, and accumulated. And even when well-accumulated and well-produced, all of the external possessions — mother, father, son, wife, servants, workers, attendants, friends, ministers, relatives, and kinsmen — and this very internal, material, gross body composed of the four great elements, nourished by rice and grain, subject to the law of constant wearing away, bathing, rubbing, breaking, cutting, scattering, and destruction — serve merely as a remedy for the suffering that arises again and again. Food is the remedy for the suffering of hunger; clothing for the remedy against the suffering of cold and heat, and for covering what causes shame; bedding and seats for the remedy against the suffering of fatigue from sleepiness; and medicine for the sick as the remedy against the suffering of disease. Thus these sense-desires are merely remedies for suffering. They should not be enjoyed with attachment, not with clinging — [they should be consumed] as a sick person afflicted by disease [takes] medicine merely for the alleviation of the disease. This is also the authoritative testimony. Thus these sense-desires are coarse in these and other ways. And my own knowledge and vision

body.text: sa evaṃ kāmānāmaudārikalakṣaṇaṃ pratisaṃvejya yaduta ṣaḍbhirvastubhiḥ prathame dhyāne śāntalakṣaṇaṃ pratisaṃvedayati nāstyetatsarvaśa audārikatvaṃ (|) prathame dhyāne yadetatkāmadhātāvityanenaudārikalakṣaṇaṃ pratisaṃvedayate | prathame ca dhyāne śāntalakṣaṇamayamucyate lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī manaskāraḥ | sa khalveṣa manaskāraḥ | śruta cintāvyavakīrṇoveditavyaḥ |
body.translated_text: Thus, having experienced the coarse characteristic of sensual desires through six categories [of objects], he experiences the peaceful characteristic of the first <s>dhyāna</s> (meditation absorption): 'This coarseness does not exist at all in the first <s>dhyāna</s> as it does in the desire realm (<s>kāmadhātu</s>).' By this he experiences the coarse characteristic, and in the first <s>dhyāna</s> the peaceful characteristic. This is called the characteristic-recognizing mental attention (<s>lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī manaskāra</s>). This mental attention should be understood as mixed with hearing (<s>śruta</s>) and reflection (<s>cintā</s>).

body.text: sa evaṃ kāmānparijñāya prathamaṃ dhyānaṃ prathamaṃ dhyānaṃ yathāvatparyeṣṭau(ṣyau)dārikaśāntalakṣaṇena śrutaṃ ca cintāṃ ca vyatikrāmyaikāntena bhāvanākāreṇaivādhimucyate | tannimittālambanāmeva śamathavipaśyanāṃ bhāvayati | bhāvayaṃśca yathā yathā tāmaudārikaśāntatāṃ punaḥ punaradhimucyataḥ | ityupapadyate | [ā]dhimokṣiko manaskāraḥ |
body.translated_text: Having thus fully understood sensual desires, regarding the first <s>dhyāna</s>, having properly investigated the coarse and peaceful characteristics, transcending hearing and reflection, he becomes convinced exclusively in the mode of cultivation (<s>bhāvanā</s>). He cultivates <s>śamatha</s> (calm) and <s>vipaśyanā</s> (insight) with that very sign as the object. And as he cultivates, again and again becoming convinced of that coarseness and peacefulness — this is called the conviction-based mental attention (<s>ādhimokṣika manaskāra</s>).

body.text: ta(ya)syāsevanānvayād bhāvanānvayādbahulīkārānvayāttatprathamataḥ kleśa(ḥ)prahāṇāya mārga utpadyate | kleśaprahāṇāya ca mārge samutpanne yastadbhagavato manaskāraḥ | ayamucyate prāvivekyaḥ |
body.translated_text: Through the continuity of repeated practice, through the continuity of cultivation, through the continuity of habitual engagement, the path first arises for the abandonment of <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions). And when the path for the abandonment of <s>kleśas</s> has arisen, that mental attention of the <s>Bhagavān</s> (Blessed One) — this is called the seclusion-inclined attention (<s>prāvivekya manaskāra</s>).

body.text: sa tatprathamataḥ kāmāvacarakleśādipraheyaprahāṇāttatpakṣye (

children.text: ) dauṣṭhulyāpagamācca | tadūrdhvaṃ prahāṇārāmo bhavati | vivekārāmaḥ | tasmiṃśca prahāṇānuśaṃsadarśīparīttapravivekaprītisukhasaṃspṛṣṭaḥ kālena kālaṃ prasadanīyena manaskāreṇa | saṃpraharṣayati | saṃvejanīyena manaskāreṇa saṃvejayati | yāvadeva styānamiddhauddhatyāpagamāya (|) ayamucyate | ratisaṃgrāhako manaskāraḥ |
children.translated_text: the departure of rigidity (<s>dauṣṭhulya</s>) — beyond that, he becomes one who delights in abandonment (<s>prahāṇārāma</s>), one who delights in seclusion (<s>vivekārāma</s>). And seeing the benefit of that abandonment, touched by the limited joy and happiness of seclusion (<s>praviveka</s>), from time to time, with the inspiring mental attention (<s>prasadanīya manaskāra</s>) he gladdens [the mind]; with the urgency-producing mental attention (<s>saṃvejanīya manaskāra</s>) he creates urgency — just for the removal of sloth-torpor and restlessness. This is called the delight-gathering attention (<s>ratisaṃgrāhaka manaskāra</s>).

body.translated_text: From the initial abandonment of the afflictions of the desire realm that are to be abandoned, and from the side of

body.text: tasya tathā prahāṇārāmasya bhāvanārāmasya samyakprayuktasya sataḥ kuśalapakṣaprayogopastambhakāmapratisaṃyuktaṃ kleśakarmaparyavasthānaṃ carato vā viharato vā na samudācarati | tasyaivaṃ bhavati | kiṃ santamevāhaṃ kāmeṣu kāma(c)chandaṃ pratisamvedayāmyāhosvidasantamparimīmānsayitukāmaḥ | anyatamānyatamaṃ prasadanīyaṃ śubhanimittaṃ manasi karoti | tasyāprahīṇatvāt sarveṇa sarvamanuśayasya tannimittaṃ manasi kurvataḥ sevanānimnaṃ cittaṃ bhavati | sevanāpravaṇaṃ | sevanāprābho(bhā)raṃ nāpekṣāpattiyutena nirvijugupsā(prati) vā niḥpratikūlatā | tasyaivaṃ bhavati | na me samyagviraktaṃ vimuktaṃ cittaṃ yaduta kāmebhyaḥ, saṃskārābhinigṛhītaṃ me cittaṃ vārivad dhṛtaṃ [|] dharmatābhinigṛhītaṃ (|) ya[n]nvahaṃ bhūyasyā mātrayā tasyānuśayasyāśeṣaprahāṇāya bhūyasyā mātrayā prahāṇārāmo vihareyaṃ | bhāvanārāmaḥ | ayamucte mīmānsāmanaskāraḥ |
body.translated_text: For him, thus delighting in abandonment, delighting in cultivation, rightly applied, engaged in the practice of the wholesome side — the affliction-producing action connected with the desire for sensual pleasures arises, as a residual trace of the afflictions. At that point, those afflictions are of limited duration; they are merely the movement [of defilement].

body.text: sa bhūyasyā mātrayā prahāṇārāmo viharati | bhāvanārāmaḥ | śamathavipaśyanāyuktaḥ | paunaḥpunyena ca mīmānsate | tasya pratipakṣaṃ ca bhāvayataḥ kālena kālaṃ prahīṇāprahīṇatāṃ mīmānsamānasya sarvebhyaḥ kāmāvacarebhyaḥ kleśebhyaścittaṃ visaṃyujyate | tāvatkālikayogena (|) na tvatyantādbījasamuddhāto bhavati | tasmiṃśca samaye prayogadhyānaprayogamārgaparyavasānagataḥ | sarvakleśaprātipakṣiko manaskāraḥ | samutpanno bhavatyayamucyate prayoganiṣṭho manaskāraḥ (|)
body.translated_text: He dwells even more abundantly in delight in abandonment, delight in cultivation, engaged in <s>śamatha</s> and <s>vipaśyanā</s>. And again and again he investigates. Through his investigation, the afflictions belonging to the desire realm that are to be abandoned by cultivation become progressively subtler. And those <s>dharmas</s> opposing [the afflictions] become progressively greater. This is called the investigative mental attention (<s>mīmāṃsā manaskāra</s>).

body.text: tasya ca samanaskārapratyayaṃ taddhetukaṃ prathamaṃ dhyānaṃ samāpadyate | maulaprathamadhyānasahagato yo manaskāraḥ | ayamucyate prayoganiṣṭhāphalo manaskāraḥ |
body.translated_text: And depending on that mental attention and caused by it, the first <s>dhyāna</s> is attained. The mental attention that accompanies the fundamental first <s>dhyāna</s> — this is called the final result attention (<s>prayoganiṣṭhā manaskāra</s>).

body.text: tatra prāvivekye manaskāre vartamāno, ratisaṃgrāhake ca vivekajena prītisukhena kāyaṃ pratiprīṇayati | kadācit kenacit pratanukasaṃmukhībhāvayogena prāyoganiṣṭhāmanaskārakālasyārati[ḥ] | kadācit kadācit dhyānavipulatarasaṃmukhībhāvena prayoganiṣṭhāphale punarmanaskāre vartamānasya nāsti kiñcidasyā(sya) bhavati | smāraṇīyaṃ sarvataḥ kāyādyuta(dyaduta) vivekajena prītisukhena sa tasmiṃ(smin) samaye viviktaiḥ kāmaiḥ viviktaṃ pāpakairakuśalairdharmaiḥ savitarkasavicāraṃ vivekajaṃ prītisukhaṃ prathamaṃ dhyānaṃ paṃcā[ṅ]gamupasampadya viharati | kāmāvacarapratipakṣabhāvanāphale sthitaḥ kāmavairāgya[tā]manuprāpta (
body.translated_text: While abiding in the seclusion-inclined attention and in the delight-gathering [attention], he refreshes the body with the joy and happiness born of seclusion (<s>vivekaja prītisukha</s>). Sometimes, through some

body.text: tatra lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedinā manaskāreṇa [|] yat prahātavyaṃ tat samyak prajānāti | prahātavyasya ca prahāṇāya prāptavyasya ca prāptaye cittaṃ praṇidhatte | ādhimokṣikeṇa ca manaskāreṇa prahāṇāya prāptaye ca samyak prayogamārabhate | prāvivekyamanaskāreṇādhimātrajña śāṃ(tāṃ)jahāti | ratisaṃgrāhakeṇa sa kleśaprakāraṃ jahāti | mīmānsāmanaskāreṇa prāptinirabhimānatāyāṃ cittamavasthāpayati | prayoganiṣṭhena mṛduṃ kleśaprakāraṃ jahāti | prayoganiṣṭhāphalenaiṣāṃ kleśaprakārāṇāṃ bhāvitānāṃ subhāvitānāṃ bhāvanāphalaṃ pratyanubhavati |
body.translated_text: Therein, through the characteristic-recognizing mental attention, he rightly knows what is to be abandoned. And for the abandonment of what is to be abandoned, and for the attainment of what is to be attained,

body.text: apica yaśca lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī manaskāraḥ | yaścādhimokṣikaḥ | ayamucyate ānulomiko manaskāro 'pi dūṣaṇāpratipakṣasahagataḥ | yaśca prāvivekyo manaskāraḥ, yaśca prayoganiṣṭho 'yaṃ prātipakṣiko manaskāraḥ | prahāṇapratipakṣagavataḥ (-kṣagataḥ) [|] tatra yo ratisaṃgrāhako manaskāraḥ (|) ayaṃ prātipakṣikaśca prasadanīyaśca [|]
body.translated_text: Moreover, both the characteristic-recognizing mental attention and the conviction-based [attention] — these are called the conforming attention (<s>ānulomika manaskāra</s>), accompanied by the antidote that corrupts [defilements].

body.text: tatra yo mīmānsāmanaskāraḥ ayaṃ pratyavekṣaṇāmanaskāraḥ | ityucyate | evaṃ sati ṣaṭṣu manaskāreṣu catvāro manaskārāḥ pravighnā veditavyāḥ | tadyathā ānulomikaḥ | prātipakṣikaḥ | prasadanīyaḥ | pratyavekṣaṇīyaśceti |
body.translated_text: The investigative mental attention is called the reviewing attention (<s>pratyavekṣaṇā manaskāra</s>). This being so, among the six [types of] attention, four [types of] attention are operative.

body.text: yathā prathamadhyānasamāpattiḥ saptabhirmanaskārairevaṃ dvitīyatṛtīyacaturthadhyānasamāpattiḥ | ākāśavijñānākiṃcanyāyatananaivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatanasamāpattiḥ saptabhireva (

children.text: ) manaskāraiḥ | tatra yena vitarkeṣvaudārikalakṣaṇaṃ pratisamvedayate | avitarkaśca dvitīyadhyāne śāntalakṣaṇaṃ sa lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī manaskāraḥ | dvitīyadhyānasamāpattaye [|] tatra dhyānasamāpannaḥ | prathamadhyānalābhī vitarkeṣvaudārikatāmpaśyati | yaḥ samāhitabhūmiko 'pyugrālambanabhārī tatprathamopanipātitayā cālambane audāriko manojalpaḥ | ayambitarkastadanubandhānucārī vyagracāryevālambane sūkṣmataro manojalpaḥ vihāraḥ | ete punarvitarkavihā(cā)rāścai tasikāścetasyutpadyamānā utpadyante | sahabhuvaḥ saṃprayuktā[ḥ] | ekālambanavṛttayaḥ | evamete adhyātmamutpadyante |
children.translated_text: [Each is accomplished] through [types of] mental attention.
